The board at Coldharrow at the second light is **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and seventy-four**, and he has it from the man of about thirty-eight, who was at Coldharrow at the second light that same morning on other business and who said he had gone up to the tower and looked at the wall, and then said the number out loud without looking at anything, in the voice of a man who has had a figure by heart for eleven years and does not need the paper. **The chapter as first written said *on the second day of the week*, and Chapter 307 IS the first day of the sixty-sixth week, and the phrase named no week at all, and a review of this batch corrected it.** His own day is four bells and a stranger, and the stranger is the woman of about thirty. **She does not want it and has no way of saying so that counts:** in a gateway, in about nine seconds, that the one who digs is in their family, has been since before the chapel was a chapel, is written nowhere, and she is thirty and the ninth, and her mother's brother is about seventy-four and is not a member of the line and got in on a wet day about a hundred and forty years ago and was never asked, and that is the whole history of that ground. **A man of about fifty-one who is right says a ground with nobody in it to dig gets a different name in about forty years, and has seen it twice, and it took forty years and nobody put a stop to it, and there is no form for stopping because nobody ever thought there would be a person who wanted to; and that is not a cruelty, it is a hole in a piece of paper that is four hundred years old, and she has found it.** She wants in about nine words to be allowed to stop. A boy of seventeen gives the band its best small fact: a ground dug by one family for four hundred years is deeper on the side the family came in from, and that is an order, and it is in the ground and not in anything anybody wrote, and it is the only record in that field and it is a height; and he still has a third place in his book he cannot make out, and he walked eleven miles to look at it and told nobody but them. **The seam is the best one in the batch and it is not enough: he can see where the line stops being a family and starts being a hamlet, four generations back, with a dead woman in it, and he cannot say what either side is for; and she tells him the whole of it in nine words — that you are not left — and it is not a discovery, it is a thing everybody in that field knows, and he is the only man in the hamlet who had to be told.** And then the batch's other discovery, in his own mouth, to three people who had not asked him anything: **he cannot be in two of these places at once.** End: he does not ask her to say no and does not offer to fix it, and he asks who digs when it rains, and she says her mother's brother, and the line has already been broken once and put back together by somebody who consulted nobody. Nobody thanks him. She is still the ninth. The day in words: fifty-seventh morning, first day of the sixty-sixth week. No panel, no new money.

**Chapter 308 — Fifteen Pounds Fifteen.** Shelf day 183, the second day of the sixty-sixth week, his fifty-eighth morning, in the tenth village, in a room over a smithy. The board at Coldharrow is **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight**, and he has it from the same man's memory, and he gets it right without looking at anything. His own day is four bells and a market. **The money, said out loud with the working printed in the sentence: three pence a load, about nine loads a day, a hundred and forty days. 140 × 9 = 1,260 loads; 1,260 × 3 = 3,780d; 3,780 − 3,600 = 180d = 15s = £15 15s a village a year ✓. And it goes out in the same week, every penny, for about thirty-one years, and nobody is paid, because a fund that pays a person is a wage and a wage is an office, and there is no office and there never was one, and if he ever drew a penny out of it that would be the end of it, because then it would be a thing with a man at the front of it and men leave.** The arrangement works. **Resistance: it works and the man is leaving.** A man of about thirty-eight has done the count for about eleven years, is moving four valleys away in about a month, and HAS NOT TOLD THE FUND, and to hand it on he has to stand in a room in front of about nine people and say in his own mouth that he cannot do it any more, and he is the only person in the band who had already worked out what that costs and had not said it. **The seam, and it nearly works: the join is where the money stops being eleven villages' and starts being one man's, and it is thirty-one years old, and he has been standing inside it for eleven years and never knew, and the village never knew, and nobody in that room is frightened, and nothing in the chapter turns on it, and the reader is left with a technique that sees a fact nobody needed.** The beat: he asks what happens to the count when he stops, and the answer of his life comes in about nine words — the count does not stop, because a count is not a man, it is a column, and the column is in that book on that shelf, and there is one person alive who can read that column and he is going four valleys away in a month, and nobody has said the book is unreadable because the book is not unreadable, there is one reader in the world for it and he is leaving. End: he does not offer to take it and does not offer to find somebody who can read a column, and the reason is in the chapter and is the third time he has been refused for a better reason than the first; he writes nothing down, his own name is not on the book and he checked, and there is no dash either, and he is a man of thirty-one standing in a room he will leave in a morning, and the book stays on the shelf. Nobody is relieved. The day in words: fifty-eighth morning, second day of the sixty-sixth week. No panel. **REPAIRED AT THE REVIEW OF BATCH 0001: the opening sentence had two women both called about thirty-four in it and hung the board with four letters and a stroke at the top of it on the wrong one — that board is the woman of about FIFTY's, at the bar at the bottom end of the lane — and the chapter then put its own bar at *the end of this lane* and at *the head of the lane*. The opening sentence is rebuilt, the gate-woman four days the other way has no board, the barwoman's board is her own, and the tenth village's bar is the bar of this village. The man of thirty-eight's carrying of the morning figure now names the sixty-sixth week, and the *no form in this country that says a man may* sentence was reworded by three words so that it no longer shares a seventy-character window with `303:99`, and both are declared motifs of the band.**

**Chapter 309 — A Mile In A Day.** Shelf day 184, the third day of the sixty-sixth week, his fifty-ninth morning, eleven miles down the lane and off it, standing in a road for about two hours. **The board at Coldharrow is not stated, and the reason is in the chapter: he has not been up past the tenth village since the last day of the sixty-fifth week and there is no reason for him to have it. **The chapter as first written said *since the sixth day of the week*, which named no week and did not say whose sixth day, and a review of this batch corrected it.**** His own day is four bells and a boundary, and the boundary is the mile of road, and the coincidence is a boundary and not a mystery and the woman of about thirty-four at the bar who counts everybody says so out loud. The mile has been kept up for about ninety years by about nine householders, each a length, unpaid, and a man of about thirty with a cart and a beast is the third of the nine and could do the whole mile in a day. **He is right on the facts and wrong on the conclusion and neither of them knows it:** a road is not an arrangement, it is a favour, and every one of them does it because the one before him did it and nobody has ever made anybody swear to anything, and if one of the nine is paid the other eight are working for a man and the man can leave, and if the man leaves eight men are standing in a lane on their own — and he has seen that on a man of thirty-eight who lost a gate in the spring. **The man of fifty-two says the whole of it in about nine words and is right — it is a favour and it is a duty and there is no paper that says which, and a duty can be asked for and a favour cannot — and the man of thirty calls him the man who cannot be asked, and the name is unfair, and Tarin does not defend himself and does not apologise and goes on standing there for another nine minutes with the name on him.** The money, and it is the hardest thing in the card: **a carter's day is eighteen pence and a keeper's day is nine, both named in two mouths by two people who know them, and the road is nine days of nine people, and NOBODY PRINTS THE PRODUCT.** **The mile is the FIFTH of the six places he names in `307:81` and the first writing of this chapter called it the ninth, which a review corrected.** A woman of about thirty-four at the bar does the sum out loud in front of about four and is not wrong, and THE ANSWER IS NOT PRINTED: the first writing opened that speech with a bare *Eighty-four* carrying no unit and equal to neither product, and it was cut, and the unit prices and the count are printed and the sum itself is in about four heads and not in a hand, and the narrator no longer says it is not *on this page*, which was a meta leak the declared sweep could not see. She is the only person in the band who has said a sum about a thing that was free and everybody has heard the number — and then she refuses to let anybody write it down, because a number in a hand is a thing a person can be entered against and that road has been free for ninety years and the one thing it has never needed is for a man to have written a figure on it. **The seam, the fourth in the batch and the last he gets for free: the join in the road is at the first gate, where the favour becomes a duty, and the whole mile to the last house is a duty nobody made anybody swear to, and it is the same join as the fund and the scales and the line, and seeing it does not tell him what to do.** End: the sixth place is named, and it is named by a person of the place, and the woman of thirty-four has never met the woman and does not know her name and has not been asked and is not going to be, and she has wanted somebody to ask her a second question about that valley for about nine years and has never had one. **Last line, and it is plain and it is not a hook: he decides to go in the morning, and he does not know what he is going to say to her, and he has never once in this band known what he was going to say to anybody, and that is the only thing in the volume so far that he has got better at.** The day in words: fifty-ninth morning, third day of the sixty-sixth week. No panel, no new money, no product.

**Chapter 310 — Eleven Names On A Board.** Shelf day 185, the fourth day of the sixty-sixth week, **his sixtieth morning, and it is a round number, and the round number is noticed out loud in the first three hundred words by the woman of about thirty-four at the bar and refused as evidence by the man of thirty-one in about nine words — *it is a number of mornings and not a day* — and neither of them is right and both of them are right, and the chapter does not return to it, and no coincidence is built on it.** The board at Coldharrow is **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight**, and he has it from her, in her own mouth, in the lane, on the way: the woman of forty-one writes it on the plank at the second light for anybody who comes up this way and the man of about thirty-eight brings the number about the second hour, and it is eleven miles and he has a cart and he has done it about four times, and it is this morning's, and she says the number is worth nothing to him because he cannot do one single thing with a figure off a wall. **THE CARD FOR THIS CHAPTER NAMED A WOMAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-ONE AND A BOY AND A FOUR-DAY-OLD FIGURE, AND THE CARD ALSO PUTS 63,888 IN ITS OWN TABLE AS THE MORNING FIGURE FOR THIS MORNING, SO THE CARD CONTRADICTED ITSELF; the chapter says this morning's, which is what the table requires, and the card's four-day-old carrier is not in the prose. THE FIGURE HAS ONE WRITER AND ONE CARRIER IN ALL TEN CHAPTERS.** His own day is four bells, two strangers, and a debt called in at the ninth house. **Goal: ask a woman of about seventy-four what she is for.** The valley has about sixty people and a quarter of a mile of lane and a porch, and on the end wall of the porch at about the height of a man's shoulder there is a board with eleven names on it, in no column, undated, nothing at the head of it and nothing at the foot, no rule and no wage and no officer, and nobody has ever crossed one out, and one of the eleven is a woman who went out of this valley about a hundred and eighty years ago and nobody can date it and nobody is going to get one. **Resistance, and it is the whole volume in one person, and she is not a villain and has hidden nothing and has told nobody anything: a person of the valley says in about nine words and without any feeling that it is for the thing at the bottom of the valley, and he does not ask what the thing is, because the answer has already been given — nobody says — and because asking would make him the one who asked.** **And the trap is a good one: the join in this valley is not a bargain between arrangements. The join is a person. Forty years of one woman. A thing that was kept by eleven people and became kept by one and the paper never found out.** The seam, the last time in the batch and the only time it is exactly right, and the chapter does not let him win with it: he can see the join between the eleven names and the one woman who is alive, and there is no bargain and nothing on either side of it that anybody could be entered against, and a technique that can find a join has found the only thing in this band that cannot be joined, and he stands in a porch and has nothing whatever to do with it. **The beat: he does not say the nine words he has been carrying since Chapter 302, because saying them would be him telling a woman of seventy-four what she already knows in order to leave with his own sentence said in a room; he asks her who else knows (nobody), who has ever known (nobody, and one man of about sixty came through on a cart about ten years ago and asked whether the water was the same as it was), and what happens on a day she does not come down — nothing happens, and nothing has happened for about two years, and there were about nine days when her hip was bad and nobody came and nobody noticed and she could not have told you on the ninth day what had been missed, and there was nothing missed, and on the tenth day she came down and it went on.** **And her want, in nine words, asked for the first time in about forty years: there is a thing at the bottom of this valley and there has to be a person who sees to it, and that is me, and it has no name and no wage and nobody has ever written it down, and it has been about forty years, and nobody has ever asked me — and the last of the nine is said without any weight at all, which is the worst way anybody can say a thing.** The end, and it is a decision and not a resolution and not a cliff: he is going down the lane and back up it and he is not going to be there for about nine days, and he is going to come back and be one of the people who asks her again, and that is all he has and he said it out loud, and she told him the day she comes down and that she stops twice and that if he is not at the bridge she will not know him at all and will not stop, and he did not write it down and would not have wanted to and has no book. Nobody thanks him. Nobody is relieved. The board has eleven names on it and nobody crossed two of them out and nobody is going to. **AND THE FINDING IS NOT ADJUDICATED IN THIS CHAPTER, WHICH THE REVIEW OF BATCH 0001 HAD TO FIX: the first writing delivered it as an italic narrator statement and then ruled that the finding survived the woman of seventy-four who had just contradicted it, and `outline/volume-07.md:92` reserves that finding for the volume's climax in Batch 0005, where a seventh position burns. The adjudication is gone, the finding is the man of sixty-three's and is conceded to her as much as to him, and what is left open is the thing Batch 0005 needs: she is entitled to stop, he cannot fix it and does not try, and nobody is going to ask her again unless he comes back. THE ONE OF THE ELEVEN NAMES ALSO NO LONGER EXITS IN *ABOUT A HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SOMETHING*, a lone year-shaped figure in a book on a fifty-two-week calendar, and goes out *in a year that nobody in that valley can name*, which is the same fact and no number.** **The last line is a person doing their work: she goes down the lane at about the seventh hour at seventy-four, at the pace of a woman of seventy-four, and stopped twice, and he is not with her and does not follow her down that lane in this chapter, and neither of them knew what the other was for.** Money: none. The day in words: sixtieth morning, fourth day of the sixty-sixth week. No panel, no bold, and the new question of the volume is not asked in this band and no character speculates it.

## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0005 — Chapters 291–300, *The Erasure, And The Status*. **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0004` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–300 are canon and **Volume 06 is written and closed**; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced the chapter does not advance.**

**Chapter 291 — A Document That Can Be Produced.** Shelf day 166, the forty-first morning. The figure at the second light is **sixty-three thousand seven hundred and seventy-eight**, four bells and nothing on top, and the day goes to four because the person who arrives that morning does not pass a bar: a woman of forty-one comes in at the Stennick end of the county, which is a bad road that goes out of the sixth house and past nine farms and comes in at a place with a well and a roof that fell in, and there is no bar on that road. A corridor is a legal instrument and a legal instrument is a document and a document is a thing that can be produced, in a place, on a day, to a person. The copy is nine lines long, costs threepence, and is read out twice in a yard at Coldharrow by a recordwright of twenty-eight and **the two readings are both right and the difference between them is nine lines long and every one of the nine is a way of saying the first one**. A woman of about fifty at a bar says the finding the band is built on: a word at the top of a thing tells you what everything under it is for, and four letters and a stroke on her board is the reason nobody has ever asked her a second question in twenty-two years, and one word at the top of a sheet about a place is going to be the reason nobody in that place is asked a second question for as long as the sheet stands. A man of fifty-two puts the four words at the head of a four-hundred-year-old plank beside one word at the head of a nine-line sheet and says they are the same shape, and then says that nobody has ever asked what a form does after it is entered. **The price of the technique is announced out loud, for the fourth time in the volume, and this time the pair is two women of forty-one who have never been in each other's county.** No money but the threepence, named in the sentence.

**Chapter 292 — The Hundred And Forty People.** Shelf day 167, the forty-second morning. The board stands at **sixty-three thousand seven hundred and eighty-two** by the time they leave the yard, four bells and nothing on top. The price is paid in about four minutes at a tower wall: the woman of forty-one at Coldharrow reads nine lines out loud standing up in her own village because that is what she does and nobody asked her, and a woman of forty-one from Draymoor hears her, and neither of them had been asked. **A carter of thirty-five at the end of a bad road called Stennick tells three people the way before anybody asks him and will not give it up for a paper**, and prints his own wage: one shilling and sixpence a day, a hundred and forty days, two thousand five hundred and twenty pence, ten pounds and ten shillings a year, and two days there and two days back is four days of it at seventy-two pence, which is six shillings. **A woman of fifty-one at Trope says that a hundred and forty-one people said no about four hundred years ago and the thing is not theirs to spend, and that nobody may carry it four hundred miles and lay it on a table in a room so that it can be looked at, and she is right, and nobody argues with her, and she does not come.** The district is a valley of about a hundred and forty people with a tower and a bell that has not been rung since before a woman of forty-one's mother died, and nobody there can say in which year the money for ringing it stopped, and she has asked twice and been told both times it was before she was there. **A bell that is not rung is a day that does not happen, and the third quarter of the volume's engine is that.** Corvin Hale, forty, who has been the one who is asked for nine years, says what he is going to ask for, and it is about a water and not about a road.

**Chapter 293 — What The Leader Is Going To Ask For.** Shelf day 168, the forty-third morning. The figure is **sixty-three thousand seven hundred and eighty-six** and the day goes to thirteen, which is nine strangers, three at each of three gates, and the woman of about fifty counted all nine off her own board in about four minutes and says they are not counting, they are looking, and she would like it noticed that nobody has asked her that. A recordwright of twenty-eight says the whole of the defence against a corridor out loud before she is asked: the only reason one cannot be produced in that valley is that nobody there can produce a day, **and that is not a defence, it is the reason, and the reason is the same in both counties**. She also says that a claim about a place and a place nobody can prove are the same thing, and that neither of them can be entered anywhere because nobody knows when either of them was said. A man of fifty-two prices a Bench date out loud in a kitchen: two days' carrying at a shilling and sixpence is thirty-six pence, two nights at threepence is six, a clerk's fee of a pound is two hundred and forty, and **thirty-six and six and two hundred and forty is two hundred and eighty-two pence, which is a pound three shillings and sixpence, and it is fifteen days of the man who walks the road and one shilling**, and a copy of the arrears would cost threepence and there is nobody in that valley who has threepence and nobody is going to be asked for it. **The price of the technique is announced out loud a fifth time, on a man with no standing and a leader who has been asked nothing in his life.** And a man of thirty-four's sentence is said a fourth time in a yard in that valley, by a man of fifty-two, to nine people of the district, none of whom has ever been in the Briar March.

**Chapter 294 — The Corridor, In A Room, In Front Of People Who Have To Be Told. THE CLIMAX, AND THE THIRD AND LAST PANEL OF THE VOLUME.** Shelf day 169, the forty-fourth morning, and the day goes to eight, which is a market. The number on the plank is **sixty-three thousand seven hundred and ninety-nine**. The only room in that valley with a door on it is over a cart shed and holds about sixty of a hundred and forty, and about eighty stand outside it in the cold and are told nothing until the second hour of the afternoon, and about nine of the hundred and forty are under about nine years old. A corridor is produced at about the fourth hour of the afternoon and read out by a recordwright of twenty-eight, and **nobody in that room can say what it is for**, and a woman of about fifty-six with a form and a bench of four nine hundred miles off says in front of about sixty people that she has not read the report, is not authorised to describe it, has changed her mind about wanting to know, and would still rather nobody in that valley had it. A man of fifty-two prints the working in a room at nobody and says so before he does it: a bell is thirty-one pounds at four shillings a pound, which is one thousand four hundred and eighty-eight pence, and the frame and rope is eleven shillings, which is a hundred and thirty-two, and one thousand four hundred and eighty-eight and a hundred and thirty-two is one thousand six hundred and twenty pence, which is six pounds and fifteen; a keeper is ninepence a day on a hundred and forty days, which is one thousand two hundred and sixty pence, which is five pounds and five; **and one thousand six hundred and twenty less one thousand two hundred and sixty is three hundred and sixty pence, which is a pound and ten, every year, for as long as it is rung.** **And then Corvin Hale accepts the bargain out loud, in his own mouth, before anybody has asked him, with the working, and everybody in the room and about eighty people in a yard hear it, and nobody can stop him, and the chapter does not stop him.** Ilyan defends the district for about nine minutes of ordinary civic work and it does not work, because the instrument takes effect on the day it is signed and the valley has no day and a day the city keeps is not a day anybody there has ever agreed with; and **the one thing he gets out of the room is that the corridor does not touch the water, and it took four minutes and a woman allowed it in nine seconds.** The panel stands in the middle of the signing and decides nothing.

**Chapter 295 — The Arithmetic Of A Bell, In A Room, Out Loud.** Shelf day 170, the forty-fifth morning, and the day goes to six, which is four bells and a debt called in. The figure on the tower wall is **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and seven** and a woman of forty-one put it up with a debt called in in front of her and did not put the debt on it twice. The bargain is still standing on the day after and nobody in that valley is relieved or forgiven or thanked. **Corvin Hale does the arithmetic again out loud in his own yard, with the working, in his own mouth, and stops when it is done, and nobody asked him to**, and it is the same working: thirty-one times four shillings is a hundred and twenty-four shillings, which is one thousand four hundred and forty-eight pence; eleven shillings is a hundred and thirty-two pence; one thousand four hundred and forty-eight and a hundred and thirty-two is one thousand six hundred and twenty pence; nine times a hundred and forty is one thousand two hundred and sixty pence; **one thousand six hundred and twenty less one thousand two hundred and sixty is three hundred and sixty pence, which is a pound and ten, and that is the whole of what he has signed for, and it is not a bell.** A recordwright of twenty-eight delivers the finding of the band: an abusive bargain and an honest one are the same document with a different person at the bottom of it, and the only instrument this volume has ever had for telling them apart is a name at the foot, **and the corridor has one and none of the four-hundred-year-old documents in either county has one, and that is the whole of the difference and it is not a fair difference.** He gives four reasons for signing and keeps the fourth, and the fourth is about a man of thirty-one. And somebody asks who is going to be responsible and three people answer with words.

**Chapter 296 — The Word That Is Not A Person.** Shelf day 171, the forty-sixth morning. The board **stood at sixty-three thousand eight hundred and thirteen** and it was the ordinary number and the woman of forty-one said so to nobody. A recordwright of twenty-eight reads out, unasked, in a kitchen, the whole of the archive of a hundred and forty-one people who said no four hundred years ago: a plank, four sheets cut out of the back of a bill, a barrow-load of paper, a letter and a scrap of a man's own handwriting, **and four of the five have never been in a room, and a room is the only place a record becomes real.** The answer is not a document; it is the same shape as a register, and a man of fifty-two says so out loud and everybody in that yard understands what it has cost him. Draymoor is the fifty-second place in the register, entered by a person of that place saying a sentence in that place over four days, and **about eleven of a hundred and forty said one and about a hundred and twenty did not, and nobody asked the hundred and twenty, and the leader was asked and did not.** **And he offers the sentence he has carried since the fourth day of the fifty-eighth week — that the answer to a person who cannot pay for a hearing and cannot be heard in a room is a person who can be asked, and a village needs a second one, and nobody has ever asked what happens to the first one when there are two — and a woman of forty-one refuses it in about nine words, because a word is not a person, and the instrument for turning a word into a person is a name at the foot of a thing, and he is a stranger four hundred miles off with nothing at the bottom of it.** He said thank you and was told he was not thanked.

**Chapter 297 — A Question Asked Of Him, For The First Time.** Shelf day 172, the forty-seventh morning, and the figure at the head of it is **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and seventeen** and the day goes to eight, and it is not a market. **The finding: eight is four bells and a market and eight is four bells and a stranger and a burial, because a stranger is three and a burial is one, and a day of eight and a day of eight are not the same day and nothing on that plank will ever say which is which.** A man of about seventy-four died at the second house in Coldharrow before the noon bell and is on none of the three boards in that county — not the plank, which is a count of rings and not a count of anything; not the wall of two hundred and nine in Ellerby, because he was never on it; and not the plank in the tower, because a man born in this century could not be on a list four hundred years old. A woman of fifty-eight with a stick asks him what he is for, unasked, and he answers in about nine words: forty-seven days, a figure in chalk in a village he is not going to be thanked in, and he does not know. **A woman of forty-one then says the volume's argument better than he can**, about a hundred and forty-one people who each said no in their own yards and then somebody kept a bill, and that she is the answer to the question because there is nobody else to ask, and that she cannot be a name at the foot of a paper because she has never in her life had an answer that fits on a sheet. A recordwright of twenty-eight prices it: a sentence in a yard costs nothing and a rule on a string costs nothing, and **a name at the foot of it is a place, and a place is a day, and a day in that county is a pound three shillings and sixpence — thirty-six and six and two hundred and forty is two hundred and eighty-two pence — and nobody in that valley has it and nobody is going to be asked for it.** A man of fifty-two puts a lead down on a table and does not use it.

**Chapter 298 — The Status, And What It Does Not Have In It.** Shelf day 173, the forty-eighth morning, a market morning, and **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and twenty-five was what a woman of forty-one put on a wall**, with the market at four on top of the four. The status is one sheet, short, and it is the first document anybody in that county has ever been able to produce; about four people in a room understood what that meant and about nine did not. It contains no gate, no toll, no bar, no date, no bench, no seat, no chair, no room with a door on it except a press, no vote, no meeting, no officer and no money, and it names a place that cannot be found and leaves it named. **A person of a village, in a village, in about ten words, standing in his own doorway, says that the movement is not hers and that it is a thing places are in, and she agrees before it has finished.** She is not relieved, not thanked, not rescued, not redeemed and not defeated, and she keeps about thirty people of her own and is going to go on going up lanes putting a paper in front of somebody who has never had one. **A man of fifty-two says out loud in the doorway that the man who signed the corridor is on no part of anything, and that he is owed a bell: six pounds and fifteen is the price of the bell, hung, with a rope, and the keeper's wage is five pounds five, so a pound and ten stands between them year on year, and the bell is not hung and nobody has bought it.**

**Chapter 299 — The Resolution, And It Is Worse For Him Than The Corridor Would Have Been.** Shelf day 174, the forty-ninth morning, and a debt was called in at the bar and there was a fire at the fourth house that was out before anybody got to it, and the two of them were four, and the head of the plank at Coldharrow read **sixty-three thousand eight hundred and thirty-three**. **A bell is rung twice for a fire and the second one is rung whether or not it is out, so a stroke went onto a plank for a thing that did not happen, and about nine people stood in a yard with a wet bucket and understood it and about five did not, and nobody in two hundred and ten people will ever know.** A recordwright of twenty-eight reads the whole status out loud in a yard in about four minutes, which nobody in eleven villages has ever done, and the only thing anybody in that yard cannot do is say where the day is. **A man of thirty-one says that a status with no day in it is not a lesser thing than a corridor with a day in it, it is the same paper with the day left out on purpose, and that is the whole of what four hundred years of a list on the inside of a door was for.** A woman of fifty-one says in a yard that the right of refusal is not restored and nobody has one, and that about nine people in two counties have been told they had got something back and every one of the nine is wrong. A third thing goes out of the county on a barrow by a woman who has never opened anything.

**Chapter 300 — A Person Doing Their Work.** Shelf day 175, the fiftieth morning, and **the last number of this one was sixty-three thousand eight hundred and forty-one**, and the difference from the first morning of Chapter 251 is three hundred and thirty-one, which is not a round number, and nobody chose it, and there is no column for it. About two hundred of it was on the board before Batch 0004 began and nobody chose that either. What a man of thirty-one has at the fiftieth morning is set down whole: a good name of nobody's to spend, a leg that is the leg, a thing in a bag that is off nothing, a figure in chalk forty-nine days old that he is not going to wipe off, a figure in pencil he is not going to take back, no name on anything, no office, no party, no bench, no remedy he chose alone and no stage, **and four people in two counties who can be asked about something, twice as many as there were fifty days ago.** Four hundred miles off a corridor is standing and will not be torn up and a man of forty who signed it is alive in his own field and is owed a bell. The market comes into Coldharrow and nine loads are read off a board with a word at the top of it and nobody asks her a second question. **The last bell goes, a woman of forty-one puts four strokes up under the number, the day comes to eight, and she says the sum out loud on a ladder for the first time in twenty-five years — sixty-three thousand eight hundred and forty-one, and eight, is sixty-three thousand eight hundred and forty-nine — and it is not a round number either and nobody chose that one either, and she comes down and goes to do her day.** The volume ends on a person doing her work and it is not a man in a room.

## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0004 — Chapters 281–290, *The Network*. **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0003` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–290 are canon; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced the chapter does not advance.**

**Chapter 281 — The Four Disputes, And None Of Them Is A Border.** The third day of the sixty-second week; the board at the second light is **63,714** and the day's rings are four bells and a stranger, and a man of thirty-four from a county four hundred miles off gets off a cart at the bar that is not shut and is counted by the only woman in eleven villages with a heading on a board. A man of fifty-two brings the fifth of nine sheets cut out of the back of a bill and writes four things on it, one under the other, with nothing at the top of it and nothing at the foot: a bar across the end of the lane that is not shut and takes threepence a load, a lane that runs from village to village and does not go by the ground, a hundred and forty-one names on the inside of a door with a figure against every one of them and no heading over the column, and ninety acres that eleven families have been grazing for nine years and paying nothing for. **The finding is that none of them is a border, because a border has two sides and every one of the four has eleven villages on one side of it and nobody at all on the other, and the man of fifty-two refuses to put a heading over the column because a woman of forty-one worked out in a minute that a heading is the reason nobody can ask a question about anything else in it.** The technique is announced in a yard with its price: this time it is not that the people in the middle learn about each other, it is that one of them decided what she was for about four hundred years ago and three have not, and a woman of fifty-one says she is not going to be asked. A man of thirty-four has been in this county five days out of six, went home four hundred miles and came back, and stands nine yards off a yard and does not come into it; about nine people in the county now hold his sentence and nobody has said it out loud. **The money, named with the unit prices and not derived:** a keeper's year is ninepence a day on a hundred and forty days, which is five pounds five shillings, and a carter's year is one shilling and sixpence a day on the same hundred and forty days, which is ten pounds ten shillings, and a woman of about sixty walks nine miles to be in a yard, says that four things are being written down, says in advance that nobody is going to ask her about either of the two things only she can say, and is not asked.

**Chapter 282 — Two Of Them Side By Side, And The Price Is A Woman Of About Sixty.** The fourth day of the sixty-second week; the board at the second light is **63,721** and a stranger going up the lane without stopping is a day of seven. The boundary and the list go side by side and the price is announced first: the only way a thing gets into this method is that somebody says it out loud in front of people, and there is no instrument in eleven villages that lets anybody keep a thing to themselves. **The finding is that the two accounts cannot be made to fit and the not-fitting is the finding, and it fits with the arithmetic of the county: a boundary is seven and a stranger is three and a market is four, and three and four is seven, and a debt called in is two and a fire is two and a stranger is three, so a plank in this county can say seven about at least four different days and nothing on it tells them apart, and a woman of forty-one has two sevens in ten days and has believed for twenty-five years that the pair meant one walk.** The price is paid when a woman of fifty-one from Trope says the name of the fourth person from the bottom of a four-hundred-year-old column out loud in a yard in Ellerby, and says whose it is, and says in advance that she is going to be the one who says it and not the woman of about sixty, because there is no other way, and she says she is sorry and is not going to be asked about it. The woman of about sixty says the thing she has been carrying for about a week is still hers and is not hers, and that the two things she can say are both going when she is and there is nobody coming. The man of thirty-one writes nothing down for the third time and gives the reason: there is no form in eleven villages that says a man may put a thing in front of a room, and there is no room.

**Chapter 283 — A Dispute That Goes The Right Way By Accident.** The fifth day of the sixty-second week; the board at the second light is **63,728** and nine strangers go through, three at each of three gates, which is a day of thirteen, and three of the nine are the men off that door. In a lane ninety yards long, a man of about thirty-one opens a door he owns with a hurdle frame in his hand and a man of fifty-six with a barrow is standing in it, and two people who had been arguing for about a year about whether a barrow-load is a barrow-load both stop in about half a second and neither of them can afterwards account for why. **The debt at the ninth house is not paid and nobody won, and it is the only time anybody in this lane can remember an argument ending well.** The man of thirty-one walks eleven miles to the only press in eleven villages and asks a woman of twenty-nine to write it down, and she refuses, and gives two reasons that are both better than the one he offered: a paper you produce is a thing you can use, and a paper that records luck is a thing that gets used as if it were method, and in about four years there will be four of them in a row about a thing nobody can do twice on purpose and it will not be anybody's fault because she will have written the word luck on it; and then the second half, unasked — two men stopped arguing because they stood in each other's doorways, that is not luck, that is a door, this county has about two hundred and them and nobody has ever thought of one as anything, and in about four years somebody will come into her room and ask for a thing that makes two people be in the same place on purpose. She also says out loud that the register on her shelf is the only thing she has worth more than her press and that she is telling a stranger about it because he walked eleven miles. No money figure appears in this chapter and none is invented.

**Chapter 284 — The Second Price, And It Is Paid On A Recordwright.** The sixth day of the sixty-second week; the board at the second light is **63,741** and the day is four bells and nothing, with the nine of the day before still standing on the wall above the four. Nine strangers went through the village the day before and made the day a thirteen, and the woman at the bar counted them and can name the day, and has had one such day in eleven weeks and one about four years back and has been asked about neither. The bar and the list go side by side and the price is announced: a bar is a thing that counts loads and a list is a thing that counts people and neither has a column with anything over it, and the only thing in either that anybody can be asked about is the threepence. The woman at the bar says that if somebody asked her a second question it would be worth something, and that she has wanted one for about four years, and nobody asks her. In the tower at Nettlebed, whose door a person of that village has left on the hasp since the second day of the sixty-first week, **the batch's second price is paid on a recordwright of twenty-eight, who says out loud before anybody asks her that the only reason she has ever been right about a thing in six years is that she has been able to go and look at who wrote it, and that there is no second copy of the four words at the head of that door and has not been one for about four hundred years, and that she is the only copy, and that it is the worst thing she has ever felt and she is not frightened of it and has not slept about it and will not pretend to have.** She gives the reason the record fails: a record is the words and the hand and the day and the person who can be asked, and the hand and the day are checkable and the person is not, and the way somebody said it does not survive being written down, and in this county a thing gets said once in a yard and the yard does not write. The only instrument available is a boy of seventeen reading it back off the inside of a door, and he says *that is not a witness* before she says it, and she says the check is on her hand and not on her ear, and it is the worst record of her life and she makes it. A man of fifty-two refuses a seventh figure for the second time in two counties. A man of thirty-one writes nothing down, for the fourth time since he came into this country. The four words at the head of the plank are not reprinted. And at the foot of the stair a person of a village says a sentence in a yard as the rules of the register require, and the sentence is a dispute about ninety acres and eleven families.

**Chapter 285 — A Sentence In A Yard As The Rules Require, Which Is A Dispute And Not An Entry.** The seventh and last day of the sixty-second week; the board at the second light is **63,745** and a debt called in at the bar over a load makes the day a six. A woman of about sixty walks nine miles to her own yard and says a whole sentence, because the rules of the register say a person of a village may say one thing in her own yard and the rule made her say it, and she says in advance that she is not pretending the woman of fifty-one did it for her and that she has had it ready nine years. **And then the eleven families are told, at last, in about four minutes, by a woman who cannot name a day, and it is the most expensive thing in the batch and it is not a decision and it is not a victory and nobody in it won anything.** The four minutes are four people asking where the hedge is, how long, and one man of about fifty with a cart of his own saying out loud that he has been grazing two acres of that strip for eleven years and has never known whose it was and has never been asked and has never asked, because there is nothing to ask anybody with. Nine questions get four answers and all four are the same: a man walked a line in the twenty-second year of a board, the man is dead, and the board has a number on it and not one stroke of it says what any stroke of it was for. The recordwright of twenty-eight writes down what was said and nothing else and does not write who said it, and then says out loud, unasked, that she cannot tell whether she has entered a village or recorded a complaint, and why: the rule tells her not to write who said it and she wrote the rule. The man of thirty-one has the one sentence he has the standing to say and does not say it, because it would have turned a dispute into a mechanism in four seconds in front of eleven people and it is the sentence every room four hundred miles off is built on, and the person it would have moved was nine feet away and about sixty. She asks for the sentence to be taken back off the sheet, the rules say nobody may go out, there is no twelfth line and there is not going to be one, and the recordwright writes down the asking.

**Chapter 286 — Contested From Inside It, And She Is Not The Villain Of It.** The first day of the sixty-third week; the board at the second light is **63,751** and a market is a day of eight. A man of about thirty-one who owns the tower at Nettlebed and makes hurdles and gates, standing against a wall with a frame he has come to sell, says in a market yard to about nine people that a hundred and forty-one people each said no in their own yard four hundred years ago and kept a list, and what they did not do was find somebody to carry it, and a thing carried by one woman and about thirty people is the same shape as a room with one person in it deciding what the rest of them are for. **He is not asking her to stop and he is not asking for it to be led by somebody else, and he sells four hurdles a year.** The woman with the board agrees before anybody asks, in nine words, and then says what changes is not the carrying: what changes is that she now knows what she is doing, and about four hundred places are going to get a paper from her in the next year from a woman who knows, and nothing has been taken off her bag, and she is not going to be relieved and is not going to be thanked. She counts her thirty for the first time and finds that nine would go up a lane with her and nine would not. The man of thirty-one says nothing for an hour, is not asked, does not offer, and takes nothing off her. And the register gets smaller by two crosses, taken off by two people nobody asked: a carter of thirty-five who would rather not be on a list than not be asked, and a miller who said the word once to a carter about ten years ago. **A cross is not an entry and a cross comes off the moment anybody in that place says anything at all.** The money: threepence a load at about nine loads a day is named with the unit price and is not derived, because it was derived in Chapter 257.

**Chapter 287 — A Village That Says Its Sentence, And A Village That Will Not.** The second day of the sixty-third week; the board at the second light is **63,759** and the day is four bells and nothing. A man of about thirty-one says four words in his own doorway in Nettlebed: *we walk this lane.* He refuses twice inside the sentence to dress it up, because a rule says what people may do and a claim says what is mine and he has got neither and is not going to invent one in a yard. **A woman of fifty-one from Trope will not have a man in a doorway four miles down the road say her village's sentence for it in a yard nine miles away, and gives as her reason that a village which has said a sentence has joined a thing and a village which has not joined a thing cannot be asked to leave it, and she has known both halves for about thirty years and has never said them out loud.** A woman of forty-one says both halves out loud in her own village and then says Coldharrow will not say one either, and will not be the one who says it for anybody, and gives the reason: this village is the one with the head in the chalk. A man of fifty-two does the arithmetic, which is the only sum printed in a yard in this batch. **What one entry in a register of fifty-one places is worth: ninepence a day for a hundred and forty days is one thousand two hundred and sixty pence, which is a keeper's year; one shilling and sixpence a day on the same hundred and forty days is two thousand five hundred and twenty pence, which is a carter's year and is also what two villages that never had a bell have been worth every year for two hundred years; eleven villages at one thousand two hundred and sixty is thirteen thousand eight hundred and sixty pence, which is fifty-seven pounds fifteen shillings, and thirteen thousand eight hundred and sixty goes into eleven exactly one thousand two hundred and sixty times, so one village's share of the whole of what this lane is worth is a keeper's year to the penny; and the register has no money in it and no gate and no toll and no officer and no vote, so four words said in a doorway are worth nothing whatever in coin, which is a lane. All three answers are correct and he does not know which one to give anybody.** The register has one place in it and a second line nobody can classify, and the eleventh name on the sheet is a place nobody in two hundred and ten people can name and cannot come off, and put side by side those are the whole of the register. And at the last of the light a carrier puts a letter on a cart's side and it is not a form.

**Chapter 288 — What The Clerk Of Forty-Four Says When He Gets Back.** The third day of the sixty-third week; the board at the second light is **63,763** and three strangers going up the lane on foot make the day a seven, and one of the three is the man of thirty-four. A letter comes back down the lane on the same barrow: about the size of a hand, sealed, and not a form, and nine people in a yard look at it and none of them has held one. **It is read out in a yard by two people who were neither of them in the room where it was written — a woman of fifty-one who cannot read and a recordwright of twenty-eight who can — and the man of thirty-one is in the yard and is not the addressee.** Four things in it: a form came back unsigned with a paper folded inside it carrying about nine words in a hand the writer does not know, and the nine words say the district in which the acknowledgment would be entered has no road to it and has never had, and there is no signature and no seal and no name, and he has four ordinary reasons and none of them is a wicked clerk; he has been at the Seat nine years, about four hundred acknowledgments a year come back, about thirty clerks do them, every one was done properly, and **nobody in that building has ever once been asked to look at what a form does after it is entered**; **nine forms have been entered without a day in nine years, and every one of the nine was entered by a person who had been in a room and had been asked what day it was and had said there was not one, and he does not know what a form does with those nine answers and there is nobody to ask**; and the column they sit in has a head over it that is two syllables, and he will not write it out, because one of the two people standing in that yard can read and the whole of what he is saying is going to arrive in a lane that has never had a building in it through a word on a column in a building four hundred miles off. The recordwright reads the word out, four people in the yard know it and five do not, and a woman of fifty-one who cannot write says on the way up the lane that she had not known a word could hold a thing up. And then the letter's last four lines, which are the batch's one asking of the volume's question: a copy of a thing goes out of a district, the district has no road to it and has never had, the acknowledgment comes back and is entered without a day because the person in the room said there was not one — and then, *is there a road inside your lane?* — and he told the yard not to write back. **Nobody answered it, nobody said they could not answer it, and a woman of fifty-one said on the way up the lane that she had been asked a thing and had not understood it and was not going to pretend she had.** The asking is in a letter four hundred miles off and not in a mouth, and the System said nothing about it and nobody says who laid a lane out from village to village in those words.

**Chapter 289 — The One Thing The Technique Cannot Do.** The fourth day of the sixty-third week; the board at the second light is **63,770** and the day is four bells and nothing. A man of fifty-six with a barrow and a man of fifty-two have walked the whole length of the eleven-village lane in a day and a half and come back with the barrow empty and say four words: there is no road at the end of it. Past the last village there is about two miles of hedge and a field and a boundary nobody has walked in about forty years, and then a road four miles off going somewhere else entirely. **The gate dispute closes because the object of it does not exist: a bar across the end of a lane is not a gate, there is no road behind it and there never was, and four people who had been arguing with each other for about a year have been arguing about a piece of wood a man put across a gap in a hedge.** A carter of thirty-eight does not say the answer in a yard, is not asked, and goes back to the ninth cart. A man of about thirty-one who makes gates says he has never once been asked what a gate is for either. A man of fifty-two refuses to do a sum about the levy in four seconds in front of about nine people, and gives the reason: a figure with a sum under it is a column, and the heading on that woman's board is the only reason nobody has ever been able to ask her a second question, and he is not going to be the one who takes it off her. **And then the man of thirty-one says the volume's method's own limit out loud in a yard in his own mouth, in about nine words: you can put them next to each other and you cannot make them agree, and a method that cannot make four villages agree is a method of evidence and is not a method of government, and if you could make them agree it would not be four villages any more, it would be one village with four names on a door.** He then counts out loud, in about nine seconds, what forty days produced: one of the four disputes is in a book, one is in a ledger at a press and it is not going in, one is in a woman's head and she is about sixty, and one is a bar at the end of a lane — and that is the whole of it and it is not nothing and it is not a settlement. **And the one non-panel trace of the volume is his, one unfinished sentence in his own interior, with no formatting and no name for it.** And a man of thirty-four comes into the yard with about twenty people in it instead of nine.

**Chapter 290 — Four Accounts Side By Side, And They Do Not Agree. BATCH CLIMAX, AND IT IS NOT THE VOLUME'S CLIMAX.** The fifth day of the sixty-third week; the board at the second light is **63,774**, which is four strokes and nothing on top of them, and that morning is the fortieth morning of a man of thirty-one in this country. A hen gets out at Trope. The four accounts are put side by side in a yard for about half an hour and they do not agree, and the chapter says the not-fitting is the finding and that it took four days to arrive at. **The batch's climax is a silence: he has the one sentence he has the standing to say, which is that a person who cannot pay for a hearing and cannot be heard in a room is answered by a person who can be asked, and that a village needs a second one, and that nobody has ever asked what happens to the first one when there are two; it is the sentence every room four hundred miles off is built on; and there is a woman of about sixty nine feet away in a yard who it would have moved, and he does not say it, and about four people watched him decide not to.** A man of thirty-four says his sentence in front of about twenty people and then does the one thing nobody expected: he asks the woman of about fifty at a bar a question, which is the only second question she has been asked in twenty-two years, and she says that a load is a thing that came up the lane and that there is no stroke in this county for a load, because a load is not a thing that happens, it is a thing a man has decided is a load, and he decides it about four hundred miles off in a building, and she finds out when it stops at her gate. He writes it on the back of his own hand in about forty seconds, and it is the only thing he has written down in about eleven years and he did not know that until a recordwright said so out loud. He then goes down the lane and out of the county and does not act on his sentence anywhere in this county, and there is no corridor here for him to act on, and that is a fact and not a mercy. A woman of about sixty says the last of hers: she is the only one who can say where it started, the two things are both going when she is, nobody is coming, and she is not relieved and nobody is going to thank her or rescue her or redeem her. The board read sixty-three thousand five hundred and ten on the first morning of the first day of his being in this country and is two hundred and sixty-four higher this morning, of which two hundred was on the board before this week began and sixty-four is ten days of a village doing things, and nobody chose any of it and there is no column for it. **And the last beat of the batch is a woman of fifty-one in a village of about a hundred and twenty people shutting her own gate bar for the first time in fifty-one years, and opening it again inside four seconds, because a hen was out, and nobody in about a hundred and twenty people heard any of it.** No money figure is invented in this chapter and the only coins named are a keeper's year and a carter's year elsewhere in the batch with their unit prices in the sentence.
