## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0003 — Chapters 271–280, *The Midpoint*. **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0002` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–280 are canon; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced the chapter does not advance.**

**Chapter 271 — The Fourth Line, Read Again.** The seventh day of the sixtieth week; the board at the second light is **63,647** and the day is four bells and nothing, the twenty-first day of a man of thirty-one in this country. The recordwright walks eleven miles to a town that keeps weeks she has never learned. **A woman of about fifty at the bar picks the Form 6 off a cart in the rain because she has a board under her arm, and she is the fourth person in this county to read that sheet and the only one who was not asked, and she gives the fourth line its own beat and says that whoever built that door in was being fair, and that being fair and being useful are two different things, and that she is not opening it and will not say one word about what is behind it.** Her own board has four letters and a stroke at the top of it — **AT THE BAR, the only heading in eleven villages** — and the finding is that a heading is a category and a category is a thing you can be asked about and only about, so that she has been at that bar twenty-two years and has been asked twice about the threepence and about nothing else, and the woman of forty-one would give eleven shillings for a word at the top of her own board and would not know what to do with it. **THE BATCH'S FIRST POSITIVE FINDING: a run of nine consecutive mornings of four, found in the grain because the strokes that are not four are longer, and nine and not ten because there is a longer stroke either side of it — and it cannot be dated, and the woman who found it has been asked twice about it and cannot say once which year of the board those nine mornings are in.** A run of fours is a length and not a day, and a bell can show that a number of days went past and can show nothing else, and she has known that for twenty-five years and thought it was a defect in her. Ends on the woman of forty-one naming the two villages up the lane that have nothing to count at, and the man of fifty-two saying he is the wrong man to be sent and is going anyway. *Money: a keeper's year named at 1,260d and not derived, and a day named at £1 3s 6d and not derived, and both named only as the prices of two ordinary things a woman at a bar already knows.*

**Chapter 272 — The Two Villages That Have Neither.** The first day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,651** and the day is four. The woman of forty-one comes up the lane because she has got a figure in her head about the two of them she has never said out loud, and a man of thirty-five with a barrow, who has heard about this before, asks how old a custom is and is told there is no why. Trope is about the fourth village on the lane and about a hundred and twenty people and it has never had a tower; **a woman of fifty-one called Isel Cardew rings a handbell at the lane end and has done for about forty years, and she is asked three times who taught her and answers once, and the answer is that there is no why and there has not been one since before she could ask one.** A man of sixty-three who sells bells has asked eleven times and has a theory he cannot finish, and the woman of forty-one says the same four sentences to him that she has said to four men from counties with roads in it for twenty-five years. Nettlebed is the sixth up the lane and has a tower about four times the height of a house with a hasp that is not in its staple and a key on a nail inside a house at its foot and **nothing in it for about two hundred years. NOBODY WENT IN.** Three people stood at a door for a quarter of an hour and did not open it, and the man of thirty-one said so and gave the reason — the tower is not his, there is no form for it, and if a stranger opens it then everything anybody finds in there afterwards belongs to the door and not to the village — and the woman of forty-one said the stronger version: you cannot make a day out of a door, and a length is worth more, and she will write three mornings of four on the end of her cloth. **The one non-panel in-world trace in the batch is here, in his own interior, one unfinished sentence, and it is not named.** Ends with a man of thirty-five telling him there is a man at the tower foot who has been asking for a day since about the fourth hour, and has been told twice that nobody there knows what a day is. *Money: a keeper's year as one of her hundred and forty days at ninepence, named and not derived.*

**Chapter 273 — A Board In A Tower.** The second day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,655** and the day goes up eleven, and the seventh of the eleven is a boundary, and the man of thirty-one is standing at the second elm when the first of the seven goes. **A man of about sixty-one who put the marks on those two elms nine years ago walks them again because a stranger asked him for a day, and he cut a fresh mark, and the woman of forty-one ends up with two sevens in ten days and nothing on the plank that says they are the same walk, and neither man will let the stranger walk with him.** At the tower foot is **a clerk of forty-four of the Seat, four hundred miles off, with a coat made for a desk and a stick that is not for walking and no cart and no dog**, and he and the man of thirty-one look at each other for two seconds and neither of them says one word about a room nine feet by fourteen four hundred miles back. He came on his own account: **his whole trade is watching what a document does when it leaves the place it was measured in, and nobody has ever once gone and looked, and a copy left a district eight weeks ago and no acknowledgment came back and there is no number on it.** He is not a Bench, not an office, not a body, and he brings nobody and no authority and he says so before anybody asks. A man of about thirty-one opens his own door because a woman of forty-one has told the stranger he cannot ask anybody else, and asks for that to be on whatever anybody is keeping. Up eleven worn steps: **a hundred and forty-one names on the inside of a door, no seal, no signature, no witness line, nothing at the foot, and at the head four words in a hand the clerk dates at about four hundred years and refuses to give a year for.** The finding is not a charter but a sentence and a list, with the list underneath the sentence. Ends on the clerk naming a column of figures against every one of the hundred and forty-one and nothing whatever over it, and the man of thirty-one counting nine of them and being unable to say what any one is a figure of. *Money: a keeper's year carried from Batch 0002 and not re-derived; no new figure.*

**Chapter 274 — The Midpoint. The Column With No Heading.** The third day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,666** and the day is four, the twenty-fourth day. The recordwright came back at the last of the light and had handed a clerk a sentence and written nothing down anywhere, because the writing of it down is what the sentence is against. **The four words are read three times in one morning and the three readings are all right** — at a bar, in a stair, and again in the same doorway with a different word in the middle of it — and a recordwright of twenty-eight says there was never a fixed one, that a recordwright's whole life is the difference between what a hand says and what a hand has been taken to mean, and that she cannot get this one and is not frightened of that. **A man of fifty-two refuses to add up the column, out loud, in front of about twenty people, on purpose**, and the reason is the instrument's opinion of itself: a column with nothing over it is not a total, and adding it gives a number that is wrong about the world, and there is one of those about once a week in this county and the woman of forty-one has spent twenty-five years not making any. **A woman of fifty-one puts her thumb on the last nine figures and says they are her grandmother's hand and that the column stops there and that her grandmother was dead when she was eleven and has been angry with her for not saying for about thirty years.** **THE MIDPOINT, AND IT IS DELIVERED TWICE AND IN TWO REGISTERS.** A clerk of forty-four, in the voice of a man reading a form: the Codification froze disputed rules and made a challenge harder to file and took the right out of the public in a printed line and gave it to nobody, and **he has never once in twenty-two years found a document that admitted to having taken something, and that is not because it is honest and not because it is dishonest, it is because the people who wrote it did not know they were in a room, because there was no room.** And then a woman of fifty-one, in an ordinary mouth, unasked: we did not lose it, nobody took it off us, we were never in a room and there was nothing to be in one — **we could not refuse the bar, we could not refuse a copy, nobody in this lane has been able to refuse one single thing at any time anybody can remember, and we cannot refuse anything now and we could not before and the two are the same; what we did was stop saying yes, and there was nothing there to say yes to, and the cost was a bell apiece, and it is in that column and there is no name over the column, and I am not going to stand here and tell you that makes it a right. It makes it a bill. Somebody kept the bill. That is all anybody did.** The four lines stop being a curiosity and start being a test. Ends with the clerk saying he has spent a good name once, about five weeks ago, in front of nine people, and that there is nothing in him that anybody in this county can spend, including him. *Money: none new; the keeper's year is not used.*

**Chapter 275 — What The Two Villages Paid.** The fourth day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,670** and the day goes up six, two of them a debt at the ninth house called in by a carter of thirty-eight. **THE BATCH'S ONE NEW DERIVATION, printed in a yard with the unit price in the sentence every time: a year of the woman who keeps the count is ninepence a day for a hundred and forty days = 1,260d; two hundred years of that = 200 × 1,260 = 252,000d; 252,000 ÷ 240 = a thousand and fifty pounds exactly; a bell is 1,620d and is not re-derived; 155 × 1,620 = 251,100; 252,000 − 251,100 = 900d = three pounds fifteen shillings. The price of two hundred years of refusing a bell is a hundred and fifty-five bells and three pounds fifteen shillings**, and the figure is absurd on purpose and the absurdity is the whole of it. The man of sixty-three is standing in the yard and **is not asked a single question about any of it**, and what he says afterwards is about his own trade and not about the March: in eleven years he has never had a village say no to him, not one, he has had two say nothing, and he has wanted one to say no, and that is what a man in his trade is for; and he is going to quote six pounds fifteen in the spring and is not going to quote it lower, and that is not stubbornness. **And the other half, which is the batch's real arithmetic and is the difference between two rows of the table: the whole margin of eleven villages is 13,860d, nine of them have a woman with a cloth at 1,260d each, 13,860 − 11,340 = 2,520d, and 2,520d is ten pounds ten shillings, which is a carter's year to the penny** — and the two villages that have never had a keeper have been worth that every year for about two hundred years off a bar that is not shut, and there is exactly one man in eleven villages who could ever have been paid out of it and he is at the end of the ninth cart and has never had a penny of it and has never once asked what a bar is for. Ends with the man of thirty-one knowing why a column with no heading is a record and a column with a heading is not, and not saying it, because he cannot produce a record and there is no room in eleven villages. *Money: 9 × 140 = 1,260 ✓; 200 × 1,260 = 252,000 ✓; 252,000 ÷ 240 = 1,050 ✓; 155 × 1,620 = 251,100 and 252,000 − 251,100 = 900d = £3 15s ✓; 11 × 1,260 = 13,860 and 9 × 1,260 = 11,340 and the difference 2,520d = £10 10s ✓, and 2,520d = 18 × 140.*

**Chapter 276 — The Panel.** The fifth day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,676** and the day goes up eight, four of them a market, and twenty-seven loads come through a bar at threepence a load. **THE SECOND OF THE VOLUME'S THREE PANELS AND THE ONLY ONE IN THIS BATCH**, in two plain lines in the flat white nothing, in a yard on a market day, and it decides nothing: **A COLUMN WITH NOTHING OVER IT AND A FIGURE IN IT AGAINST EACH OF ONE HUNDRED AND FORTY-ONE NAMES IS THE ONLY RECORD IN THIS COUNTY OF WHAT ANY PERSON PAID, AND NO PERSON ALIVE CAN SAY WHAT THE FIGURES COUNT. WHAT IS NOT DECIDED: WHETHER A THING KEPT FOUR HUNDRED YEARS IN A VILLAGE THAT HAS NO BELL MAY BE READ BY ANYBODY, AND BY WHOM.** The bar-keeper says the heading on her board is the reason nobody in two hundred and ten people has ever been able to ask her a question, and that she has said no to a date about nine hundred times and has never once said the word no to anything else. **A recordwright of twenty-eight puts her satchel down on a cart's side, which she has never done, and says out loud before she is asked that she has read a document no bench in this country has ever seen and cannot tell anybody in a room what it is for, and that this is the fourth time in her life she has read something she could not account for and the first time she has wanted it, and that a recordwright who has spent six years believing that the mark of a real record is that it can be produced in a room has got a plank on the inside of a door that nobody has ever produced anywhere.** Ends with a woman at the bar saying that three men have come into the county and are at Trope and the argument about that door is going to happen in a yard on the day after tomorrow and is not going to be the one he has been having. *Money: nine loads at threepence = 27d, called aloud in a yard, and it is on a plank with a word at the top of it.*

**Chapter 277 — The March Argues The Pressure Again.** The sixth day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,684** and the day goes up thirteen, and three men from four hundred miles off came up the lane rather than in on any road. **THE VOLUME'S CENTRAL PRESSURE, ARGUED A SECOND TIME AND IN FOUR MOUTHS, AND NONE OF THE FOUR IS A VILLAIN AND THE MAN OF THIRTY-ONE IS NOT ASKED.** A carter of thirty-eight gives up the whole of nineteen years of wanting a road for a road that has a day on it, which is a different sentence from the one he said in Batch 0002 and is further along. A woman of about sixty says *take it out* and then tells the yard that there are now **two** things only she can say — where the boundary started, and that the fourth name from the bottom of a four-hundred-year-old list is her grandmother, which nobody has told her and which she has kept for four days and is not going to be asked about — and that she is about sixty and there is nobody coming. A woman of forty-one refuses to say a hundred and forty-one names out loud in a yard, having been a person in a record for one morning, and says she would rather be a coward about it for the rest of her life. **And the fourth thing, which is not a position: a thing four hundred years old is not the March's to spend, and you cannot use it, or expose it, or take it out, and the reason there is no room in this county is on the inside of a door in a village of about ninety people.** Then the woman with the board says the thing nobody asked her: she has carried about four hundred pieces of paper in nine years and has never once asked a single person what they wanted, and the eleven villages have been deciding this for four hundred years without a road and a bell and a bench and are not waiting, and she is not going to start asking now, and she would like it written down by a woman of forty-one. The clerk of forty-four tells three strangers only what a document is, and one of them is a man of thirty-four who cannot read the thing he reads out and says that if it cannot be produced then it has not happened. Ends with four sheets of paper cut out of a bill and a recordwright who is not going to be asked to keep them. *Money: none new; the sum a carter does in his head is named and not derived.*

**Chapter 278 — A Register Anyone May Read And Nobody May Enter.** The seventh day of the sixty-first week; the board says **63,697** and the day is four, the twenty-eighth day. **FIFTY-ONE PLACES ON FOUR SHEETS CUT OUT OF THE BACK OF A BILL**, in the hand of a man of fifty-two, with a second hand on the fourth and a cross on the first from a woman of fifty-one who cannot write, and thirty-five of the fifty-one were got out of a miller and two carters and about nine conversations in a week and four of them are marked with a cross meaning a person of that place said the word once and has not been asked twice. The eleven lines of rules are read out of a cart's side, and the substance of them is that anybody of any country may read all four sheets and nobody may be stopped, and nobody may go in without a sentence said by a person of that village in that village, and the recordwright writes down what was said and nothing else and does not write who said it — **and that there is no gate on it, no toll, no bar, no day on it, no date, no bench, no seat, no room with a door on it except the press it stands on a shelf in, no vote, no meeting, no officer, and no money in it anywhere, and it was cut out of the back of a bill.** **Not one of the four of them is on it, and not one of the eleven villages on the lane is in it and none has asked to be, and that is right and is going to stay right until a village says a sentence in its own yard, and nobody has.** **AND THE SENTENCE THAT TAKES A SOLE AUTHORITY OFF A WOMAN WITH A BOARD IS SAID BY A PERSON OF A VILLAGE, IN A VILLAGE, AND NOT BY HIM: you have thirty people in this country who will do what you tell them, and in eleven weeks you have not asked this village one single question about what it wants, and a thing that eleven villages decided four hundred years ago cannot be carried by one woman with people who follow her. And she agrees with it before she is asked, and says she would have said it in about four days and is glad she has not had to sit on it, and says she is not relieved.** A clerk of forty-four, who has been in the county nine days, points out in a yard that the man of thirty-one has said nothing for an hour and that a register is a document and is the first one in this county that is not a count and not a name. Ends with a carter of thirty-five putting a lane that is on nobody's list on a cart's side, and a carter of thirty-eight saying *do not*. *Money: none; and a shelf in a press that is not let and is not charged for and whose cost nobody has asked about.*

**Chapter 279 — The Lanes Put Side By Side.** The first day of the sixty-second week; the board says **63,701** and the day goes up five, and the fifth is a stranger, and the stranger is a man of thirty-five called Petrow Sill who lives at the end of a bad road called Stennick and has come up nine miles because a woman of fifty-one told him in a lane that there was a list. **The technique with its price, the second time, and with different people, and the price said out loud in a yard before it is paid: the two men at the end of the lanes will find out about each other and neither was asked.** **THE FINDING, and the proof is arithmetic and not opinion: the walked lanes are one thing going round and not a set of lanes, and the same round of eleven villages is in three instruments that have got nothing to do with one another** — the order the debts go round in at a bar, which is not the order of distance, and which a man of fifty-two has known for about four years and never asked anybody about; the order the two hundred and nine names are in on the outside wall of the last house in Ellerby, **which holds for the about seventy names of people who were not in Ellerby when it was written, and that is the part that took a day**; and a line a boy of seventeen has run since he was twelve, in the same order every year, which does not go by the ground. **And no man's cart would choose it, because a cart goes where there is ground and this goes where there is a village.** And the price, which is not the price anybody expects: it is not that the two men find out about each other, it is that neither of them has anybody to put the round to, and there is a third thing about a hundred and forty-one names on a door that neither of them will ever see. The volume's question is not asked a third time; it is referred to once as a mark at the end of a question in a book and nobody in that yard asks anything. Ends with a boy of seventeen going to a tower with his book and a man of thirty-one agreeing to come and not to help. *Money: none; a carter's year is referred to and not derived.*

**Chapter 280 — A Boy's Book And A Hundred And Forty-One Names.** The second day of the sixty-second week; the board says **63,706** and the day is four, the thirtieth day, and a clerk of forty-four goes down the lane on a cart to a town that keeps weeks he has never learned. Four things are named as still sitting where this batch put them: the third hand in chalk, twenty-nine days without an addition; the figure at the foot of a sheet in a stranger's hand; two names on one thing and no room in four hundred miles that has asked about either; and ninety acres that eleven families are grazing and paying nothing for and have never been told about. **THE CLIMAX, AND IT IS A FAILURE OF AN INSTRUMENT AND NOT A DISCOVERY OF A POWER. A boy of seventeen takes his line book to a board of a hundred and forty-one names and cannot read it, and the finding is about his book and not about the board: it has two places in it, what crossed and what did not, and there is a third place on that door and he can see it and does not know what it is for, and the order on that plank is the order somebody decided about four hundred years ago and his book is the order things happened in, and those are two different orders and he has no way of reading one with the other. The finest thing such a book can say about that wall is that one of these came before that one, and there are four hundred years between them, and not one of them is a day he can name, and there is not one instrument in eleven villages that could turn that into a day, and he has had five years. HE WRITES NOTHING. He says he will think about it and will not be hurried and he can be asked in about six weeks, and that is a proper answer, and he goes and does his day.** A woman of fifty-one says that a person of seventeen has just said a thing that was a fact about the county and not about himself, and that she is not going to thank him or tell him what it is for. **And the thing the man of thirty-one could have done and did not: if he had said read it out, and the two hundred years of a woman's wage in that column is a figure he gave a woman of twenty-nine in a press, and if she had put that on the foot of a sheet the way she put his number there, then this plank would be a document — and nobody in that tower thought of asking him, because nobody in that tower had any reason to, and he stood there and let it not come up.** Ends on the round number nobody chose: **the board reads sixty-three thousand seven hundred and ten on the first morning of Chapter 281, and it read sixty-three thousand five hundred and ten on the first morning of Chapter 251, and the difference is exactly two hundred, and it is four bells a day for fifty days, and it is two hundred and nine names on a wall in a village nine miles off against a hundred and forty-one on a door four miles off a woman of fifty-one's gate, and sixty-eight of that difference is nobody's business and is not a mistake in anything, and there is no column for it and no heading over it and no name against it and no year at the top of it and there never was one, and nobody in two hundred and ten people chose it.** *Money: none; the two hundred is a count and not a coin.*

**AND TWO OF THESE TEN PARAGRAPHS WERE TOUCHED BY THE REVIEW OF BATCH 0003, INSIDE THEIR LINES, AND NEITHER PARAGRAPH ABOVE IS WRONG AS A RESULT.** **`276` had a timber-cart morning on the fourth day of the fifty-ninth week at a bar and it is the fourth day of the sixtieth, which is Chapter 268; the nine is right and is the nine strangers out of that day's thirteen, and the paragraph above says nothing about that morning, so it stands.** **`275` promised a press eleven miles off on a day this batch never went there and gave an argument to a woman who was not in the room; the woman is Isel Cardew, fifty-one, and the day is gone and the chain — a heading over a column is a category, a category is a room — is exactly as the paragraph above records it, which is the test a repair has to pass: the summary of a chapter must not have to be rewritten because a sentence in the chapter was wrong.** **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0001` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–270 are canon; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced that the chapter does not advance.**

## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0002 — Chapters 261–270, *The Price Of A Date*. **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0001` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–270 are canon; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced that the chapter does not advance.**

**Chapter 261 — The Day After A Piece Of Paper Leaves.** The fourth day of the fifty-ninth week; the board at the second light is **63,579** and the day comes to five, and the one on top of the four bells is not a stranger and is not anything else on the list. The sealed copy goes back under the seat of a timber cart at the first of the light and out of the county unread, and the man of fifty-one has four days of road in front of him, no reason to stay and no reason to go, and both of those are true. The finding of the chapter is that **a day is finished the moment somebody decides it, and the finding of its second half is that three people got a hand on one rope inside two seconds and a pull is one ring and not three, and the woman of forty-one can prove three reasons and one number, and one is a burial, and nobody died.** And the sentence the batch turns on, in his mouth: **a number that anybody can move is not a record, and the count is the easiest thing in this county for a person to move and the hardest thing in it to argue with afterwards.** The only arithmetic in the chapter is hers and it is the volume's: in twenty-five years the board has gone up **54,750** times, the four bells a day over twenty-five years is **1,460 × 25 = 36,500**, and the difference is **18,250**, which is every burial, boundary, debt, market, stranger and fire anybody in that village has rung for since she was sixteen, so about two rings a day sit on top of the clock, and about two rings a day does not touch most days at all, and the days it does not touch are the days the board says four on. **Four is therefore the ordinary number in this county and not a remarkable one.** No panel.

**Chapter 262 — A Second Day Of Four.** The fifth day of the fifty-ninth week; the board reads **63,584** and the day's rings are the four bells and nothing else. Four people account for last night's one and the four accounts agree with each other and agree with nothing on the list: a woman of about thirty-five whose hens were out, a boy of about nine shouting a friend in out of a field, and a man of about fifty who was in a state and does not know what he rang for and would do it again tomorrow. **The brass is spent once here, in the form the volume planned and in no other: four bells, a rope, and anybody who can reach it.** Two findings and they are the same finding. First, from the route-man, who refuses his own test out loud and says why — **the only way to keep a thing in this country is to write it on somebody else's board, and he is not going to be the fifth hand on a board in a village he has been in eleven days** — and then goes and asks a man of about forty at a door what day it is and gets, in about nine seconds, the same answer four men from counties with roads in it have got out of the woman of forty-one in twenty-five years. Second, and worse, from her: **a day of four and a day of nothing are the same number, and a number that anybody can move is a number that has to be asked about, and there is exactly one person in this county you can be asked, and for twenty-five years that has been a comfort, and it is a door, and she heard somebody walk up to it this morning.** The last line is her sending him to find out what asking a question costs in this country. No panel.

**Chapter 263 — A Date Bought By Somebody Else.** The sixth day of the fifty-ninth week; the board reads **63,588** and the day's rings are the four bells and seven for a boundary, and it is the first boundary walked in this county in nine years. The man of thirty-one goes out with them and one of the four who came from Ellerby is a woman of about sixty who is **Wenna Skell**, and she says where it started and does not know what any of the days are called, and the seventh ring goes on a board that cannot say it is the same seven. He and the route-man then walk eleven miles to the press at Coldharrow-edge and he buys a date for the day a sealed copy was read out in a yard in Coldharrow, in the grain year the clerk uses, at **a pound, three shillings and sixpence**; and a woman of twenty-nine says the price first because that is the only honest part of the business, and says that **two people who bought the same day have not made a day twice — they have made one day with two people standing in front of it, and a room will take whichever of the two it likes, and it has never once in my life taken the one I would have chosen.** **THE SUMMARY SAID *in six years* ON DELIVERY AND THE CHAPTER SAYS *in my life*, AND THE SIX YEARS IS THE RECORDWRIGHT'S UNFILED FAMILY CLAIM AND HAS NO PLACE IN A WOMAN OF TWENTY-NINE'S MOUTH AT A PRESS; THE CHAPTER IS RIGHT.** The working is printed on a press bench because that is where this volume prints its working: **two days is two hundred and eighty-two pence, two of them is 564d, and 564 − 480 = 84d = 7s, so two dates is two pounds and seven shillings exactly; and 564 ÷ 18 = 31 remainder 6, so two dates is thirty-one days of the man who walks the road and sixpence; and a year of the woman who keeps the count is 9 × 140 = 1,260d = five pounds five shillings, and 1,260 − 564 = 696d, and 696 − 480 = 216d = eighteen shillings, so two dates is a year of her less two pounds and eighteen shillings.** A carter of thirty-eight has bought a second one out of his own money, for a day that is no use to him, after asking a woman of twenty-nine for a date for the lane and being told: tell me the day it was laid out — he said it was always there — then I cannot help you. The recordwright's line is the batch's: **two names on one thing is not two witnesses, it is one thing with two people standing in front of it, and a room nine days from this field will take the one it likes.** And on the road he says out loud, and writes down afterwards, that he had a moment on that bench at which he could have told the woman of forty-one what he was doing and he bought the day instead. No panel.

**Chapter 264 — A Thing From A Building With A Yard.** The seventh day of the fifty-ninth week, a market day; the board reads **63,599** and the day's rings are the four bells and four for a market. **A market is the only day anything at all comes up the eleven-village lane**, which nobody in the county had ever had cause to notice, and what comes up is a printed sheet, four days late, out of a drawer under a cloth with a list of eggs on it: **Form 6 of the Water-Seat of Sallowby — the delivery spelled it Sallyby, which is not the name at `259:33` — acknowledgment of a copy carried out of the district**, dated in a year this county does not keep. The chamber's answer is **correct**: a copy is not evidence, a copy is paper, an acknowledgment is evidence of one thing only, which is that a person was in a place and read a copy and is willing to say so afterwards. It is **wrong about the place in three ways and in the same three ways in every country it has been in, and not one of the three is anybody being a villain**: it asks for a room and the reading was in a yard; it asks for a day in the grain year of the seat and the fell year is not a day and the woman who could give the fell year has said the same four sentences about it to four men in twenty-five years; and **it says the acknowledgment will be entered in the district named in the copy, and that district is four hundred miles off, so this county would put the only name it has got into a record in a valley that has never heard of it.** Its fourth line is a door built into it by somebody who was being fair: **where no day can be shown, the acknowledgment may be entered without one, and the entry will be marked as made without a day**, and it is not a door anybody has to open. It asks for one person present at a reading and the county has exactly one, and nobody can ask her, because nobody in eleven villages has a person to ask. **The first half of what the batch costs is said here, to a wall that cannot hold it: she has been the only one who can be asked in this county for twenty-five years and it has been a comfort, and she did not know until about a minute ago that a thing like that can be spent, and now she does, and she has not told anybody, and she would like it written down somewhere that is not a wall.** A woman with a board sent for that form eight weeks before she came and told nobody and is not thanked and is on no paper. **The only figure is a pound three shillings and sixpence and fifteen days of a man's road.** No panel.

**Chapter 265 — The Use, And The Expose, And The Destroy.** The first day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,607** and the day's rings are the four bells and two for a debt, and a March day with a debt in it is finished before the noon bell. **The volume's central pressure is said out loud in full by three ordinary people in ordinary mouths before anybody is asked: use it, tell the eleven families, take the hedge out.** A carter of thirty-eight says *use it* in one word for the first time in nineteen years and works out the price of it in the same yard, out loud: **three thousand seven hundred and eighty pence a year off one gate, and ten pounds ten of it is what a man earns walking it and five pounds five of it is the woman who keeps the count, and none of it keeps anything because there is no surface, and a road wants a date kept on it, and a date is a pound three shillings and sixpence, and four of them in a year is four pounds fourteen, which is a year of the woman who keeps the count less eleven shillings** (4 × 282 = 1,128d; 1,260 − 1,128 = 132d = 11s ✓), and nobody in that yard had ever said it. A woman of about sixty says she wants the hedge and the two elms and the line taken out, and the reason is her own life and not the record: **being the only one who can say where it started is not an honour, it is a job nobody gave her and nobody can take off her and she is about sixty.** A woman of forty-one says she wants the eleven families told, in nine seconds, having carried the fact for nine years because nobody ever asked her for it. **He is not asked, and the reason is his own finding from the fifth day of that week: a place with no party is a place that can be done to.** The finding of the chapter is his and it is the volume's: **they are not three positions, they are three prices — using it costs the levy and the levy keeps nothing, exposing it costs a date this county cannot make, and destroying it costs eleven families the water off ninety acres they have had for nine years, and it is the only one of the three there is no figure for anywhere, and it is going to be the one somebody pays.** **THE ELEVEN FAMILIES ARE NOT TOLD ANYTHING IN THIS CHAPTER** and the reason is printed: the batch's problem is that nobody in eleven villages can produce a day, and a fact told to eleven families without a day on it is eleven families in a lane with nothing to be right about. A boy of seventeen says the thing nobody in the yard had thought of — he has run a line since he was twelve and has never once crossed the strip — and then says, before anybody can use it, that it does not help. The leg is used once, as a consequence, with no explanation and no count. The chapter ends with the woman of about sixty stopping a woman with a barrow at a gate and asking for a thing to hold. No panel.

**Chapter 266 — A Village With A Different Arithmetic.** The second day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,613** and the day's rings are the four bells and one for a burial, and the burial is the one ring on the list with a name on it and it works, because a woman of forty-one stands in a yard and shouts a name at two hundred and ten people. Nine miles up the lane is Ellerby: about a hundred and forty people, a bell in a frame on two uprights in a field rung by whoever is nearest under a custom of about four hundred years that everybody in the village can describe and nobody in it can date, and **a board with two hundred and nine names on it and no figures and no total and no date and no column, in the order they happened, with nobody ever struck a name out, about thirty-one of the about hundred and forty people not on it, and a name on it of a man in a blue coat there is nobody in the village for, left there because a name with nobody at the end of it is still better than a number.** The copy is fetched on the way up, in about four minutes, from a drawer in a press, because a woman of about forty with a barrow says a woman of about sixty wants a piece of paper to hold, and a woman of twenty-nine who copies for a living gives her a copy of the four lines and says that a copy that has been in a country for an hour is worth nothing. **The same four lines are worth nothing in Ellerby, and not for the opposite reason, and the reason is arithmetic and not opinion: in Coldharrow a document is a lever with two hundred and ten people's names nowhere on it, and in Ellerby a thing that happened is a thing somebody was standing near enough to see, and every one of those two hundred and nine names is a person somebody can go and ask.** The finding in one sentence: **a number says how many times and names nobody, and a name says who and can be asked; Coldharrow has the first and cannot produce the second, Ellerby has the second and does not know that is what it has; and the four lines are worth something again the moment a person in Ellerby stands in a doorway and hears them read out, which is the one thing he knows how to do and the one thing he cannot make anybody do.** A woman of about sixty reads them with her thumb under the line, gets to the second line, and says: there is no river in this county. The recordwright says the thing about herself before he does: there is a person standing in a doorway in front of him and she is the only one in this county he can put anything in front of that comes back with an answer, and I think it is a waste, and I am telling you now before you do it. No panel.

**Chapter 267 — Two Cases Side By Side, And The Price Of It.** The third day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,618** and the day's rings are the four bells and three for a stranger, and the stranger is a man of about forty with a grey coat who gave his name when the woman at the bar asked him to and was written on a wall in Ellerby yesterday without anybody asking. **THE TECHNIQUE IS DEFINED ONCE, IN THE FICTION, IN HIS OWN MOUTH, AND IT IS NOT A LESSON: you may put two things next to each other, you may not make them one, and the price of putting them next to each other is that the two people in the middle of them find out about each other, and neither of them was asked, and there is no instrument in this country that stops it happening, and he had looked for one, and he did it anyway, because the alternative is two things in two counties nine miles apart that are each worth nothing.** He does it in a doorway in about nine minutes with a woman of forty-one in it and a woman of about sixty nine miles off in it, and what comes out is one true sentence nobody in this county could have said: **the only proof in this county that a strip of ground was ever decided is a number one village keeps and a name another village keeps, and the two of them are nine miles apart, and neither village can use what the other one has.** And the price arrives inside the same minute, because the technique works. What a woman of forty-one says about it, and it is not anger and she is not being magnanimous: **you have made me a person in a room and I did not ask to be one, and I have been one for nine years, and I did not know it was a room until a man of thirty-one stood in a doorway and put me in it in front of nine people**, and she asks for it to be written down somewhere that is not a wall by somebody who is not in it, and does not say him. What he wrote down afterwards and gave to nobody: **he was right about the mechanics, the mechanics were right, the human meaning arrived late as it always does and arrived on two women in a county of two hundred and ten people, and he did not find out he had done it until the second of the two had already said it back to him; and he has had this before, twice, both times it was a hand on a table and both times he took the hand away again, and this is the same failure in a different medium.** No panel.

**Chapter 268 — Sable Venn And Ilyan Work Beside Him And It Goes Badly.** The fourth day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,625** and the day's rings are the four bells and nine for three strangers at each of three gates. **They work together for the first time and it goes badly, and the badness is that the method works.** The method is that a person reads aloud and two people who are neither of her decide what it means, and because the two who decide cannot read they have to agree out loud in front of four witnesses, and there are eleven disagreements, and the eleven disagreements are the reason the sentence came out the shape it did. The reader is a woman of about sixty who was not asked and did not know what any of the days are called and got the third line right the second time and was not told. What comes out is two hundred words and four lines with no name at the foot of it and no day on it, and **the not putting of the day is the only protection anybody in that kitchen has got, **AND IT BELONGS TO SABLE VENN, WHO WROTE THE DOCUMENT, IN HER OWN HAND, IN ABOUT ELEVEN MINUTES, AND COULD NOT READ IT BACK, AND IT IS THE FIRST USEFUL THING SHE HAS DONE IN ABOUT FOUR HUNDRED. THE DELIVERY GAVE ALL OF IT TO THE RECORDWRIGHT, WHO WAS IN THE COLDHARROW YARD AND NOT IN THE KITCHEN.** **The consequence in Sable Venn's own mouth, and she does not apologise for it and is not going to:** you have made a woman of sixty read one out, and she is not a document, and I know the difference, and it has taken me nine years and a copy to learn and it has taken you eighteen days, and it has cost her nothing at all, because nobody asked her either, and I was one of the people who did not ask her. The recordwright's observation is the volume's next turn: **it is the first route out of this county that anybody has chosen, and a man of thirty-one has just started one, and I have written a clause into a charter once and never thought of it as the same thing.** Nobody is thanked, nobody is on anything, and the sheet goes down the lane on a barrow with a woman of about forty who has never opened another person's paper in nineteen years and has said out loud, unprompted, that she has not read it. **The only money named is a pound three shillings and sixpence, twice, as what the woman of sixty could not lay down for a day out of a village, and as what a woman of twenty-nine at a press makes forty of a year.** **THE DELIVERY ATTRIBUTED THAT TRADE TO THE RECORDWRIGHT, WHO IS NOT A PRESS.** No panel.

**Chapter 269 — The Figure He Wrote Because He Had Nothing Else.** The fifth day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,638** and the day's rings are the four bells and nothing else, and the day he leaves behind added thirteen, three at each of three gates, and about half the nineteen days he has been here added nothing at all above the clock, and the board says four on those the same as on any other, and there is no way of telling which. **THE DELIVERY SAID THE DAY BEHIND HIM WAS *A DAY OF NOTHING* AND CALLED THE WHOLE OPENING *THE FIRST THING THIS VOLUME HAS TO BE A RECORD OF*, WHICH IS BOTH WRONG — THE DAY ADDED THIRTEEN — AND META-NARRATION; THE OPENING IS REWRITTEN.** Eleven miles off the lane, in a press in a village that is not in the March, a woman of twenty-nine is making the second of a copy and asks for the two things a copy has to have under it: **the number of the thing you are copying, and the day of it, both, because a copy that cannot be told from the thing it is copied from is not a copy, it is a second thing, and a second thing is a lie about there being two.** He has a figure and he does not have a day, and he says so, and she says: I have been selling dates into that county for six years and there has not been a single day in it that I could have put at the foot of anything, and put the number or do not pay me. **THE BATCH'S COST IS PAID HERE AND IT IS PAID IN FOUR SECONDS: the only figure he has ever put into this country in his own hand is the chalk at the foot of a board from the first morning of his being here, reading sixty-three thousand five hundred and ten, and it is EIGHTEEN days stale — he is on his nineteenth day and the delivery said nineteen — and he gives it, and he stops in the way a man stops when he has heard himself, because there were two numbers he could have said and he gave the one with his hand in it, and a number with a hand in it is a person, and a person is what two hundred words and a woman of twenty-nine not putting a day on it were for.** He does not take it back, and the reason is in his own words on a leaf torn out of a book: **a man who takes a thing off a board in front of two hundred and ten people has admitted he had no business putting it there, and the only thing that would have made it not a different act is if he had never done it, and he had, and he did it in four minutes on a first morning in a country where nobody had asked him anything, and he gave it because a woman asked him for a figure and he had nothing else to give.** The book with two halves in it is named once, and the second half was not opened. A woman of about forty reads the figure back off the bottom of the sheet when he asks her to, in the way he asks for things, and nobody in that press remarks on the asking, which is the second time in eighteen days and has become a thing people in two counties have stopped remarking on. The thing underneath Sable Venn's nine words is said here at last: **it worked four hundred times because of what she would not know and not because of what she could not do.** No panel.

**Chapter 270 — What He Wrote On A Board In A Place He Was Not In.** The sixth day of the sixtieth week; the board reads **63,642** and the day's rings are the four bells and three for a stranger at about the fourth hour, and a stranger is three. The sheet comes back down the lane on a barrow and is read out at the board, at the woman's own asking, by the recordwright, and at the foot of it, on the left, in pencil, in a hand that is not any hand in eleven villages, is **sixty-three thousand five hundred and ten**, and the figure at the head of the board on the wall of the tower that morning is **sixty-three thousand six hundred and forty-two** — **which the delivered chapter printed as sixty-three thousand five hundred and forty-two, out by a hundred, and which is the number the batch turns on** — and about nine people in that yard know it at a glance and nobody is told and nobody says a word. **The arithmetic is the wound and the man of fifty-two prints it on the side of a cart: a hundred and thirty-two, and a hundred and thirty-two is not a figure of anything, it is the shape of nineteen days — five, eleven, five, six, eight, five, seven, four, thirteen, five, and five, four, eleven, eight, six, five, seven, thirteen, four — sixty-nine and sixty-three, which is a hundred and thirty-two, which is what the board has done since the morning he chalked it (5+11+5+6+8+5+7+4+13+5 = 69; 5+4+11+8+6+5+7+13+4 = 63; 69 + 63 = 132; 63,510 + 132 = 63,642 ✓). And the last of the nineteen is a four, and four is what the board says about most days in a year, so the one day nearest the sheet is the one day out of the nineteen you could not find with a lamp and a boy.** **What the woman of forty-one says, and she does not say it is his: there is a number inside a piece of paper in this county, and a number on a wall is a thing about a village and a number on a piece of paper is a thing about a person, and on the wall it is ours and on the paper it is his, and there is no column on that board that says whose hand anything was and there is never going to be one, and she has been a person in a record for one morning and did not ask to be one and is not going to be able to undo it and is not going to be told she is sorry for it.** He does not explain and does not apologise and does not offer to take it off. The recordwright says the nine words a third time, word for word, and says that was the point of it, and says she is going to carry the sentence to a town that keeps weeks she has never learned and hand it to a clerk and would like him to have a bad afternoon. **And then the volume's question, asked a second time, in a different mouth and a different shape, and not answered: a boy of seventeen asks it in a doorway, to a person, having run a line since he was twelve, and it is longer than the carter's and it has a mark on the end of it, and he writes it in a book that has never had a question in it because a question is not a thing that crossed, and turns the book round so a man of thirty-one can read it, and the man of thirty-one has the one sentence he has the standing to say and does not say it, and nothing comes, and he says I do not know, and the boy says that is two of us, and goes to do his day because there were about four bells left and somebody in that village had to count them.** He has been in the country twenty days, the leg is no better, the thing he is carrying is still off nothing, and nobody has thanked him and nobody is relieved. No panel.

# Chapter Summaries — **open `state/index.md` first.** The live record is the top block, `## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0001`; everything below it, from `## VOLUME 05 IS CLOSED` down, is archive.
## VOLUME 06 BATCH 0001 — Chapters 251–260, *The Bell, And A Count With No Date In It*. **The live block. The block below it, from `## VOLUME 05 IS CLOSED` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–260 are canon; Volume 05 is closed; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-06.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced that the chapter does not advance.**

**251 — A Country That Counts In Rings.** The first day of the fifty-eighth week, Shelf day 126. He comes down off the last ridge into the Briar March and the cart turns about at a posting yard, because the last four miles is not a road. **Bram Orren, seventeen, rings a bell at a stile before he speaks, and then says the March's rule — that a runner rings what he crosses — before anybody can accuse him of touching the rope, and it is worth noticing that he says it because he was told to, by a man of sixty in a yard eleven miles off, in the same words, in the same number of seconds, and that is how a thing travels in a country with no paper in it.** Coldharrow is about two hundred and ten people in thirty-eight houses with a tower and a bell and **no market day, because a market needs a day and Coldharrow does not have the kind of day a market needs.** On the north wall of the tower at chest height is a board, about as wide as a door, painted and unpainted so often that the grain has come up through it, two hands in it, **thirty-one years, six of them the father's and twenty-five her own, and a figure of sixty-three thousand five hundred and ten with no year at the head of it and no column and never a column.** A woman of forty-one keeps it, says *four hundred and ninety-two since the last of the year before the fell came down*, and says the plainest thing in the batch: **she has never been asked what the number is a number of and has answered nobody because nobody has asked.** He puts a figure in chalk at the foot of the board, the same figure as the head of it, four inches apart, **and does not put his name on it and does not put a date on it, and the reason he does not put a date on it is that he does not know what date to put.** She says *that is not what I asked for* and *I have not asked you for anything* and *you have put a figure in chalk at the foot of a board that has been going thirty-one years and there are now three hands in it and it is in chalk and it will come off in the rain*, and then: **that is not what I asked for, and I have not asked you for anything.** She does not tell him to wipe it. She says *it is on the board.* **No money. No panel. The batch's device is spent here and it is a mistake he makes in his first four minutes.**

**252 — Four Bells A Day And Two That Are Not The Clock.** Shelf day 127. Board **sixty-three thousand five hundred and fifteen**, five more, four bells and a stranger, and a stranger is three. **Ottily Roke, forty-one, twenty-five years, ninepence a day for a hundred and forty days, and she says the price before the fact because the price before the fact is the only honest part of it.** The four bells are the clock — the first, the change, the noon, the last — and the first is when the day starts and the last is when it stops and **nobody in eleven villages has ever said what either one is a height above.** The other two a day are the problem, and she gives the whole of it in one sentence: *I cannot tell you what the other two a day are for, and neither can anybody else in this village, and it is not because we are hiding it. It is because nobody has ever written down one of them.* **They go and watch a boundary being walked, and she counts it out loud the whole way and says why: seven, once to start and once at each corner and once at the end and twice coming back, and it is seven every time and there is no way to do it in six and nobody has ever tried.** And the man of thirty-one understands a mile in that a strip of ground's only proof is a woman saying a number on a hedge in a particular year, and puts side by side a printed index in a room eight weeks ago and this, **and the finding is that a thing which happened once, whose only record is a woman saying a number out loud, is not a record and is not not a record; it is a third thing, and the Bench has no word for the third thing, and the Bench's word for the fourth thing is a column headed with a year — and he does not say it out loud, because the sentence that separates them is the sentence that protects the institution.** She finishes the sum he has been doing in his head: four a day is 1,460 a week is 460 and about six a day is **2,190 a year; a carter rings once at each of eleven villages; 2,190 ÷ 11 goes in a hundred and ninety-nine times with one over; a year of that board is a hundred and ninety-nine whole passages of a man with a cart and one ring, and the one ring is most likely a stranger and the one ring might be anybody.** She refuses in the end to explain the three: *I would rather say that in a road than have somebody come back in a year with the answer and find that I wrote it down.* **Money: 140 × 9d = 1,260d = £5 5s a year, given in her own mouth. No panel.**

**253 — What A Burial Gets And What A Stranger Gets.** Shelf day 128, a burial. Board **sixty-three thousand five hundred and twenty-six**, eleven more, and the eleven is the largest single day's rise in the eight mornings he has been here. She tells him her name **because she can see that two of them are going to write something down eventually**, and she has never said it out loud in a yard. Three days becomes eleven, because three is not enough to show anybody anything. **THE FINDING, in about four seconds, agreed to by the woman in one sentence and not argued with: a day's figure is not how many things happened, it is how much they weighed.** The list is complete and it is short and they do not ring for a christening or a marriage, and the four a day are on top of it and are not in it. He goes up the board with the lead and finds that the same week nine years back reads nine, four, eleven, four, four, thirteen, four, and the same week eight years back reads four, four, four, six, four, four, two, **and that he can tell which strokes are which because the ones that are not four are longer and the man who made them put the downstroke first, and a man who is nearly out of the day puts the upstroke first. She can tell you the strokes. She cannot tell you the day. She has been asked twice why she does not write down what it was for, and both times she said it was in the tower, and it is in the tower and she can read it, and the answer is that it is in her and she is fifty-nine when this is finished being her job and there is nobody coming.** **Then Garrick Terrel, sixty-three, the bell-founder's agent, twice a year, in a coat that had been good eleven years ago, quotes a price and the price is the batch's second arithmetic: metal at four shillings the pound on thirty-one pounds, 31 × 48 = 1,488d = £6 4s; frame and rope eleven shillings = 132d; together 1,620d = £6 15s; and against her year of 1,260d = £5 5s the difference is 360d = £1 10s. The working is printed in a cart yard by a man of fifty-two and he gets a unit wrong once and corrects it before anybody else can.** And Terrel says the sentence nobody in a yard would say: **nobody has ever set the bell against the woman, and you would have to be a fool or a bastard to do that in a yard, and there has never been a fool or a bastard in this yard that I know of, and I would not be one either.** And that the two villages with no bell have no board, and the last man in a village who wanted one went without about thirty years before Terrel was born, and **the money went the other way about thirty years before that and he has never worked out how.** He ends by saying it is not going to be asked for, which is the batch's device twice over. No panel.

**254 — A Boy's Book With Days In It.** Shelf day 129, a debt called in, and a debt in this country is not a matter of money. Board **sixty-three thousand five hundred and thirty-one**, six more, and the figure is not named in the chapter. **THE BATCH'S THIRD DEVICE AND THE SERIES' OWN MILESTONE: Bram Orren refuses him, in about nine words, before he has got as far as asking — *you want it in a room, and rooms are what it is for* — and the boy is right.** The man of thirty-one does not argue, and the chapter is explicit about why in his own words: he came into the country to find a thing a person can hold and put in front of a room, and a boy of seventeen has told him in nine words the difference between his kind of good and the boy's, and he has got no answer and a man with no answer has no business making an argument at a hedge. **He then tells the boy the whole of the reason he would hand the lane over, and it is not sentiment: a person who cannot pay for an appeal and cannot be heard in a room is a person whose problem is the most real kind there is, and he decided in four days that the answer is to get a second person who can be asked, and he did not ask himself what happens to the first one when there are two.** In the afternoon a debt is collected: two men knock and stand there and a woman of about sixty does not open the door, and the two rings went at dawn and the whole village knew by the noon bell and knew by the last bell whether it had been paid. **There is no form and there is no court. There is a bell, two men and a door, and the door is the woman's, and she can stand behind it for as long as she likes, and if she does, everybody in two hundred and ten people knows there is a debt and does not know whether it is paid — and the woman of forty-one refuses the reading of it that the March is soft: we have a thing for it and the thing is that the whole of a village is standing in the lane, and that is a thing no clerk can do.** The man of thirty-one says, to the recordwright and not to anybody else, that this is the one that has no column. And the boy explains his book without opening it: **the four bells at the top of every page and a mark against the one he is at, and what crossed and in what order, and what did not, and two pages lost in the ninth year because he was ill, and his father said a book with a hole in it is a book with a hole in it.** The finest thing it can say is that a thing happened before this and after that, **and that is not a date.** And the refusal, at its full length: a date is what a room needs, and a thing said in a room can be written down, and a thing written down can be produced, and a thing that can be produced can be used, and a formal appeal is a thing that is produced, and a formal appeal costs money, and a family that cannot pay for one does not appeal, **they walk** — and this lane is the only thing in this county nobody can be asked about, and you are the first person in two years I think would hand it over for a good reason, **and I would rather it was somebody rude.** A recordwright of twenty-eight, who has said nothing for two days, says nine words at the end. No panel.

**255 — Nine Words From A Recordwright.** Shelf day 130, a market. Nine loads at a gate, threepence a load, a stroke of the board and a word to the man and nothing kept, and the ninth is a man of thirty-eight's and the woman at the post has him out by one in a month and is right. The argument is not until the last bell and it goes on after the last bell, which is the only time anything does. **Sera Quill gives him her family claim in about eleven words, and only because he asked in front of a witness: it is unfiled, it has been unfiled for six years, it is going to be unfiled in six weeks, and nobody knows about it but her and a clerk who could not help her and has since died, and that is all he gets, and she would have said nothing at all in a lane.** She refuses the whole of his case, and her own reason, which is that she is a recordwright and a recordwright's whole trade is a count that leaves the board, and she has made that argument to herself first and lost to it. **THE BATCH'S FINDING, said by her and not by him, in two parts, and the second part is the volume's engine: a place that cannot be dated is a place that cannot be named in a room.** A bench that is sent nothing does not write nothing down; it writes that it was sent nothing; that is a sentence about a place and not about a person; there is nobody in it to answer it, because to answer it you have to have been in it. **And a place with no party is a place that can be done to.** He does not argue with it and instead says his own plan out loud in a yard, in full, and warns her: **he is going to find out what a date costs, and pay it, and have somebody else pay it too so that it is not him, and have two people in the county who can put a name on it in a room, and he knows that two is worse than one and that they will then be able to be argued with and that she is the one who will be worst at by that — and he asks her to say now rather than in a letter in a month.** And the route-man says the only thing nobody had said: you cannot fall out of a bell, and nobody in a room nine days from that field can put a hand on this village, and **a person who cannot be put a hand on is not free, and the woman of thirty-eight in that valley said it before she was asked and he did not get it out of her and has not got it out of anybody since.** She answers that two is worse than one, that he has known it since about the fourth volume of his own life, that he has never once done the sum on it out loud in a yard, and that she has now said her nine words twice and would like it noticed. **He writes none of it down**, and gives the reason: he learned once what happens to a thing you write in your own hand to be careful with, where it goes, and who is holding it. No panel.

**256 — A Woman Who Sells Days.** Shelf day 131. Board **sixty-three thousand five hundred and forty-five**, eight more than the morning before, which was four bells and four for a market, and the day itself came to five and the fifth of those was a stranger. **Nell Callow, twenty-nine, says her name in a yard without being asked, because a person who carries paper to a village that has never had a date has to say who she is before the price, and then says the price before he asks, because that is the only honest part of the business and everything after it is her being quick.** The money, printed in full and checked twice: two days out at eighteen pence is 36d, two nights at threepence is 6d, a clerk's fee of a pound is 240d, and 36 + 6 + 240 = **282d = £1 3s 6d**, and the pound does not go anywhere in particular, it goes into a box, and the box is the reason a county seat has a seat, and **you are buying a seat at a table in a room and you are not buying a friend and you are not buying anybody's attention.** Then the conversion into the only money a March village has: **282 ÷ 18 = 15 remainder 12, so a date is fifteen days of the man who walks the road and one shilling**, and the woman at the gate says *about half a month*, and the man of fifty-two has had nine such days a year for nineteen years and has never once said that to a person who was selling him something. And **four dates is 1,128d = £4 14s, and a year of the woman who keeps the count is 1,260d, and the difference is 132d = eleven shillings** — and the yard goes quiet in a way a yard in Coldharrow does not get quiet, because about four of the people standing in it understood that sentence as being about their own road. **She puts her own year in the same money unasked: about forty dates a year is 11,280d = £47 exactly, which is about nine times a keeper's year, and she has not slept especially well about it for two years and has not stopped, because the alternative is not sleeping at all and there are thirty-one houses here that cannot pay a man with a cart to come up the lane once.** And then the thing she came to say, unasked, and it is the batch's incompleteness: **she cannot put a date on a boundary.** A date is for a thing that happened on a day. A boundary is a line and the line is there before you walk it and there after you come back; put a Shelf date on it and you have proved a man walked it, and he did, and it is true, and it is worth nothing, because a man can walk a boundary twice and the second time is the one that counts, and a room nine days off will take the second one. **Fourteen in six years, all fourteen gone against the man who asked, and she knows about eleven of them and has not gone looking for the other four, because she is twenty-nine and has a press and a woman and two children and has never done a thing in this county she could not do on a day she could name.** And the incompleteness is named, **by a woman of forty-one in a yard and not by the man**: a boundary is a thing that can be walked twice, and that is the whole of why that girl is the way she is, and it is not because she is wicked and not because she is careful, and nobody has ever asked her to sell anything else, **because we are all waiting for somebody to come and make the room stop wanting them.** No panel.

**257 — The Whole Of The Margin, With The Working Printed.** Shelf day 132, the last day of that week. Board **sixty-three thousand five hundred and fifty**, five more, four bells and one stranger, and the fourth time in a week that he has put a figure in chalk at the foot of somebody else's board. Nine men in the cart yard have watched a man say a figure out loud on a cart's side twice and have concluded he is a fool, and the man of fifty-two decides the best use of the second hour of the fifth day is to be wrong in front of nine men who think he is a fool. **Everything is printed and nothing is taken on trust from a ledger.** A day of a man on this lane is one shilling and sixpence, told to him by a man of forty-two who has counted carts for twenty-two years and checked against a man of thirty-eight who does it; a hundred and forty days, and he names that it came from a man of fifty-two in a yard four hundred miles off who was wrong, and that the true figure in a year about every seven is a hundred and ten, and that he has not corrected it and is saying where it came from. 18 × 140 = 2,520d = £10 10s. The levy is threepence a load on every day there is a load, and the price has not moved in nineteen years and he has been told it is a foundation. **He says eight loads and the woman at the gate has said nine and told him in front of five people and he did it again in a yard because he counts the road and the road and the gate are not the same thing.** 140 × 9 = 1,260 loads, × 3d = 3,780d = £15 15s. **THE BATCH'S CENTRAL ARITHMETIC, out loud in a cart yard: 3,780 − 2,520 = 1,260d = £5 5s, and the woman of forty-one is paid ninepence a day for a hundred and forty days, and 140 × 9 = 1,260d, and it is the same figure, and it is not nearly the same figure, and he has got it twice from two directions and read it twice.** And then the man of thirty-eight says *eleven villages* and the whole of it: **1,260 × 11 = 13,860d = £57 15s a year, and that is the whole of the margin, and it is the whole of what this lane is worth to the people who own it, and it is the whole of what is left after paying the people who walk it, and there is not one other penny in it anywhere in this county and I have been on it nineteen years and I know.** He wants it to be a road, and **the whole of his reason is a gate: a road has a gate on it, and this gate is a post with a bar across it that is not shut, and he has been over it about four thousand times and never once been stopped, and it has taken three pence off him nine times a day for nineteen years and he has never seen it do anything at all, and there is no road here, there is a lane and a bar and a woman with a stick and a man who counts, and the man who counts is me, and if I stop there is nothing, and nothing is not a road.** The recordwright, who has said nothing in a yard in seven days, says one thing: **a gate takes three thousand seven hundred and eighty pence a year and does nothing, and the whole of the reason it does nothing is that there is no road for it to be the gate of, and that is a sentence and not a figure, and she is not going to write it down, because if she does somebody in a room nine days off will use it, and she has watched a room use a sentence like that in another county and she is not doing it in a country that has a woman of forty-one in it.** And the man of thirty-eight asks the last question of the day: **nineteen years and he has never once been able to say what a gate is for, and nobody in the yard can tell him, and he has asked in four counties and stopped expecting an answer and started keeping a list.** No panel.

**258 — The Day That Added Four. THE PANEL.** Shelf day 133, the first day of the fifty-ninth week, and **the day's rings go to four**, and the man of thirty-one is in a yard at the second light for the express purpose of finding out why that is worth walking into, and finds out in about nine minutes that it is not worth anything and that the woman of forty-one has known for twenty-five years and has never told anybody because there has never been anybody to tell. He asks at the noon bell and she comes down off the ladder before he has finished the sentence, which she does not do for anybody. **THE PANEL, in two plain lines, in about two years of his life spent in a place like this, in a yard, to about eleven people at a board, and it says not one word about any of them:** a count of four on a board in a country where every day is four bells is a count of nothing, and a figure that cannot be told apart from another figure is not a record, it is a number — **and what is not decided: whether a boundary walked twice in thirty-one years has been walked, and whether the man who walked it the first time is the man who walked it the second.** It is the correct shape of a thing and not a thing anybody can do anything about, and he has never found a way to make the shape of a thing do anything at all. **Then the discovery, at the board, in the shade, over an afternoon: a stroke takes about a second and four strokes is a good hour and thirty-one years of four strokes a day is a board about the size of a door and a man of sixty-one and a great deal of paint, and that is not a metaphor, it is the whole of the labour.** The same week nine years back reads nine, four, eleven, four, four, thirteen, four; the same week eight years back reads four, four, four, six, four, four, two; **and she can put her thumb on a day of four nine years back and cannot tell you whether it is the same four she is looking at.** **THE FINDING, IN HER OWN MOUTH, AT `258:60`: a quiet day and a day with nine strangers on it are four rings apart, and I have been counting for twenty-five years and nobody has ever asked me which of them it was.** And then the concrete cost, laid out in the order of how sure it is, and it is thought about for about nine years: in the twenty-second year of the board her father walked a boundary, about ninety acres between Coldharrow and Ellerby along a hedge with two elms on it, with four men, of whom two are dead and one is a woman of about sixty in Ellerby who was **twenty-one** and who was asked once, four years ago, on a market day, by a woman of thirty-seven who thought she was entitled to, and who said he did and said where it started and said it was on a day with a name on it that she does not know the names of, and that she was somebody's aunt. **We do not know whether the strip is a boundary.** If it is, about eleven families have been grazing it and paying nothing and using the water off it for nine years and were never told to stop, and they are not thieves, they are eleven families. If it is not, it is ninety acres of common they were told nothing about and their fathers told them nothing, and the man who could have told them is four years dead, **and the only record that they were told anything is a woman of forty-one's hand, and her hand is not a witness, her hand is a count.** The recordwright refuses to write it down and says so **as a thing she has done and not as a thing she has refrained from**, and when he asks what the sentence is for she says it is for the eleven families and the woman of sixty in Ellerby and the four of them at the board and **not for a room, and those are the same eleven families whichever way I write it and I have never in my life found that to be a satisfying answer at four o'clock in the afternoon.** The woman of forty-one says that is the correct answer and that she is not going to get a better one out of her. And the route-man, out of nothing: **that was four, and a week of four is a week you do not talk about, and it is the same rule in every village he has been in in nine counties and nobody could say where it comes from, and he is not going to be the tenth thing that comes up that wall** — and he asks to be asked again at the first bell tomorrow. And the board, at the second light on the first day of the fifty-ninth week, was sixty-three thousand five hundred and fifty-seven, and sixty-three thousand five hundred and sixty-one on the second, and the rings in between were four bells and nothing else at all. **And the next morning it goes up thirteen.**

**259 — A Woman With A Board, Second Time.** Shelf day 134. The thirteen that take the figure from sixty-three thousand five hundred and sixty-one to sixty-three thousand five hundred and seventy-four are four bells and nine more, and the nine are three strangers at each of three gates, and a man with a cartload of timber and two men with a barrow went through together and rang at three because that is what you do. **Sable Venn is in the yard by the fourth hour and about four people know it and about thirty do not, and the man of thirty-one finds out in about nine minutes that she is not a stranger in this country and never was, and that the whole of what he has been doing for a week — standing in a yard waiting to be an outsider long enough to be told something — was the wrong shape for the room he is going to be in.** She gives the device in nine words before he has asked anything, **because he has the face of a man who is about to be polite at her: I put four lines into the March and I did not read them.** A recordwright says out loud that this is a thing she has never said anywhere in nine years, and the woman agrees: no, it is not, and **it is the whole of my standing in this world and I have never had it questioned once in nine years, and I have just questioned it myself standing in a yard to a man of thirty-one, and I would like it noticed that it took nine days and a copy.** What it is: four lines of an order made in a market town called Sallowby about a dam and a height and a day and a party to pay, complete, no hole in any of it, about a valley four hundred miles off, **not about this county, not naming this county, and true.** Mine to carry, not mine to have got hold of, and she says that is the only difference she has ever had and she has been on the wrong side of it about four hundred times. **And the two of them, and it is the volume's engine in about ninety words and neither of them says it: a ruling is a weapon the moment it leaves the place it was measured in, and this is a county where a day is four bells and a height is measured from nothing, and he says that he is the man who is going to be stood in front of a room about this county, and that he has no party and no name on anything, and
