that if there is a document about this county in a room nine days off with his hand nowhere on it, then there is a person they can ask who was here — and that she has built him a box and put him in it and has done it in the only way anybody could, which is by handing him a true thing.** And it is the carter of thirty-eight, at the end of a cart, unasked, who says the true thing: **a thing carried into a country is not a thing anybody in the country can be shown. That is not an opinion, that is what carrying is.** So she has not given this county a door; she has given it a thing it cannot open and a man it will be asked about. Then the woman of forty-one comes down at the last bell, says *no* — the shortest word anybody said that day — and asks for three things and has not got the days for three, because it is a hundred and forty days and she is at about the hundred and sixth: whether the four lines are sealed, what a piece of paper is worth in this county, and who put them in the cart, **and she wants it today and not on the last day, because on the last day she has been the last day for six years and it has never once turned out to be the last day.** The answer: sealed, threepence at Sallowby, five shillings and four days to a man of about fifty-one who buys paper in four counties, and a woman of thirty-three copied it in about four minutes because she is fast and because she asked no questions, which is a thing Sable has relied on four hundred times. And the man of fifty-two saw the satchel at the first bell and did not think anything of it. No panel.

**260 — The Copy Arrives.** Shelf day 135, a burial, the fifth of five. The satchel is under the seat of a timber cart two hundred yards down the lane and the man is asleep with his boots off, and it takes about a minute and a half of standing in a shed door to get him up and to the yard with the bag still on his own arm, and a woman of about forty with a handcart stands at the back and does not come forward, and **it is not that she is hiding.** He puts the satchel on a cart's side because everybody in this country does, and does not open it, and then works backwards through the yard and recognises the board from a market town eight weeks ago, and says there was a gate on it with a river and a boy of about seven who ran off with a dog. **Ottily Roke says it was eight weeks ago and that she has not thought about it once since the following morning, which is a thing he should not tell anybody, and that she has thought about it about four times since the second of this week.** He says he was given five shillings and four days, does not know what it is, was told it was a thing to carry and not a thing to read, and **looks at Sable Venn for about four seconds and says he does not know her, and asks her not to tell him he does not, and she agrees and says she has known for about eight weeks and did not know it until that morning.** **Who will read it out?** He asks it in the way he asks for everything, in every yard and every room and every lane, for about a month, and it is read out, **and nobody in the yard says one word about the asking.** The woman of forty-one reads it, and a boy of seventeen could have read it and did not offer and was not asked, and a woman of twenty-nine did not move and was not asked, and it is worth saying that both of those were choices and not absences and that neither of them made a sound. **THE FOUR LINES, block-quoted, and the second line and the third line are the whole of the volume's engine:** the order of the hundred and fifty-fifth day stands and no person in that basin is to dispute it; the schedule named in it is the schedule named in it and a schedule is not a river and no person is to treat it as a river; **the height named in it is eleven feet and NO SILL IS NAMED IN IT and a height with no sill named in it is a height above whatever the reader is standing on**; the party named in it shall pay at the closing of every year until the matter is reviewed and the review is not appointed. She reads it twice and gives the eleven feet its own beat, because a man with nothing in his hands gave her that habit in a market town four hundred miles off eight weeks ago. **And then the finding of the batch, stated exactly, because a great deal rides on it: nobody said no, and nobody said yes, and nobody put it down, and nobody carried it to a room, and nobody rang a bell about it, and there is no bell in this country anybody could have rung about it, and that is the entire reason nothing happened, and it is not a decision anybody took.** She folds it along the seal and gives the satchel back and it goes under the seat where it has been for four hundred miles. **And then the argument, and it is not what he prepared: not about us, and a careful statement of why, and the second line says a schedule is not a river, and a bell is a schedule, and the four bells of a Coldharrow day are four bells and they happen and they go nowhere, and the first bell is a height above nothing and the last is a height above the first, and nobody in eleven villages has ever said what either is above, and there is not a thing in this country that would tell you.** And the third line is a completely true sentence about a height, printed, nine years old, the rule a bench of four works under, in four hundred and sixty lines of a printed index under a heading — **and a sentence that means a thing four hundred miles away can be true about a man in this yard, and there is no way on this earth to hand it back.** The recordwright corrects the man of thirty-one, who has had it backwards: **it is load-bearing here, and that is the whole of it, and you have had it backwards and I have had it backwards and the woman with the board has had it backwards since the day she copied it — in that valley it was a curiosity, and here it is a sentence about a height, and the only public thing anybody in this county has ever had is a height that is a height above nothing, and a height above nothing is a height above whatever is standing nearest, and what is standing nearest to a bell in a village of two hundred and ten people is two hundred and ten people.** **It is a lever with our names nowhere on it.** And the woman of forty-one says the last thing: no, it is not, she is not going to have it in this village and not on her board, **and she has not written one word of it in chalk and she is not going to, and the last thing he wrote in chalk on anything is a number.** And he says he did not write it, did not want to, and had worked out about four hours earlier that he was not going to, and had not said so out loud, **and that is the only thing he has done in ten days that he would call work.** And the batch ends on a list of what Coldharrow had at the last bell, and a satchel that is going to be under a seat on the day it goes, and a piece of paper about a river that has come into a country where there is no river at a cost of fourpence, **and which nobody in two hundred and ten people has done anything about** — and a man of thirty-eight at the end of a cart asking the last question of the first ten days of this country, in twenty-five words, at the last bell, and he had had them ready for nineteen years, and nobody answered him and he did not appear to want one: **it does not run north to south, it runs from village to village, and I have never found out who laid it out that way.** No panel.

**THE BATCH'S FOUR SPENT DEVICES, AT THE CHAPTER THAT SPENT THEM: a counter with no units in it, `252`; a hand written in chalk at the foot of somebody else's instrument, `251`; a refusal made by a young person against the man who is helping and the young person is right, `254`; and a copy of a document arriving in a place it was not measured in with nobody having read it, `260`. A fifth, a question asked out loud in a yard by a carter, is spent at `260:87` and is the volume's new question in its civic form and is not answered.**

## VOLUME 05 IS CLOSED — the volume-level record for Chapters 201 to 250, *The Red Basin*. **The live block. Everything below it, from `## VOLUME 05 BATCH 0005` down, is archive and is not edited by this phase.** Chapters 1–250 are canon; Volume 04 is closed, audited and repaired; `outline/series.md` outranks `outline/volume-05.md` and this file. **This is a summary and not a re-narration: one paragraph per chapter, the finding each one carries, the money with its working where the chapter has a figure, and nothing advanced that the chapter does not advance. The per-chapter blocks for Batches 0001 to 0005 are below and are not to be copied.**

**The run: Shelf day seventy-one to one hundred and twenty, the second day of the fiftieth week to the second day of the fifty-seventh, which is basin day one hundred and forty-nine to one hundred and ninety-eight since the second shaking, on the formula basin day = Shelf day + 78, both ends checked: 71 + 78 = 149 and 120 + 78 = 198. He is in the valley fifty days and forty-nine nights. Eighteen day-count figures. Three panels. Twelve block-quoted documents. Twelve day-phrases naming a day of seven or less. Two chapters carry a day that the volume's own table does not carry, at 231 and 238, and both are recorded and neither is repaired — see `state/current.md` §1 and §11.**

**Chapter 201 — The Road That Is Not Where It Began.** Shelf day 71, basin day 149. Three people come to the end of a nine-day road and the basin is red and low and has a floor. Tarin Keel measures the road twice, throws the first set away and refuses to say which of three explanations it is; one word, *common*, is defined differently in the margin of each of two deeds and both men were telling the truth; and the chapter ends not on a ruling but on a finding about a room, that nobody in this basin can be in the room when four true pages are read, which is why the plan of four pages was said on a road instead. A man of thirty-one writes a hundred and forty-nine at the head of a page in his own hand, which is the first of eighteen figures of that kind, and the finding of the chapter is that a valley's standing is a room and not a person. *Money: none in this chapter.*

**Chapter 202 — Fifty Saltings, And A Count Nobody Keeps.** Shelf day 72, basin day 150. The salt-pans above Coldbeck, eleven of them, and a man of sixty-one drawing a board through the fourth pan, talking because they came up a bank for water. He says the thing the volume's engine is: the clocks do not convert — a pan-book year is a year and nine is a year, a salting is a drying and has no length, seven weeks in a dry year and eleven in a wet one — and he says it without knowing he has said anything, and the reason he can say it in front of people who could contradict him is that the pans are the only count in the basin that has never been out. A hundred and forty-nine notches on a board, one a day, and a hundred and fifty the day before that is the second day-count figure. *Money: none.*

**Chapter 203 — Two Halves Of One Deed.** Shelf day 73, basin day 151. Sallowby, a room over a chandler's shop, Wenna Skell, thirty-three, who has copied about six hundred and forty deeds in eleven years and about ninety for the Anner, at a penny a page and threepence a sealed copy, and who says the price before the fact because the price before the fact is the only honest part of it. **A deed in this basin is not a paper; it is an agreement between two papers** — the strip is longer than a skin, the two halves were written about eight years apart in two towns four miles apart, and neither man saw the other. Block-quoted documents one and two, the two halves. *Money: a penny a page and threepence a sealed copy, and nothing is added to it.*

**Chapter 204 — The Sluice, And The Half Wage.** Shelf day 74, basin day 152. Hollow Sallow, and the Sallow comes down all at once and not gradually. **Ilma Treen, thirty-eight, eleven years in the job, says the whole of her wage before she is asked anything:** nine shillings a week for the sixteen weeks the water runs and nothing the rest of the year, which is £7 4s, of which four shillings and sixpence is the pit's and four is the seat's, and three years of it unpaid. She has been opening the sluice eleven days early for eleven years to keep nine carts a day off a causeway, and she is the person in this basin who holds the burden and is the worst paid for it. The question nobody had asked her was asked by Tarin Keel in nine words, and not by the man who came nine days for a different thing. *Money: 16 × 108d = 1,728d = £7 4s ✓; the pit's half 16 × 54d = 864d = £3 12s ✓; a hundred and twelve of a hundred and forty days worked and ninety paid is fifty-two unpaid, which is about two years and four months at the same rate ✓.*

**Chapter 205 — A Bond Keeps A Thing True By Costing Somebody Money.** Shelf day 75, basin day 153. The water-seat's one room over a shuttered shop, eleven seats of which eight have never had anybody in them, a table down the middle of it and a press in the wall. **Hollis Nance, forty-four, says in his first nine words that he is not a Bench clerk, not a recordwright and not an advocate, and that the price of taking a paper to Orison and bringing it back is five pounds and six.** A dead man named in the bond, his widow, and a penalty of forty pounds that stopped being paid in the fourth year while the thing the bond was holding up went on being true, and nobody noticed for three years, because a thing that keeps being true does not announce itself. Block-quoted document three, the bond. *Money: 240d + 960d + 72d = 1,272d = £5 6s ✓; the penalty of forty pounds and the forty pounds unpaid ✓.*

**Chapter 206 — The Eleven Houses.** Shelf day 76, the last day of the fiftieth week, basin day 154. Eleven roofs on a lane four hundred yards below the sluice, a mark cut on each doorpost about the height of a man's shoulder, cut in one day in a year when the Sallow came up nine feet in a night by a man of seventy-four with a stick and a string and a bucket of tar. **The eleven houses are not a category**, and the reason nobody has asked them is that asking eleven people costs three days and three days is not a figure. **A height is a height above something:** there are three sills inside four miles and the same figure means two different things in two rooms, which is the first appearance of the volume's whole arithmetic. The first price for anything in this basin is said out loud here, in front of a person who was not going to buy it, and the district of Ryefold is named once as four hundred and eighty-five pounds a year in the hole in a county this village has never heard of. *Money: four pounds ten and one pound eight on a lath in chalk, and the Anner's sixty tons at seven pounds a ton is four hundred and twenty pounds a year, which is five and seven-tenths in the hundred of the trade ✓.*

**Chapter 207 — The Four Pages.** Shelf day 77, the first day of the fifty-first week, basin day 155. Nine people in the Seat's one room, four more than have ever been in it, none sent for. Hollis Nance says the order is his hand and not a clerk's before anybody has said anything. **The quick ruling is four lines and all four are complete and there is no hole in any of them, and he says so out loud before anybody else has worked it out, and nobody notices.** The order names a dam, a height, a day and a party to pay, and it names nobody else, and the party it names is the only body in the basin with enough men to hold a dam, and it does not name the person who will hold the height on the night the water comes, because there is no such person. **Panel one, at `207:67`–`68`,** and it is the panel's subject and not a rule anybody in this basin has ever heard of. Block-quoted document four, the order. Day-count instance four, a hundred and fifty-five. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 208 — Three Rulings And A Column Head.** Shelf day 78, basin day 156. A rider's bag comes to Sallowby on the morning the four pages went on the wall, addressed to the Bench of Orison **at** the water-seat of Sallowby, in that order, which is not an address, and nobody opens it. **A record can be perfectly kept and still be wrong about a place**, and the reason is on the head of the abstract, where the referral is signed by a man who is not of this basin. Three rulings of the chamber in nine years, consistent with each other and not with this valley, and the second of them says a height marked on a doorpost is not a measurement and no order may name a height without naming the sill, which is nine years old, was never in this basin, and the four pages break. A column heading of two words sits in a stranger's eye at the back of the Seat's own hand-book. A letter from a clerk of thirty-four about a fourth hand is in the bundle and nobody opens it and the chapter says so out loud. Block-quoted document five. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 209 — A Trench Taken Out In A Straight Line.** Shelf day 79, basin day 157. Anner Pit, the under-manager's office, the chain-book about nine hundred pages in a hand nobody in the valley can read, and a woman of twenty-six who has been in the oldest workings since she was seventeen and who was not asked to be anywhere. **The first missing anchor position is identified by two ordinary records that do not meet:** a take-out of eleven chains and sixteen links taken in a straight line and not sunk in a pit, six cuts in a floor, and a drain aimed along that line. **Four hundred and six feet is the pit and is not the void, and under the low end there is a void of depth not yet found.** **Nobody goes down**, and the reason he gives is not the water and not the steps, and he tells nobody what the reason is. The System puts nothing up and says nothing whatever about it. Block-quoted document six, the fourth turn of the tithe book. *Money: a pound and four for eleven days and he did not find a void in it ✓.*

**Chapter 210 — A Person Doing Their Work.** Shelf day 80, basin day 158. Four days after the four pages went on the wall: the causeway shut, nine carts a day on the high road, the dam dressed with forty loads of clay and a hundred and forty of rubble in about four days by four men and a barrow, and three pounds and five of the Anner's money gone on clay in a month. The order stands, the mine is stable, the eleven houses are dry and nobody goes down. **And the new question is written down once, in his own hand, in a penny exercise book in a cart shed, with a place and a form of words, and he does not ask, and the sentence breaks off in the middle.** A woman who maps a country without asking anybody is named once in a mouth by a man who has not met her, and one person in the room repeats the name wrong. The chapter's title is its finding and it is a person doing their work. *Money: three pounds five of clay, forty loads and a hundred and forty of rubble ✓.*

**Chapter 211 — The Slow Is Down.** Shelf day 81, basin day 159. The causeway at Hollow Sallow is a hundred and forty years old and stood dry for the first time since the second shaking, and a carter of about forty is standing on it with a crowbar. **A girl of seventeen, who has been in that lane since she was born, reads a four-line order out to a lane and asks the first question anybody in the Red Basin has ever asked about a document.** The order breaches the chamber's own second ruling on its face, and the under-manager says it is not void and he is right. A second matter goes to Orison in a bag with a knot cut with a knife, dated on the outside with a day out of the water-book, because the Shelf's grain year does not exist in this basin and a deed that arrives with one on it is a different kind of arrival. Day-count instance six. *Money: the second matter is the five pounds and six of `205:7`, paid out of a man's own pocket ✓.*

**Chapter 212 — The Standing Order Nobody Has Read.** Shelf day 82, basin day 160. The frame at Hollow Sallow is oak and has been in the same place since before the first shaking, and behind the gate in it there is a second frame, newer, that came at the same time and does nothing at all. **The standing order of the sluice names a weather and not a day** — *the day the pans are turned at Coldbeck* — and it is the eleventh salting of the forty-ninth year while the bond is the eleventh salting of the fortieth, which is the same salting nine years along, so the order is legal and arrives on the wrong day every time. And the turn is in a book and not in anybody's mouth: the sluice was shut and the water was in the hollow and nobody came, written by the woman who keeps the sluice three weeks and a day before it happened, every year, and nobody has ever asked her how she knows. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 213 — The Last Day Of The Fifty-First Week.** Shelf day 83, basin day 161. The water is against the ninth doorpost at the second light and about two feet in the lane, and about nine people are on the bank, which is four more than had ever been there at once. **A height put on two doorposts by the same water is a foot above one old mark and a foot below the other, so the two old marks are two feet apart**, and a joiner of forty-one has had his own shoulder against both of them for nine years. **The lane asks what the number is a number of, out loud, on a bank, and it is the first question anybody in that village has ever asked about a document.** Day-count instance seven, a hundred and sixty-one, said out of the water-book by a man of thirty-four. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 214 — Asking Eleven People.** Shelf day 84, basin day 162. The Seat's one room has a table with nine things on it and **no form in this basin for any of them**: a sheet, a second sheet, a stub of lead, twine, a pot of tar with a brush, a rule, the water-book, a sheet with the chamber's second ruling on it. **Asking eleven people costs three days and three days is not a figure**, and the person who keeps the sluice has not been in the Seat's room in eleven years. A clerk of a seat reads a four-line order out in a lane he has no authority to read it in, on eleven chairs carried down a hill by nine people, and nobody signs anything. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 215 — Eleven Feet, Held Exactly.** Shelf day 85, basin day 163. Four men and a barrow on the Anner dam. **The height is held exactly and on purpose** — eleven feet and an inch at the low end and ten feet and eleven inches at the high end, with a string and a barrow and most of a morning, because the paper says so. **A thing that is void and unread is not a protection, it is an absence**, in the under-manager's own mouth, in ochre dust. And nine words in the same mouth, in ochre dust: *I have been given a number and never a reason.* He is right, and a thing held exactly is a thing held to a figure, and a figure is not a decision. **The Anner is the only body in this basin with men enough to hold a dam, and a man with men enough to hold a dam is not looking at eleven houses, and that is the arithmetic and not a fault.** *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 216 — The Night.** Shelf day 86, basin day 164. **THE MIDPOINT, PART ONE.** Four men and a barrow and a string on the dam at the second light, and there have been four men on that dam in the working years of every year since the bond was lodged. The height is held exactly, as instructed, lawfully, by the only body with enough men, and four men and a barrow do what the paper says, because that is the whole of what anybody has ever asked them to do. **The arithmetic of it is one subtraction and it is printed where a reader can do it in their head: the frame's sill is nine feet above the Anner's sill, so eleven feet above the Anner's sill is two feet above the frame's sill.** **Nobody drowned, and that is not a mitigation and is not written as one.** Day-count instance eight. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 217 — Nineteen Houses.** Shelf day 87, basin day 165. **THE MIDPOINT, PART TWO.** They count it at the first light and the people who count it are the people who live in it, on foot, because there is nowhere in Hollow Sallow a cart can go that the Anner's carts could not have gone on the causeway nine days ago. **Nineteen houses and not eleven**, about a hundred and forty people, and the eleven were right about the eleven and the eight are a barn that became a house and seven others, and the man who turned the barn into a house cut no mark because nobody asked him for one. **Nobody in this valley is a villain, and it is said plainly: the bond's promise is its first two sentences and the promise was kept exactly by the party it names**, and a woman who is not a lawyer says nine words — *it named a dam, it named a height, it named a day, it never named the water*. **Panel two, at `217:35`–`36`.** *Money: a roof wet through is £9 and not broken into parts, and nineteen of them is £171 exactly ✓.*

**Chapter 218 — The Person The Order Did Not Name.** Shelf day 88, basin day 166. **THE MIDPOINT, PART THREE.** The Sallow turned in the night and is falling about a foot a day, and there are nine people in the Seat's one room, four of them there on the day the four pages went on the wall. **A rule that names no bystander is carried by whoever is nearest with hands on it** — said by the man of thirty-one in his own mouth, and it is not the sentence he said once and he does not say it again and he does not explain it and nobody asks him to. **The four pages stay on the wall**, and the person who says why is a woman of about forty who washes the pen: a basin with no document on a wall has nothing for the next person to argue with. **And his name is not on the four pages and never was, and the space at the foot is neither filled nor dashed.** *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 219 — What Is Under, In Money.** Shelf day 89, basin day 167. There is no word in this basin for what a man does when his house is under water, and no book that could be opened and no office nine days off that does this. **The money is not the difficulty, and the chapter proves it by asking the wrong question on purpose: not one of nineteen answers about nineteen houses is money.** **The list of nineteen is a document and it is the first document anybody in this basin has ever written about itself** — the back of a leaf of the hundred-year-old water-book, with a mark under every answer and not one address. *Money: the nineteen answers, none of them money, and the wage that keeps coming whatever the water does ✓.*

**Chapter 220 — A Person Doing Their Work.** Shelf day 90, the last day of the fifty-second week, basin day 168. **The water is down and the mud is not**, and the chapter is careful about the difference: the water goes down a bed that has a shape in it and the mud does not, and there is a crust on the top of it and mud underneath the crust and three inches of it. **The second matter came back in nine days as a letter of two paragraphs from a clerk of the chamber who did his job properly**, saying the bench is seized of the matter and will consider it in its own time and giving no time. **He reads the Shelf side of his own book out loud on a bank to nine people and stops at the tenth item and says he is not going to say it, and nobody asks him which year it was, and he is not relieved of the not being asked.** The chapter ends on a gate at the closing of the water and a chair put back at a table, and neither is a ruling. Day-count instance nine. *Money: 1,272d = £5 6s, the same matter, twice priced, and it does not stop ✓.*

**Chapter 221 — The Order The Nineteen Gave.** Shelf day 91, basin day 168+1 = 169. **A list of what nineteen people need is not a list of work**, and it took a morning, and eighteen of the nineteen answers cannot be bought and the one that can is a roof, and the order of the work is bed, boards, salt, and then the roof. **A man may put a day on his own act and may not put one on another person's speech**, in his own hand, as the second line under the eleventh day-count of his exercise book. And the Shelf half of that book is not opened, and the new question is not raised, and nothing this chapter carries from the other side of the book is carried. Day-count instance ten. *Money: nine pounds a roof and the roof is second, because a wet roof over a wet floor is a wet floor ✓.*

**Chapter 222 — Nobody Names A House.** Shelf day 92, basin day 170. The question is whether the settlement names the nineteen houses, and there are two doors in the lane with no mark on either — one a house that was a barn in the year the marks were cut and one a house whose door was replaced in the winter before the water came. **A list of houses is a list of people, and the day there is a list of people the next house is a house that is not on the list.** **A list of answers with no addresses on it is nineteen opinions, and a list with addresses on it can be argued against the wrong door in a person's own front door**, and that was found at the ninth door of a walk that took four hours. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 223 — What The Anner Can Pay.** Shelf day 93, basin day 171. **Let it all be the Anner**, in about six minutes, by a man who had been waiting six days for somebody to come up the hill and ask him a question about money. **And what the Anner can pay is nothing: £178 13s 4d out of the £7,700 a year that is the whole of what has been argued about in this basin is two and three-tenths in the hundred.** The figures are his own and all of them are true. *Money: 19 × 2,160d + 1,728d + 112d = 42,880d = £178 13s 4s ✓; 1,100 tons at £7 a ton at the market = £7,700 ✓; 42,880d × 100 ÷ 1,848,000d = 2.32% ✓.*

**Chapter 224 — The Wage That Comes Every Week.** Shelf day 94, basin day 172. The three years owed to a woman of thirty-eight are paid in one week, in an envelope, at the closing of the water, and she counts it twice on her own sill and says it is the first money anybody in that lane has handed her in eleven years and she is not going to say thank you in the road. **It is not the four and six: the Seat did not fail to pay her, because nobody promised her the other four and six.** And **the first money in this basin ever paid anybody for looking at water is nine shillings and fourpence a year**, named by the girl of seventeen who keeps the second hand, who said it twice and had it checked on the page. **A book of a river kept by four people who have not stood at the frame keeps what they were told**, and on the night the water came the mill hand and the Seat's hand disagree about that frame by about two hours and both are right. *Money: 16 × 108d = 1,728d = £7 4s ✓; the second hand 16 × 7d = 112d = 9s 4d ✓; 3 × 864d = 2,592d = £10 16s ✓.*

**Chapter 225 — A Man Who Lost A House Is Not A House.** Shelf day 95, basin day 173. **Nobody asked Coll Ferren anything for eight days after the counting — 173 − 165 = 8, and the chapter prints the subtraction —** and the reason is that there is no form in this basin for standing in a doorway. The under-manager asks the wrong question in a lane, wanting a list of nineteen doors and numbers so that nobody could be left out, and it is the wrong question. **A paper with a man's name on it is read out in a year when he is gone**, in eighteen words at the bottom of a lane, and it is the reason the name came out, and he said they were right and did not put it back, and the space at the foot is empty and not dashed. Day-count instance eleven. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 226 — What He Drafted.** Shelf day 96, basin day 174. **His version, block-quoted, document seven: seven lines, a struck first line left on the paper, and three words under a name at the foot.** Five objections, in order, and every one made by a person the draft names or does not name, and not one by a man from four hundred miles off. A scrivener of thirty-three who copied it for nothing asked that a struck line not be left on a piece of paper. The under-manager asked for the word *asked* — not that the Anner shall pay again, asked — and wanted it read out four times and his own hand on that line and not a clerk's, and wrote it in ochre dust. **And the woman of about forty said, in nine words, that if he put a name at the foot of that paper it was a paper about a man from four hundred miles off**, and he agreed with her before she had finished. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 227 — Six Lines, And Eleven Hands.** Shelf day 97, basin day 175. **THE BATCH'S MIDPOINT: the remedy is rewritten in eleven hands that are not his and he is not one of them**, and the eleven hours were not in a room, and the eleven people were asked one at a time in eleven places, and four of them who could be found together did not sign in front of each other. **There are eleven hands on that sheet and it is not the eleven houses and it is not the eleven marks and it is not the eleven feet and it is not the eleven seats in this room and it is not the eleven men at the pit.** The part of the sheet nobody will agree on is the part that cannot be carried by anybody. **Panel three, at `227:53`–`54`,** and its subject is the finding and not a rule. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 228 — The Sheet In The Lane.** Shelf day 98, basin day 176. **Their version, block-quoted, document eight: six lines, one hand, and three hands on a struck line that do not agree,** printed on the face of the paper because a clerk of forty-four wrote a sentence about it at somebody else's request. About forty people in the lane at the closing of the water, because nobody in Hollow Sallow has ever had a paper read out in it. **The order's fourth line has said since the hundred and fifty-fifth day that a copy is to be kept in the lane by a person of the lane, and nobody had ever asked what happens to a copy that is kept by a man who cannot read it.** And he put in *and every week*, after nine shillings a week, and said before he said it that six people had argued for two days about four and six and had never once written down the half of the argument. *Money: 16 × 108d = 1,728d ✓; the second hand 112d ✓.*

**Chapter 229 — What The First Year Costs.** Shelf day 99, basin day 177. The first roof comes off the second house from the bottom, the one with the door on its hinge, in about four days, four days longer than a roof on dry ground, and the man of fifty-six does not price that and is not asked to. The timber goes up on the backs of about eleven people over two days. **The settlement costs more than the flood**, and the excess is a hair under one part in eight of the whole thing and is not roofs. **And nobody carried it to Orison**, and a clerk of forty-four put it in about eleven words: the bench is seized of the matter already and would come back with two paragraphs. *Money: 19 × 2,160d = 41,040d; + 1,728d + 112d = 42,880d = £178 13s 4s ✓; the gate 1,080d + 336d = 1,416d = £5 18s ✓; the arrears 2,592d ✓; the first year 42,880 + 1,416 + 2,592 = 46,888d = £195 7s 4s ✓.*

**Chapter 230 — What The Sheet Does Not Say.** Shelf day 100, basin day 178. A gate of five pounds eighteen hung in one day by two men, one of them on ten shillings a week, on his own time, telling nobody, not thanked. The oak came up on a cart and about nine people carried the rest, and a joiner of forty-one who measured that frame in the fourth year after the marks were cut watches a thing he has charged for three times go past him. **And the whole of what the sheet does not say is a height** — eleven feet above the Anner's own sill is the number that put two feet of water into nineteen houses, and it is on a wall, in a bond, in a chain-book and in about nine heads, and it is not on the paper, **and he did not put it in because a recordwright said nine words and was right, and because he is not a party, and because there is no form in this basin for a man with nothing in his hands to have a paper in front of him.** The chapter ends on a gate, a chair and a lath gone in a cart shed. Day-count instance twelve. *Money: 1,416d = £5 18s ✓.*

**Chapter 231 — The Copy In The Lane.** Shelf day 101 as the volume's table has it, **and the chapter says the first day of the fifty-fourth week at `231:3` and `231:7`, which is a conflict and is recorded and not repaired.** The second roof comes off the third house from the bottom of the lane in about four days at nine pounds the man will not split, and eighteen roofs are wanted. **A document in this valley is used rather than observed**, for the first time in this volume, and the use is that a man of thirty-four cannot read the copy he keeps and reads it out at the closing of the water because it is the only thing he can do with it. **It is not a ceremony; it is a promise about a day is what everybody thought it was.** **A paper kept in a lane by a man who cannot read it has no second copy**, said by a woman of thirty-eight in a road four miles up a hill, and she named the reader's own nine words. *Money: 2,160d × 19 = 41,040d ✓; a gate 1,416d ✓.*

**Chapter 232 — A Road That Does Not Go Through Orison.** Shelf day 102, basin day 180. Market day at Sallowby. **The tradesmen of the basin price a route that does not go through Orison**, named once in a cart yard and not followed, and the chapter says out loud that the money behind it is more than the whole of the trade. **There is no gate on it**, and every trade in this basin has carried salt and ochre past the gate at the top of the pass for eleven years and not one of them has ever asked what is at the other end of it. **And the first person in this volume says out loud that the water-seat is the reason there is a seat and not the other way round**, in a cart yard, in the mouth of a woman of thirty-three who copies deeds for a penny a page. *Money: nine carts a day, about a hundred and forty days a year, a morning and a half each way, and the Anner bears the whole of it ✓.*

**Chapter 233 — The Word That Means Not Sent.** Shelf day 103, basin day 181. The man with the bag comes up the high road the way he does, twice in the year, and a clerk of forty-four weighs it in the hand and says the same sentence he has said twice before about having no authority to open it, and the sentence has not got any shorter, and being in a hurry is what he has instead. **Block-quoted document nine, the back of the last page of the Seat's own hand-book: a printed heading of two words, about four hundred and sixty entries, one rule ruled under all four, and under the fourth four lines.** All four are about this basin. **The reason the hand-copy is empty and the original is not is the volume's own method and not a conspiracy: a hand-copy of what was sent has nothing to copy, and the material under a column headed *not sent* is exactly what does not get copied.** **Thirty-two papers went nine days up a road and did not come back and nobody in this valley has ever been told.** **Nobody asks**, and the chapter lists the five people in that room who could have asked and did not, by name and by reason, and the fifth is a man of thirty-one who could have opened it and did not. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 234 — Nobody Asks.** Shelf day 104, the last day of the fifty-fourth week, basin day 182. The four lines come out into about four hundred and ten people over three days in the ordinary way, one at a time, in four different mouths, and the first is said by a woman of thirty-eight at her own gate. **The basin's answer to a record that was not sent to it is to go on doing the work**, and that is neither indifference nor heroism, and it is the plainest thing about this valley in about a month. **And the first person of the Red Basin to ask the man of thirty-one a direct question about a thing he is carrying** is a man of fifty-six with a ladder on his shoulder, and the answer is nine words, and it is true and it is not a form of words and it is not help, and then nine words of his own: *a roof does not care and neither do I.* *Money: 2,160d × 19 = 41,040d = £171 exactly ✓; a gate 1,416d ✓; the matter 1,272d = £5 6s ✓.*

**Chapter 235 — A Record Perfectly Kept.** Shelf day 105, basin day 183. The second thing in the bag comes out of the bag because the bag was on a shelf and a clerk went to put the sheets in a drawer; it was at the bottom under nine printed sheets and the man with the bag did not point at it, and a man with a bag who points at a thing in his own bag is a man who has been asked to. It is two paragraphs and it is consistent with itself. **A record can be perfectly kept and still be wrong about a place**, and the reason is that nobody who kept it was ever in it, and the first time this volume said it a man of thirty-one said it about a building and the second time a man of fifty-two says it about four people standing in a room. **And the only figure anybody anywhere has ever written down about what this valley trades** — one thousand and forty tons, written four years ago four hundred miles off by a man who has never been in the Red Basin. **A mine is now a body with a standing interest in a number**, and the under-manager said *not the height* twice before anybody could get it wrong. **And there is now nowhere in this basin to put a number a person wrote themselves**, and a girl of seventeen found it, in her own hand, off a frame at the closing of the water. **Chapter 236 — A Good Name, Four Hundred Miles Off.** Shelf day 106, basin day 184. **Nine people in a valley of four hundred and ten are afraid of a bench of four they have never met**, and four of them said so in four places in one day in four different voices and none of the four would use the word. **Being afraid is not a matter**, said a clerk of forty-four, who has looked for a place to enter nine people being frightened of a bench and there is not one in this basin. **Their good name is public and it is free** — nine words from an under-manager of fifty-two at the end of a day he was not asked for — and being right is the whole of the danger. And the Anner's standing interest in eleven feet stops being an arithmetic fact and becomes a thing a man of fifty-two has to think about at about four in the morning, in a house at the top of a hill and not in the chain-book. *Money: 1,272d = £5 6s, the same matter, a third time ✓.*

**Chapter 237 — Named Twice, At A Distance.** Shelf day 107, basin day 185. A name is said in a kitchen in Sallowby by a woman of about fifty-four making bread, who has had it for two years and never had a use for it, and the woman came through the north before the water with a board, asked for nothing, took a loaf and did not pay for it, and gave her name when asked, which is more than most of them do. **A name travels four miles in about two years on about four mouths and nobody in this valley spent nine days carrying it and nobody was paid anything for it and nobody put it in a book.** And the column point was made a month ago and is not being made again; what is new is only that the name has started to move on its own, and nobody went looking for her. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 240 — Shut, And Going To Be Opened.** Shelf day 110, basin day 188. **The column is shut**, and the whole of what has happened about it in ten days is that about thirty people in this basin know a page exists four hundred miles off with four lines in it that are all about this valley's water, and nobody has asked for it, nobody has opened it, nobody has been asked about it, and no person in this basin has asked him when he is going to. **And nobody went down**, and the position is where it was identified in the fifty-first week. **The System put nothing up and said nothing whatever about any of it**, and a man of thirty-one has stopped expecting it to and did not tell anybody that he had stopped. **And a clerk of forty-four says to a shelf that somebody is going to open that column and it is not going to be me**, and nobody answered it and nobody was asked. **Chapter 241 — What Four Hundred And Ten People Do With A Thing.** Shelf day 111, basin day 189. Seven days after a printed page came down in a bag, about thirty people know there is a record about their water that was not sent to them, and the other three hundred and eighty have not asked anybody about it. **The valley's answer is to go on doing the work**, and the chapter's whole job is to say that without pretending to know which. **The first thing a valley does with a withheld record is to try to get at it the cheap way, which is to ask somebody who has been there, and nobody in this basin has been there.** And the question is not *how do we get it* and is *what would we do with it if we had it*, said out loud on a bank by a woman of about thirty-one with a house at the ninth door, and the woman of about forty who washes the pen called it the most expensive thing anybody has said in this valley in a month, and the clerk of the Seat wrote nothing down. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 243 — Sixty Tons Is Two Counts.** Shelf day 113, basin day 191. **The sixty tons is probably not sixty tons of anything and is a difference between two people's arithmetic**, in nine words from a man who has counted carts on roads for nineteen years, and he says the second half of it too: a figure four years old cannot be put against a memory of nineteen years by anybody in this valley. **And it is the first time in about a month that a number in this valley has got smaller rather than larger**, and nobody thanked anybody for it. **A man of sixty-one who has kept a count of every salting in this basin for thirty years has never once been asked what comes up off a road**, and nobody in this valley has written down a single load coming in, and therefore the sixty tons is a hole in a record and not a hole in a wall. *Money: 60 × £7 = £420 a year = 100,800d, and 100,800 × 100 ÷ 1,747,200 = 5.77, five and seven-tenths in the hundred ✓; 60 × 20 = 1,200 cwt and £1 4s = 288d and 1,200 × 288d = 345,600d = £1,440 ✓.*

**Chapter 244 — Who May Speak For Four Hundred And Ten People.** Shelf day 114, basin day 192. A basin of four hundred and ten people is to be represented and there is no form for the question. The room has a man of thirty-one with no standing who has said so out loud in four rooms and been right; a man of fifty-two who is a party because he is paying; a man of thirty-four who cannot read the paper; and about nine frightened people. **The standing of a valley is not in a person but in a document**, and the only document in this valley anybody is on is a settlement of work and days, and it can be ended tonight by eleven people saying one sentence in a road at the closing of the water, and nothing whatever can be done to them for saying it. **A frightened valley does not send anybody.** **A woman of about forty refused this basin a third time and was right a third time and was asked about a different thing, which was herself.** And **a paper nobody is on cannot be asked anybody anything**, said by a man of thirty-four who cannot read the paper it is about, and the copy has no person on it and neither has the original. *Money: none new.*

**Chapter 245 — He Opens It.** Shelf day 115, basin day 193. **THE CLIMAX, AND IT IS NOT A FIGHT AND NOT A RESCUE.** A man of thirty-one opens a rider's bag on a table in the Seat's one room, with no authority, out loud, in front of about nine people, and nobody had asked him and nobody is asked. He says out loud that he has no authority, that the bag is addressed to a body that has no seat, that he is not its clerk and not an advocate and not a person of this district, and that the sentence has not got any shorter and he is not going to shorten it today. **What makes it a choice and not an accident is that he could have gone up the hill and nobody in four hundred and ten would ever have found out**, and what he had instead was nothing whatever: no money that is his, no party, no form, no line with his name on it, and a good name belonging to four people four hundred miles off which is a public thing and is free. **He could have said the sentence that splits the thirty in a building from the four in a room and he did not, and he says so out loud in his own words**, and the reason is that the sentence that separates them is the sentence that protects the institution. **Block-quoted document ten, the chamber's own printed index, the original, opened flat on a table nine feet by fourteen and held open at the back page by one finger: a printed heading of two words, about four hundred and sixty entries, one rule under all four, and under the fourth four lines and no more.** All four are about this basin and one of them is the printed rule the chamber worked under for nine years and that this basin has had on a wall since before the water. **Nobody has hidden anything** is said out loud in the room by a clerk of forty-four and it costs him something this time. **Nobody thanked him and nobody was relieved.** A page went up on a wall at a penny. Day-count instance sixteen. *Money: a penny for the copy out of the press, corrected from four pence before delivery ✓.*

**Chapter 246 — A Woman With A Board.** Shelf day 116, basin day 194. **Sable Venn arrives on foot from the north with a board under her arm**, and the clerk of the Seat recognises her from a name that has been in four mouths in this valley for two years with no document under it. **She refuses the sheet on the wall before anybody offers it**, and says she does not read other people's records and that that is why nobody has ever been able to use her. **Her alternative is good and it is better than the thing this valley has**, and the proof that it is good is that she left the dam's height wrong on the board on purpose and said so before anybody asked her, and about four people in that room understood what she had just done and one of the four was a man of fifty-two. **And it is also genuinely worse for a person who needs a rule enforced against somebody**, and the person it is true about said so herself, at her own gate, before she was asked, and gave the working, and would like it written that she said that first. **He could not prove her wrong, only incomplete**, and the incompleteness was named by an ordinary person in the room and not by him: a rule-free valley cannot be given anything, and the honest name for that is a person who is not in the instruments. **And he had the standing to say the sentence he learned once in a room in another county and did not say it**, and the reason is printed and it is not a rule: it would be cheaper the second time than the first and it would be worth about half. **She did not win and she did not lose**, the room kept the paper, the paper is not hers and she is not on it. *Money: 16 × 54d = 864d = £3 12s a year, the pit's half of the wage, which is what she was talking about ✓.*

**Chapter 247 — What The Water Did At A Frame In A Year Nobody Was Watching.** Shelf day 117, basin day 195. The first of the four lines came the last four miles and got itself said out loud in a lane, and it is the only one of the four anybody had ever been in the same street with, and a man of thirty-four says first that he cannot read a word of it, and there is no other reason and no clerk came with it. **The figure in the return is two feet four inches above the sill of the frame**, and in inches it is 108 less 28, which is 80, which is six feet eight inches below the sill of the Anner's own dam, and the two numbers are both true and are not the same number of feet, and the chamber's own second ruling says no order may name a height without naming the sill it is taken from, and a man of thirty-four arrived at that in a road in about four minutes. **A figure at a frame is of a river and not a height, and a height is a thing you decide to be above**, and a valley which has spent a month arguing about a height had never once been told what the water does — and a woman of thirty-eight put a rule to a dark line on the north post of a frame in her own hand and wrote the day over it in chalk and **did not write the eleventh year.** Day-count instance seventeen. *Money: none new, and the arithmetic is in inches: 108 + 28 = 136in = 11ft 4in, which is four inches above the bond's line ✓.*

**Chapter 248 — What The Four People Who Keep The Record Say About This Valley.** Shelf day 118, basin day 196. **Nothing came back from the chamber and nothing can**, and the reason was said out loud: a man with a bag comes twice in the year, and the first paper went into the gap on the first day of this week and nine days is nine days in the wrong of the year. **The four people who keep this valley's record read nine years of it out loud to each other in an hour**, and there is no column anywhere in any of it for what this valley trades, and two of the four have been down the lane and two have not and the two who have not are the two who keep the numbers. **And the Anner's standing interest in a number is settled in public and it costs the mine something**, and the something is not six shillings and eightpence a year: it is the right to stand in a room in a year's time and say the chamber got this valley wrong, and the mine gave that up on purpose, out loud, and would like it written that it gave it up and not that it was taken. **And the chamber's rule comes down the last four miles and is the rule this basin has had on a wall in its own words since before the water**, and it is a reason for thirty-two papers. *Money: a pitman's week is 120d, 120 ÷ 6 = 20d, four of them = 80d = 6s 8d, and 80 × 100 ÷ 6,000 = one and a third in the hundred of a pitman's paid year ✓.*

**Chapter 249 — A Paper That Says In Its Own First Line That It Can Be Ended.** Shelf day 119, basin day 197. **THE RESOLUTION, PART ONE, AND NOBODY DRAFTED IT IN A ROOM.** Eleven people said one sentence each in their own houses, a scrivener wrote down what was said in her own hand, the clerk copied it out fair and put it on the wall, and there is not a clause in it that anybody in a room improved. **A revocable local charter, one sheet, one hand, with no name on it and no dash on it**, which says in its own first line that it can be ended, and that any person of the valley may go from it at any time and shall lose nothing by going but the charter, and that it is reviewed at the closing of the water one year after the day written at the head of the page in the water-book for that day, by any person of the valley who brings it. **And the eleven feet goes into a third document in three copies in three places, both sills named, the difference of four feet written down in it, on the strength of the chamber's own second ruling, and it does NOT go on the settlement** — and the reason is not a secret: the settlement is eleven people's and the height is the one thing about it that eleven people do not agree on, and there are three hands on a struck line under it and they do not agree. **A bad answer in three copies can be argued with by three people and a good answer in one can be argued with by nobody**, said by a joiner with a rule who has spent nine years trying to get somebody to measure a line of chalk on a doorpost. **And the figure the charter cannot hold is the wage**, said in a lane by a woman of thirty-eight and not written down by anybody. **And about nine people in this valley were afraid of a good name and are not afraid of that good name any more**, not because anybody was made safe. Block-quoted documents eleven and twelve. *Money: a roof wet through is 2,160d and nineteen of them is 41,040d = £171 exactly ✓; the whole wage 1,728d; the second hand 112d; 42,880 − 41,040 = 1,840d = £7 13s 4d ✓; the third document 1d + 1d + 3d = 5d ✓; 60 tons × £7 = £420 = 100,800d, and 100,800 × 100 ÷ 1,848,000d = 2.35, two and a third times the settlement ✓.*

**Chapter 250 — An Exit Review, And A Position Nobody Stood In Front Of.** Shelf day 120, the second and last day of the fifty-seventh week, basin day 198. **It does not end with anything, and the not-ending is the point.** The exit review has a date on it: the closing of the water, one year after the day written at the head of the page in the water-book for that day, by any person of this valley who brings it. The settlement stands with no name at the foot of it and no height in it. The third document is in three places. The four pages are on the wall. The column is open and the good name that paid for it is spent. The mine is a mine, bound in advance to a figure of a thousand and forty tons written down in a city four years ago by a man who has never been in the valley. **And the position beneath this basin is a bearing, a depth and a page number, and it has not moved**; four hundred and six feet is the pit and is not the void; the way down is a chamber with water in it; the last hundred and forty feet of the water at the low end of the pit has been under to the roof since before a woman of twenty-six was seventeen, and her name is Alo Vearn and she does not know that a sentence about her is in a book six miles off that nobody has ever been in this basin to write. **Nobody went down**, and that is the plainest sentence anybody said that week and nobody answered it. **He put down nothing under the day** — the eighteenth figure of that kind, in his own hand, and there has not been an answer under any figure in that book. **The leg is used once, in that same passage, as a fact about a wall and not a discovery.** And the other half of his book was not opened. **The volume ends on four ordinary things and none of them is a ruling:** a gate opened at the closing of the water, a chair put back against a table leg, a barrow put down a bank, and four men and a barrow at a dam at the second light. Day-count instance eighteen, and it is the last. *Money: 9,700 × 12d = 116,400d = £485 ✓; the second notice of 5s 4d unpaid, 4 × 16d = 64d ✓; the claim of £45 2s 8d not producible, 406 × 32d − 2,160d = 10,832d ✓; the ninety-one numbered sheets; about nine hundred doors; the box of about nine hundred and forty forms; the minute of the first of the forty-eighth week; and a dead man in the fourth line of a list of two hundred and forty and his wife — all named once, in one paragraph, and none of them advanced.*
