### Chapter 241 — What Four Hundred And Ten People Do With A Thing
**Shelf day 111, the seventh and last day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 189.**
Seven days after a printed page came down in a bag, about thirty people in a valley of four hundred and ten know there is a record about their water that was not sent to them, and the other three hundred and eighty have not asked anybody about it. **The basin's answer is to go on doing the work, and the chapter's whole job is to say that without pretending to know whether it is a decision or a habit, and the honest answer is both.** The gate opened at the closing of the water; a girl of seventeen was paid a penny in a jar and wrote a day at the top of a fresh page; the sixth roof came off the sixth house from the bottom of the lane; forty loads of clay went on at the dam. **Then the trying, which took seven days and went badly: the first thing a valley does with a withheld record is try to get at it the cheap way, which is to ask somebody who has been there, and nobody in this basin has been there, and that was established in a cart yard in about four minutes by a man of about forty-two who has been to Orison four times in thirty years on a chandler's business and has never been in the building.** About four people here can put a question into the gap in the wall and not one of them has a form, and the form has one box on it and the box is for a figure. **Being frightened has a shape and it is not cowardice: a valley of ninety houses where everybody knows which house everybody lives in.** A woman of thirty-one with a house at the ninth door says out loud that the question is not how we would get it and it is what we would do with it if we had it, and the woman of about forty who washes the pen calls it the most expensive thing anybody has said in this valley in a month, and the clerk of the Seat writes nothing down. Ends on a person doing their work: a pot off a fire behind the ninth door.

### Chapter 242 — The Price Of A Second Paper
**Shelf day 112, the first day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 190.**
The matter to the chamber is five pounds and six shillings and the working is printed in the clerk's mouth: a pound for entry, four pounds for the day, nine days' board at eightpence, and 240 and 960 and 72 is 1,272 pence. **The chapter's real subject is why nobody has paid it, and the reason is not the money.** It is ten weeks of a pitman's pay and seventy-two pence over, and eleven weeks of a sluice-keeper's pay and eighty-four pence over, and the second of those is about three quarters of the sixteen weeks a year she is paid for. The second reason is a man of fifty-two's: **a second paper puts a second date on a matter, and a second date is a thing a bench can use to close a first one, and a bench that is seized of a matter and is doing its job properly will do it, and every one of the four of them will be right when they do.** He says out loud that he is not going to pretend five pounds and six is nothing and that he has said that once in this valley and is not going to say it twice. Tarin Keel prints the working and corrects him twice, and is right twice: the price goes into the settlement thirty-three whole times with nine hundred and four pence over and not thirty-four and not a hundred and forty. **The Anner pays, out of the Anner's own cost of the high road, and the amount and the payer and the thing wanted go on the outside of the sheet in a clerk's hand, because a matter nobody is paying for comes back in nine days; and the man of fifty-two says out loud that he is buying a date and not a conscience and would like it written that he is not asking to be thanked, and the man of thirty-one does not thank him and does not stop him.** Ends on a person doing their work: a scrivener copying a fair sheet at a penny a page, not paid for it and not asked.

### Chapter 243 — Sixty Tons Is Two Counts
**Shelf day 113, the second day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 191.**
The only figure anybody anywhere has ever written down about what this valley trades is 1,040 tons and it is four years old and a stranger's; this basin says about eleven hundred and has for nineteen years; the difference is sixty tons and at seven pounds a ton that is four hundred and twenty pounds a year, which is five and seven-tenths in the hundred of the seven thousand two hundred and eighty the seven pounds a ton comes to. **The finding is in nine words from a man who has counted carts on roads for nineteen years, standing in a cart yard with his coat off: we counted the pit, nobody ever counted the valley.** And the second half of it: a figure four years old cannot be put against a memory of nineteen years by anybody in this valley, and not one man here can do it, and he has been doing the other thing for nineteen years and knows what a memory of nineteen years is worth, which is nothing after about the fourth year and very good for about a week. **There is no weigh-book at the pit, at Sallowby, in the Seat's room or in a cart shed, and a ton on paper is a ton on paper and a ton in a yard is whatever came off a cart that day, and neither of the two men was lying.** Sixty tons is twelve hundred hundredweights, and a hundredweight of salt at the pans is a pound and fourpence, which is two hundred and eighty-eight pence, and twelve hundred of those is three hundred and forty-five thousand six hundred pence, which is one thousand four hundred and forty pounds, and nobody in this basin has ever bought twelve hundred hundredweights of anything. **THE TWO HUNDRED AND ONE THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND EIGHT HUNDRED AND FORTY THAT STOOD HERE UNTIL 27 SEPTEMBER 2026 CAME FROM A WRONG CONVERSION — £1 4s IS 288d AND NOT 168d — AND WERE CAUGHT BY THE REVIEW OF BATCH 0005.** A man of sixty-one who has kept a count of every salting in this basin for thirty years came down off the flats because a carter told him his count had been counted wrong, and asked the question that turns the whole thing over — how many of what — and the answer is that he has never once been asked what comes up off a road and nobody in this valley has written down a single load coming in. **The number stops being a scandal and becomes a question, and it is the first time in about a month that a number in this valley has got smaller rather than larger, and nobody thanked anybody for it and the man who counted carts would not say the word scandal again in a room on purpose.** Ends on a person doing their work, and **this is the first notch this volume prints since `218:71`, and the chapter says in its own words that it is a count of notches and is not a count of days.**

### Chapter 244 — Who May Speak For Four Hundred And Ten People
**Shelf day 114, the third day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 192.**
A basin of four hundred and ten people is to be represented, and there is no form for the question. The room has: a man of thirty-one with no standing who has said so out loud in four rooms and been right; a man of fifty-two who is a party because he is paying; a man of thirty-four who cannot read the paper; and about nine frightened people. **The shape of the fright is printed by a man of fifty-six with a ladder on his shoulder and nobody had asked him: every one of them knows which house everybody lives in, and a valley of ninety houses cannot send anybody to a bench of four four hundred miles off and keep it private, and the thing that comes back in about a month is two paragraphs or nothing, and then this lane has to live with the fact that it spent itself.** **The finding is the woman of about forty's and it is that the standing is not in a person but in a document: the settlement is the only paper in this valley anybody is on, eleven hands, and it can be ended tonight by eleven people saying one sentence in a road at the closing of the water, with nothing whatever done to them for saying it, and that is the whole of what standing in this valley is.** **And her third refusal, about a different thing, which is herself — she will not go, because the room in that market town has one clerk in it who knows what a document is and that is exactly one too few already — and she is right for the third time and says afterwards that those three were three different things.** And then the finding of the chapter, out of a man of thirty-four with no preparation: **a paper nobody is on cannot be asked anybody anything, and the copy has no person on it and neither has the original, and that is the whole of what is wrong with this valley.** Decided, and not his decision: the standing is the settlement, so the only people who can be sent are people the eleven have sent, and he is not one of the eleven and said so and was not put forward. **The nine frightened were not asked, and the eleven have not been asked anything yet, and nobody in that room had been to any of them.** Not a completed beat.

### Chapter 245 — He Opens It
**Shelf day 115, the fourth day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 193. Block-quoted document one.**
**He opens a rider's bag.** Not a fight, not a rescue, not a monster: he says out loud that he has no authority, that the bag is addressed to a body that has no seat, that he is not its clerk and not an advocate and not a person of this district, and that the sentence has not got any shorter and he is not going to shorten it today, and then he asks anybody in the room to stop him and nobody does. **He cannot read a word of it and asks for it in words, slowly, with the numbers read twice.** **Block-quoted document one: the chamber's own printed index, the original and not the two-inch hand-copy, opened flat and held open by one finger — a printed heading of two words, some four hundred and sixty entries in the three columns beside it, one rule ruled under all four, and under the fourth four lines and no more.** The first is a return of the water in the Sallow at the frame at Hollow Sallow, taken in the eleventh year. The second is forty-one papers out and nine answers, so thirty-two never answered. The third is a tonnage and prices in the eighth year. **The fourth is a printed notice of one line — no matter of a Seat is to be sent out of its own district — and it is the rule this basin has had on a wall in its own words since before the water, and the clerk says so himself and says this time it costs him something.** **Nobody has hidden anything is said a second time, by the same clerk, and what it costs him the second time is that then it was a thing in a book and now it is a thing in a bag a man from four hundred miles off has opened on his table, and he adds that he put a good deal of it there himself without once asking what it was for.** Then the part that makes it a choice: nobody asked him, there is a door and nobody would have known, and what he had instead was nothing — no money that is his, no party, no form, no line with his name on it, and a good name belonging to four people four hundred miles off which is a public thing and is free and cannot be spent by the people it is about. **He could have said the sentence that splits the thirty in a building from the four in a room, and he did not, and he wants that on the record in his own words, because the sentence that separates them is the sentence that protects the institution.** What he said instead is the volume's engine, in his own mouth: about thirty people in a building four hundred miles off have been right three times in nine years and have not been in this valley once, and a record can be perfectly kept and still be wrong about a place, and the reason is that nobody who kept it was ever in it. **Nobody thanked him. Nobody was relieved. The good name of four people does not survive the asking and was never going to.** Four lines copied, one page, a penny, out of the press. Day-count instance 16, day 193. **The work of that morning was not enough.** No panel, and the second half of the volume's question is not asked out loud and is not even a whisper.

### Chapter 246 — A Woman With A Board
**Shelf day 116, the fifth day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 194.**
**Sable Venn arrives, on foot from the north, with a board under her arm, and the clerk of the Seat recognises her from a name that has been in four mouths in this valley for two years with no document under it.** She refuses the sheet on the wall before anybody offers it and says she does not read other people's records and that that is why nobody has ever been able to use her. **Her board is this valley and it is not good drawing and it is mostly right and she leaves the dam's height wrong on purpose and says so before anybody asks her, and about four people in that room understand what she has just done.** Her offer: no bench, no chamber, no order, no date, nothing anybody has to do because a piece of paper says so — genuinely better for people who want to be left alone. And genuinely worse for people who need a rule enforced against somebody: if the mine takes your water in the night you will have a bad night and no remedy and nobody to complain to, and that is what you are buying. **A woman of thirty-eight stands up before either of the two men does and says she wants to be left alone, has wanted it since the day before the first shaking, and gives the working, and that every one of those pence comes out of a piece of paper that somebody can be made to keep, and she would rather have a paper she can see the end of than a paper she cannot, and would like it written that she said it first.** **He cannot prove her wrong, only incomplete, and he does not name the incompleteness: the woman of about forty does, and what she says is that a rule-free valley cannot be given anything, and a woman who wants nothing is not a woman who gets what she wants, she is a woman who gets no answer at all, and the honest name for that is a person who is not in the instruments — and she has been the only person in that room in that position since before the water and she washes the pen. Sable Venn says yes and does not argue.** **And he had the standing to say the sentence he learned once in a room in another county and did not say it, and the reason is printed and it is not a rule: it would be cheaper the second time than the first and it would be worth about half, and a woman of about forty said it instead and had never paid a penny for knowing it.** She did not win and did not lose; the room kept the paper; the paper is not hers and she is not on it; about four people in that room will remember and about six will not. Ends on a person doing their work, and it is a pot on a fire, and **it is not the same pot.**

### Chapter 247 — What The Water Did At A Frame In A Year Nobody Was Watching
**Shelf day 117, the sixth day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 195.**
The first of the four lines came down the last four miles and got itself said out loud in a lane in front of about forty people, because a man of thirty-four says first that he cannot read a word of it, and there is no other reason and no clerk came with it. **The figure is two feet four inches above the sill of the frame on three days together, and the mark by which it is known is on the inside of the north post and there is nobody living in this valley who put a rule to it.** **The arithmetic, in a road, under the geometry the review of 27 September 2026 ruled: the frame's sill is nine feet ABOVE the Anner's, nine feet is a hundred and eight inches, two feet four inches is twenty-eight, and a hundred and eight and twenty-eight is a hundred and thirty-six, which is eleven feet four inches. So the highest the water has ever stood at that frame is eleven feet four inches above the sill of the Anner's own dam — four inches ABOVE the line in the bond, on three days together, in a year before anybody in this valley was born, with nobody deciding anything — and this valley has spent a month with one figure of eleven feet in it and three sills under it and had never once been told that the river had already gone over it.** And the chamber's own second ruling of nine years ago — no order may name a height without naming the sill it is taken from — arrives at by a man of thirty-four in a road in about four minutes. **What a woman of thirty-eight does with it is the finding: a return of a river is a thing that already happened and a height is a thing you decide to be above, and this valley has spent a month arguing about a height and had never once been told what the water does; and she says it was a mark on a post that somebody put a rule to and wrote down and sent nine days to a city to be kept, and that there is nobody in it but her and a rule and a wet post.** She does not celebrate. She names the second step at the sluice, which she put in herself in the fourth year, which she has been standing on in the dark twice a winter for eleven years thinking it was a step. **At the eighth hour she goes down to the frame with a rule and puts it to the mark and it is two feet four inches, and she writes the day on the post in chalk, and she does not write the eleventh year, because there is no conversion and she is the last person in this basin who would try to make one in chalk on a post.** Day-count instance 17, day 195.

### Chapter 248 — What The Four People Who Keep The Record Say About This Valley
**Shelf day 118, the seventh and last day of the fifty-sixth week. Basin day 196.**
**Nothing came back from the chamber and nothing can**: a man with a bag comes twice in the year and the first paper went into the gap on the first day of this week and nine days is nine days in the wrong of the year. And the bench is seized of the matter and will consider it in its own time, and a bench doing its job properly is a thing with no face on it, and that is the reason nine people in four hundred and ten spent a fortnight afraid of a piece of paper. **So the room does the only thing available: the four people who keep this valley's record read nine years of it out loud to each other, and it is not interesting, and it took about an hour, and it is the first hour the scrivener has spent on her own valley in eleven years.** And the end of it is a hole: **there is no column anywhere in any of it for what this valley trades, and two of the four have been down the lane and two have not, and the two who have not are the two who keep the numbers.** And here the volume's engine is said the second time and by a different person in a different register, by a man of fifty-two standing up in about four minutes, about four people who keep this valley's record and have never been in it: **a record can be perfectly kept and still be wrong about a place, and the reason is that nobody who kept it was ever in it, and there is no form for anybody to say I do not want to be that person.** He says the same of himself — he counted nineteen roofs from a bank in the second hour of the flood and did not go into one of them — and says he has no speech about himself and is not going to make one. **And the mine's standing interest in a number is settled in public: four times a year a man at the Anner gate writes down what goes out and what comes in in a book the seat keeps, at four days a year of a pitman's time, which is eighty pence, which is six shillings and eightpence and one and a third in the hundred of a pitman's paid year; and what it really costs the Anner is the right to stand in a room in a year and say the chamber got this valley wrong, which it gave up on purpose, out loud, and would like it written that it gave it up and not that it was taken — and it costs the four their name.** Nobody in that room is satisfied. Not a completed beat.

### Chapter 249 — A Paper That Says In Its Own First Line That It Can Be Ended
**Shelf day 119, the first day of the fifty-seventh week. Basin day 197. Block-quoted documents two and three.**
**Nobody drafted it in a room.** Eleven people said one sentence each in their own houses and a scrivener wrote down what was said in her own hand and the clerk copied it out fair and put it on the wall, and there is not a clause in it that anybody in a room improved. **The eleven feet goes into a third document and not onto the settlement, and the reason is not a secret: the settlement is eleven people's and the height is the one thing about it that eleven people do not agree on.** **Block-quoted document two: the difference of two lines, one sheet, one hand, three copies in three places** — the bond's line is eleven feet above the sill of the Anner's own dam; the new line is eleven feet above the sill of the bed below the village, which is thirteen feet below the sill of the frame at the sluice, which is nine feet above the sill of the Anner's dam and is therefore four feet below that sill; the difference is four feet, which is the distance between the two sills and is the whole of what the document can say; no house stands on those four feet; and nobody has agreed to the difference and nobody has refused it. **THE CHAIN THIS DOCUMENT PRINTED UNTIL 27 SEPTEMBER 2026 — a bed four feet below the frame's sill, a frame nine feet below the Anner's, and a difference of four feet — COULD NOT YIELD FOUR FROM THE FIGURES IT NAMED, AND IT WAS THE BATCH'S RESOLUTION AND IT WAS IMPOSSIBLE ON ITS FACE. THE REPAIR CHANGED THE DEPTH OF ONE SILL AND THE DIRECTION OF ONE RELATION AND CHANGED NO FIGURE AND NO PLOT.** **It cost five pence — two copies at a penny and one sealed copy at threepence — and the Seat paid it out of the press, and the three copies are in the press, in a lane in the hands of a man of thirty-four who cannot read it, and on a table under a chain-book at the pit, and the three people who can hold them cannot read one another's.** And a joiner with a rule says the volume's last civic finding: **a bad answer in three copies can be argued with by three people and a good answer in one can be argued with by nobody, and he has spent nine years trying to get a good answer out of this valley about a line of chalk on a doorpost and cannot argue with a good one at all.** **Block-quoted document three: the charter, one sheet, one hand, on a wall, and not in the press, because the press is for deeds and bonds and the things that are owed.** It says in its own first line that it can be ended and that any person of the valley may go from it at any time and shall lose nothing by going but the charter. **It carries no name and no dash**, and the reason is a paper nobody is on cannot be asked anything, and the answer the valley gives is not a name and is a date, and anybody in four hundred and ten can bring it to the review. **And the price of it, printed in full by the woman it concerns: nineteen roofs at nine pounds is 41,040 pence, the whole settlement is 42,880, the difference is 1,840 pence which is seven pounds and thirteen shillings and fourpence, and 1,840 is the whole wage plus the penny a day — so the charter is worth the roofs and is not worth the wage, because a paper that can be ended cannot hold a wage, and a wage is the only one of these things that is still going when the roofs are done. And the same 41,040 pence is what the flood cost, to the penny, and one of the two things it is put water in nineteen houses.** And about nine people who were afraid of a good name are not afraid of it any more, and it is not because anybody was made safe. Ends on a person doing their work.

### Chapter 250 — An Exit Review, And A Position Nobody Stood In Front Of
**Shelf day 120, the second day of the fifty-seventh week. Basin day 198. Day-count instance 18, day 198.**
It does not end with anything, and the not-ending is the point, and the list of what is standing is the list of a place and not of a resolution: the charter, the third document in three places, the settlement with no name at the foot of it and no height in it, the open column and the spent good name, the mine bound in advance to a figure of a thousand and forty tons, the wage and the risk to it. **And the position beneath the basin, which is a bearing and a depth and a page number, in two books whose two writers cannot read one another's entry, unmoved since the fifty-first week, with a chamber at the bottom of it and water in the chamber, and four hundred and six feet is the pit and is not the void, and the last hundred and forty feet at the low end of the pit has been under to the roof since before a woman of twenty-six was seventeen, and her name is Alo Vearn and she does not know that a sentence about her is in a book six miles off that nobody has ever been in this basin to write. Nobody went down, and that is the plainest sentence anybody said that week, and a man of thirty-four said it on a bank and nobody answered it.** **And the rest of it, four hundred miles off, none of it came out of this valley and none of it stopped:** the carrying, off nothing; **the leg, used once in fifty chapters, in the passage where he puts down nothing — he had to put his weight on a wall to get at a board and it is a fact about a wall and not a discovery**; the day at the head of a page, one hundred and ninety-eight, the eighteenth figure of that kind and a count of figures and not a count of anything else, and nothing under it but the reason; the second half of the book not opened; the four hundred and eighty-five pounds on nine thousand seven hundred, named once, in his own hand, on the other side of a board, in nobody's mouth in this valley; the second notice of five shillings and fourpence unpaid; the claim of forty-five pounds two shillings and eightpence not producible and the carter of fifty-one is right; ninety-one numbered sheets and about nine hundred doors; a box of about nine hundred and forty forms; the minute of the first of the forty-eighth week; a dead man in the fourth line of a list of two hundred and forty and Nesh Arrad, thirty-nine, four children and a stove and no paper at all, whose clock is still running and which he is going to hand on in a book with two halves in it without stopping it and without asking about it. **And a name that went four miles in two years on four mouths with no document under it, and a woman with a board who is not on any paper in this valley and did not ask to be, and about four people who know she exists and can do nothing whatever about her.** Ends on four ordinary things: a gate opened at the closing of the water, a chair put back against a table leg, a barrow down a bank, and four men and a barrow at a dam at the second light. **A person doing their work. Not a ruling, not a discovery, not an answer.**

### Chapter 231 — The Copy In The Lane
**Shelf day 101, the fourth day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 179.**
The second roof comes off the third house from the bottom of the lane, in about four days, at nine pounds the man will not split, and eighteen roofs are wanted. The timber goes up on the backs of about eleven people over two days and a man who counts carts writes it down and has about nineteen paid days a year and none of them are this one. **On the second of that week the reading did not happen, because the copy was up the hill being copied, and about eleven people came down the lane at the closing of the water and there was nothing to read, and the man of thirty-four stood in the road and said *I have not got it*, and about nine people said *that is all right* at the same moment and none of them said it to him.** The finding is his and not the protagonist's: it is not a ceremony, everybody has been treating the sixth line as a promise about a day, and it is the only way anybody in that lane finds out whether a thing has been done, and if the paper is not in his hand he will read it out of his own head and cannot help getting a word wrong. A woman of thirty-eight says in a road four miles up a hill that he has just described a thing with no second copy and that she is not going to tell a man of thirty-four he is doing it wrong, because he is the only reason about forty people knew a roof was coming. **The copy was never once in a man of thirty-one's hands in the whole of that week and he asked for it to be read out and could not follow a word of it from the paper, and a clerk of forty-four's question — which of those two is the document — is still open and nobody in that lane has asked it.** Ends on a person doing their work: a roof put back on.

### Chapter 232 — A Road That Does Not Go Through Orison
**Shelf day 102, the fifth day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 180.**
Market day at Sallowby. The high road is the long way round and adds a morning and a half each way and about nine carts a day make that addition for about a hundred and forty days a year because the causeway is shut, and the Anner bears the whole of it, and it is the second line of a four-page order on a wall that nobody outside about thirty clerks has ever read. A carter asks a question out loud about carting, and a man who counts carts has had a figure in his head about a road on the map for nine years. **There is a road on the shoulder, four miles, a bend at the second ford, a market four days short of Orison, and no gate on it, and that is the whole of the argument, and every trade in this basin has carried salt and ochre past the gate at the top of the pass for eleven years and not one of them has ever asked what is at the other end of it, and the answer is a room with a yard in it and about thirty clerks and a bench of four above them.** The market at the end of it has no court in it, and the man who counts carts has been carrying the shape of a market with no court in his head since before the water. **A woman of thirty-three who copies deeds says out loud, in a cart yard, that everybody in this valley thinks the water-seat is there for the water and that it is the other way about: there is a room because there is a press, and the press is because a bond of forty pounds is in it, and the water has been brought to that room every year and nobody has ever gone the other way. That is the first person in this volume to say it.** The route is on a cart's side in chalk in nine or ten hands, and the chapter says out loud that it was named once, in a cart yard, by a man who counts carts and who said it because he had counted the carts, and that it is the shape of the next book in this valley and that nothing else in that week was about it. Ends on a person doing their work: nine carts on a high road and a carter checking his horses twice because it was the fourth morning of the fifth week and he had been doing it eleven years.

### Chapter 233 — The Word That Means Not Sent
**Shelf day 103, the sixth day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 181. Block-quoted document one, and the batch's only one, at `233:29`–`31`.**
The man with a bag comes up the high road the way he does, and a clerk of forty-four weighs it in the hand and says the same sentence he has said twice before about having no authority to open it, and the sentence has not got any shorter, and being in a hurry is what he has instead. Nine printed sheets, of which eight are the ordinary list of decisions and the ninth is **the chamber's own printed index, which comes once a year and of which every Seat in nine districts keeps a hand-copy, and the hand-copy of this one is the book on the shelf under the window, and the two of them lie side by side on a table nine feet by fourteen.** The hand-book is block-quoted: a printed heading of two words at the head of a fourth column, about four hundred and sixty entries in the three beside them going back to the first shaking in a small hard hand, one rule under all four, and nothing whatever under the fourth. **The heading is NOT SENT, and a clerk of forty-four says it in an ordinary voice, the way he says a price, and says he has had his eye on it every working day since he came because it is the last page and you cannot tell a finished book from an unfinished one without it.** Nobody asks him about it, and the chapter says so out loud and lists the five people in the room who could have asked and did not, by name and by reason, and the fifth is a man of thirty-one who could have opened it and did not, and put his hand on the table about a foot from the printed sheet and took it away again, and has not told one person in this valley he was in the room. **Under the same heading in the chamber's own book there are four lines and all four are about this basin**, described in prose and not block-quoted: a return of the water in the Sallow at the frame, taken in the eleventh year, with a figure nobody here has ever seen; a list of the papers this Seat has sent, being forty-one, and of the answers, being nine; a sheet of the tonnage and prices of this basin's trade in the eighth year; and a printed one-line notice which is the rule the first of the three rulings was made under. **Thirty-two papers went nine days up a road and were never answered, and a clerk says nobody has hidden anything and that not being sent is a worse thing for a valley than being lied to, because nobody did it, and nobody in the room says that either.** Ends: the bag on the shelf under the window beside a bundle with a knife-cut end, neither in the press, because a printed sheet is not owed to anybody.

### Chapter 234 — Nobody Asks
**Shelf day 104, the seventh and last day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 182.**
The four lines come out into about four hundred and ten people over three days in the ordinary way, one at a time, in four different mouths, and the first is said by a woman of thirty-eight at her own gate: there is a number about my gate in a town I have never been to and I have wanted to know what it said for six of eleven years and there has never been anybody I could ask. The second is forty-one papers and nine answers, said badly by a man with a crowbar to a carter. The third is a tonnage, said by a scrivener in a shop, and if they wrote ours down four years ago then somebody four hundred miles off knows more about what this valley trades than this valley does. The fourth is a rule, from the clerk, who had the rule on his own wall in his own words every working day for nine years and had never read it as a reason for thirty-two papers. **And the basin goes on doing the work, which is the batch's subject, and the chapter says it is neither indifference nor heroism.** There is no form in this basin for asking a chamber for a thing, and the working is printed: a pound for entry is two hundred and forty pence, four pounds for the day at the chamber is nine hundred and sixty, nine days' board at eightpence a day is seventy-two, and the three together are one thousand two hundred and seventy-two pence, which is five pounds and six, and there is no price on the list for asking for a thing about thirty-two papers. **Being afraid of a bench is not a matter and there is nowhere to enter it.** Then, on a bank above a lane, **Brann Slee, fifty-six, with a ladder, asks the first question any person of the Red Basin has asked him: *What is it you are carrying?* The answer is nine words — *A matter for a district four hundred miles off* — and what he gets is *Then you will carry it home, and I have four roofs*, and the leg is used once, as a fact, and the reason is not given.** And the argument in the lane is ended by the same man in nine words — *A roof does not care and neither do I* — and the finding is his: he has been up that roof a long time, there has been a room in a city four hundred miles off this whole time, and he is not going to be the man who brings a bench to a lane. Ends on a person doing their work: four men and a barrow at the dam at the second light, and the clay in the same order for eleven years.

### Chapter 235 — A Record Perfectly Kept
**Shelf day 105, the first day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 183. Day-count instance 13, at `235:53`.**
The second thing in the bag comes out of the bag because the bag was on a shelf and a clerk went to put the sheets in a drawer; it was at the bottom under nine printed sheets and the man with the bag did not point at it, and a man with a bag who points at a thing in his own bag is a man who has been asked to. It is two paragraphs and a head, dated in a turn this basin cannot place, nine days old at the door and two days in the room. **It is true, it is consistent with the three rulings, it is consistent with the four pages and with the sheet, and the whole of it is wrong about this place — and the chapter says out loud that that is not a discovery, it is the same finding for the second time and the second time it is duller and worse, and that being careful with a true thing is not the same as being right about it.** The third of the four lines has a figure in it and a return quotes its own file, and the figure is **one thousand and forty tons where this basin has been saying about eleven hundred for nineteen years, and the difference is sixty tons, which at seven pounds a ton is four hundred and twenty pounds a year, five and seven-tenths in the hundred, and a clerk says he is not going to be the one who says where sixty tons went because he has been in that room since before the water and it was not him.** An under-manager comes up the hill unasked and says the mine is now a body with a standing interest in a number, and says *not the height* twice before anybody can get it wrong, and a clerk asks whether that is a complaint against the sheet and he says it is not and wants it written down in the order it was said. **A man of thirty-one opens a penny exercise book he shut on the third of the last week, having told himself the next figure would be a hundred and ninety-something in the first week of a month he cannot name, and it is a hundred and eighty-three, and the four days in between are not in the book, and the reason is written under it: a day goes on a thing when it arrives and a day does not go on a thing when it was done, and there is no column anywhere in this valley for when it was done, and four hundred miles off there is a turn and a day and nobody here can place a turn.** And the batch's real discovery, from a woman of thirty-eight in a lane: there are things in this valley that are true in every room and are not on any page, not hidden and not kept back, and there are about nine of them and she counted twice and is not counting a third time, and one of them is a height, and nobody asked which nine. **A girl of seventeen then finds one of them in her own book in her own hand: a figure of the water against the frame that she wrote off the frame herself and nobody asked her for, and the water-book has four columns and they belong to four hands and not one of the four has ever stood at that frame, and there is nowhere in this basin to put a number a person wrote themselves.** Ends on a person doing their work: a book kept in two hands and a third begun.

### Chapter 236 — A Good Name, Four Hundred Miles Off
**Shelf day 106, the second day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 184.**
Nine people in a valley of four hundred and ten are frightened of a bench of four they have never met, and four of them say so in four places in one day in four different voices and none of the four will use the word. A woman of about thirty-one with two children, at the ninth door, with a sentence of hers on the settlement under a strike she did not put there for this, lies awake doing a sum that is not the point: she knows nothing about the four men and they have four lines about her lane and a number about her gate. A man of about forty with a crowbar has been a boy at a winch for nineteen years and has started thinking about a bench, and can only say it to a carter. A carter reconciles nine days and four hundred miles and says what a bench of four would say about this valley is nothing, and writes it under a number in a clerk's book with the line NOT ENTRY, and says a person cannot be entered anywhere for a thing they have not done. A woman of about forty who has been in that room nine years says it is nothing and that she is the one who has been frightened for two days, and that the two are in the same sentence. **An under-manager of fifty-two, who came up the hill for nothing, says the whole of it in nine words: *Their good name is public and it is free* — and a recordwright of twenty-eight names the reason on the way out: a public thing that costs nothing cannot be spent by the people it is about. Nobody in the room writes it down.** And on a shut causeway in the wind at the fifth hour, **the Anner's standing interest in eleven feet stops being an arithmetic fact — two and three-tenths in the hundred of the seven thousand seven hundred — and becomes the right to be described, by four people whom none of us has ever met, in a way we would have to live in, and it happens at about four in the morning in a house at the top of the hill and not in the chain-book, and he does not write it down.** Nobody in that chapter has said that he is a good man. Ends on a person doing their work: four men and a barrow at the dam at the second light, and the man of fifty-two puts the barrow down himself and says nothing about a good name to anybody.

### Chapter 237 — Named Twice, At A Distance
**Shelf day 107, the third day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 185.**
A name is said in a kitchen in Sallowby by a woman of about fifty-four making bread, who has had it for two years and never had a use for it, and the woman came through the north before the water with a board, asked for nothing, took a loaf and did not pay for it, and gave her name when asked, which is more than most of them do. The same name is said the same day at the sixth hour in a cart yard at Hollow Sallow by a man of about forty-two who is on no paper in this basin, and the two places are about four miles apart and **the two men have never seen each other and do not know there is another one, and neither can say where he had it, and the man in the yard has been in that lane twenty-two years.** **The finding is not about her. A name travels four miles in about two years on about four mouths and there is nothing anybody in this basin could produce if anybody wanted to argue about it — not in the Seat's list of drains, not in the water-book, not in the chain-book, not in the hand-book with a fourth column in the head of it, not in the four hundred and sixty entries in the three beside it, not in the four lines under the fourth, not in the thirty-two papers.** The column point was made a month ago and is not being made again. Nobody went looking for her. An under-manager was asked and does not care. A clerk was asked by the girl of seventeen and says there is no column for her and there never has been. **A man of thirty-one has the name written once on the basin side of a penny exercise book under a line with nothing under the line, and he did not write it again and did not ask anybody, and he has not asked whether she knows about a column with four lines in it that are all about this basin, and nobody in this basin has told him or anybody else whether she knows.** About four people in a valley of about four hundred and ten now know a name. Ends on a person doing their work: a pot on a fire.

### Chapter 238 — A Cart Is Not Where It Was
**Shelf day 108, the fourth day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 186.**
**THE BATCH'S REVERSAL, AND IT IS NOT A FLOOD AND THERE IS NO VILLAIN IN IT.** A carter went over the shoulder on the second of that week with a load of ochre, because the customer is four days short of Orison and the shoulder is two days shorter for that one place, and he had known the road was on the map since before the water and had never had a reason to try it, and he was a day and a half late and lost about a hundred and twenty miles of high road that the Anner pays for. The second line of the four-page order is quoted, in prose and not as a document, and it is one sentence and it is about a road: the causeway shut for so long as the sluice stand, about nine carts a day by the high road while it is shut, and the Anner to bear the whole of the cost. **Nobody in Hollow Sallow had read it, and the reason none of them had is that it is on a wall in a market town, and the reason it is on a wall in a market town is that it is the only document this basin has produced in about a year, and a document a village has to read all the way through before it can know what has been done to it is not a document a village can act on.** A woman of about forty reads it out loud in a lane at the closing of the water, to about seven people, because a carter asked her a question about a cart, and she does not change a word of it, and a carter at the back says *that is not a river, that is a schedule.* The under-manager has the number out loud, the settlement, and the other one, nine carts a day and a morning and a half each way, and says there is no villain in this and wants it said in the room before anybody else says a word: that carter did not think about a paper and did not think about a dam. **And the thing that comes out of it, said on a shut causeway in four minutes to about seven people on a bank: eleven people built a piece of paper in eleven places over about a week and a mine paid for it, and a man of thirty-one took his own name off it because he was right to, and a mine has a standing interest in a number that put water in nineteen houses — and there is a number on a dam and a number on a road, and the two are on two pieces of paper on the same wall in the same room, and neither paper has ever mentioned the other, and a carter has just taken one of the nine off the high road, and nobody in this basin can say whether the mine is paying for eight carts or nine.** Ends: the fifth roof on, four days later than the first, and four facts of four different sizes in the same week. Not a completed beat. **A cart is not where it was.**

### Chapter 239 — What A Road Costs When There Is No Figure For It
**Shelf day 109, the fifth day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 187. Day-count instance 14, at `239:59`.**
There is no figure for that road in any book in this basin, and the man who would have had one was asleep behind a cart shed because he had been on a dam until the middle of the night. He comes down at the sixth hour on his own account and does the sum out loud on a bank and prints the working, and the whole of it is twenty-one figures and every one of them is checked. **He uses the chamber's tonnage, one thousand and forty, and not this basin's eleven hundred, and says why out loud: a number somebody said is worth nothing by the second day, and a number somebody wrote down is worth something for about as long as the paper lasts, and he would rather subtract from a number written down by a stranger than from a number his own yard has been saying since before he could count.** The working: one thousand and forty tons at two hundred and forty pence to the pound is two hundred and forty-nine thousand six hundred pence to the pound; four pounds a ton at the mouth is nine hundred and ninety-eight thousand four hundred pence, which is four thousand one hundred and sixty pounds; eleven at the market is two million seven hundred and forty-five thousand six hundred, which is eleven thousand four hundred and forty; and the seven between them is one million seven hundred and forty-seven thousand two hundred, which is seven thousand two hundred and eighty. The settlement is forty-two thousand eight hundred and eighty pence a year. **And the road, which nine men priced at the mouth figure, because a road is not a carrying: the seven pounds a ton is the carrying, the four pounds a ton is the trade, and a road is the ground itself, and ground is paid for out of what the thing on the ground is worth before anybody moves it.** The sum: forty-two thousand eight hundred and eighty plus nine hundred and ninety-eight thousand four hundred is one million forty-one thousand two hundred and eighty pence, which is four thousand three hundred and thirty-eight pounds, thirteen shillings and fourpence. **The whole of what the Anner takes out of this basin in a year is nine hundred and ninety-eight thousand four hundred pence. The excess is forty-two thousand eight hundred and eighty pence, which is a hundred and seventy-eight pounds, thirteen shillings and fourpence, which is the settlement, to the penny, and the settlement and the road are the same money counted once.** The ceiling is printed too: nine hundred and fifty-five thousand five hundred and twenty pence, which is three thousand nine hundred and eighty-one pounds, six shillings and eightpence, and the nine men came in a hundred and seventy-eight pounds over it, and a man who counts carts says there is nothing behind that difference and he is not going to be the one who says what it means. A board goes up against the outside of a cart shed and is going in about a month and he knows it and did it anyway. Day-count instance fourteen, a hundred and eighty-seven, in his own hand, on his own act, and not on a bank. Ends: about seven people walked past the board and two stopped and nobody has asked what it is for, and the sheet on the wall has not been touched since the seventh of the fifty-third week.

### Chapter 240 — Shut, And Going To Be Opened
**Shelf day 110, the sixth day of the fifty-fifth week. Basin day 188.**
The column is shut, and the whole of what has happened about it in ten days is that about thirty people in this basin know a page exists four hundred miles off with four lines in it that are all about this valley's water, and nobody has asked for it, nobody has opened it, nobody has been asked about it, and no person in this basin has asked a man of thirty-one when he is going to. The settlement is on the wall with no name at the foot of it and no height in it and a seventh line that exists only in a lane. The route is in chalk on a cart and in about nine mouths with no money behind it, and the money that would be behind it is more than the whole of the trade. A cart went over the shoulder for a good reason and was a day and a half late, and nobody in this basin can say whether the mine is paying for eight carts a day or nine. The Anner is to be asked again in one year and the asking is a year off. **Nobody turned the year, the six debts on the Shelf side of a penny exercise book are listed in a paragraph as things that do not stop, the new question is on the other half of that book and is not raised and he is not relieved of the not being asked, and the System put nothing up in ten days and said nothing whatever about any of it, and a man of thirty-one has stopped expecting it to and told nobody.** **And nobody went down, and the position is where it was identified in the fifty-first week, and four hundred and six feet is the pit and not the void, and the sill at the Anner is nine feet above the frame and the two numbers have never once been in the same sentence in this valley, and the last hundred and forty feet of the water at the low end of the pit has been under to the roof since before a woman of twenty-six was seventeen, and nobody in this valley said any of that out loud this week and nobody thought about it this week.** A woman opens a gate, a roofer comes down a ladder, a girl is paid a penny in a jar, and a man of thirty-four reads six lines and a struck line and a seventh line with no figure on it out loud in a road to about forty people, and it is a different paper every time it is read out and nobody in this valley can check it. A clerk of forty-four puts a chair back at a table and says the plainest sentence anybody said that week, to a shelf: **somebody is going to open that column, and it is not going to be me.** Nobody answers it and nobody is asked. A gate was opened at the closing of the water, a chair was put back at a table, a bag went on a shelf that nobody has asked about.

Everything below is archive and is not edited.** Chapters 1–220 are canon; Volume 04 is closed, audited and repaired; `outline/volume-05.md` is the volume outline and `outline/series.md` outranks it.

**The run: Shelf day ninety-one to one hundred, the fifty-third week and the first three days of the fifty-fourth, which is basin day one hundred and sixty-nine to one hundred and seventy-eight since the second shaking, on the formula basin day = Shelf day + 78. Arrival was basin day 149, so he is in the valley twenty-nine days by Chapter 230: 178 − 149 = 29.**

### Chapter 221 — The Order The Nineteen Gave
**Shelf day 91, the first day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 169. Day-count instance 10, at `221:11`.**
A list of what nineteen people need is not a list of work. Eighteen of the nineteen answers cannot be bought and the one that can is a roof at nine pounds from a man of fifty-six who will not split it. **A woman of about sixty, unnamed and unrecorded, says *the roof is second*, because a wet roof over a wet floor is a wet floor for four months, and the order of the work is bed, boards, salt out of the plaster, and then a roof before the frost.** The sheet comes out of the cart shed and he dates his own act of taking it out at a hundred and sixty-nine and writes under it that a man may put a day on his own act and may not put one on another person's speech, and there are nineteen people in that lane who have not been asked for a day by anybody in their lives. **Coll Ferren, thirty-four, four people, named here for the first time, standing in his own doorway, the fifth of the nineteen, who says that a house is not a cost, it is a house, and it is me.** The walk of the nineteen takes a day and a half of his time, out of a week he is not paid for, and Tarin Keel says out loud that it is the same condition as the woman who opens the gate. Ends on a person doing their work: the book shut, under a board, with a stone on it.

### Chapter 222 — Nobody Names A House
**Shelf day 92, the second day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 170.**
The question is whether the settlement names the nineteen houses, and there are two doors in the lane with no mark on either. **Jory Vellan, from the top of the lane, in about a minute: a list of houses is a list of people, and the day there is a list of people the next house is a house that is not on the list, and you will have a lane in about four years in which the two ends of it are argued about on the grounds of a piece of paper and neither end of it is a person.** Ilya Kever, seventy-four, born in the second house up the lane, says they are not houses, they are the ones with the tar on them, and that a line is a mark somebody cut once. **The finding is at the ninth door of the walk: the ninth answer is not the woman's, it belongs to the house across the lane, and a list of nineteen answers with no addresses is nineteen opinions while a list WITH addresses can be argued against the wrong door in a person's own front door.** She strikes the answer through and does not take it off. The question goes up the hill in a clerk's fair hand in four words, **ARE THE HOUSES NAMED**, and nobody answers it. Ends on a person doing their work: the pen washed and the board turned over.

### Chapter 223 — What The Anner Can Pay
**Shelf day 93, the third day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 171.**
The under-manager says **let it all be the Anner** in about six minutes, having waited six days for somebody to come up the hill and ask him about money, and every figure is his own and all of them are true: about eleven hundred tons a year, four pounds a ton at the pit's mouth, eleven pounds a ton at Sallowby, and the seven pounds between them is seven thousand seven hundred pounds a year and is not a profit, it is the road. **Nineteen roofs at nine pounds is forty-one thousand and forty pence, which is a hundred and seventy-one pounds with nothing over.** The frame at four pounds ten and the oak at one pound eight is one thousand four hundred and sixteen pence, five pounds eighteen. The three years owed to a woman of thirty-eight is two thousand five hundred and ninety-two pence, ten pounds sixteen, and it goes in this year. **And then the sentence he came up the hill to say, in about nine words: nineteen years and I have not spent a pound of the road on this valley, and a mine that pays a wage once a week is a different kind of mine than the one I have been the under-manager of since I was thirty-three, and I am not saying it is a reason to refuse.** Tarin Keel does the sum: forty-one thousand and forty, plus one thousand seven hundred and twenty-eight, plus one hundred and twelve, is forty-two thousand eight hundred and eighty pence, **a hundred and seventy-eight pounds, thirteen shillings and fourpence a year**, and out of one million eight hundred and forty-eight thousand that is **two and three-tenths in the hundred, and a man in a good coat would call that nothing, and it is nothing, and the thing the mine can pay is not the difficulty.** Two pages at a penny and a sealed copy at threepence is five pence and the woman who copies it is not paid for it. Ends on a person doing their work: four lines and a total in the Anner's own chain-book, which nobody will ever read.

### Chapter 224 — The Wage That Comes Every Week
**Shelf day 94, the fourth day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 172.**
The three years are paid in an envelope at the closing of the water in about ten minutes, and she counts it twice on her own sill and says it is the first money anybody in that lane has handed her in eleven years and she is not going to say thank you in the road. **And then the sentence the whole day is for, in nine words: it is not the four and six. Nine shillings a week for the sixteen weeks and nothing the rest of the year, and the half that is not the pit is the half she plans on, and what she has learned in eleven years at about four in the morning is that she does not need more money, she needs the money she has already been given to arrive on the day it is due.** **The second hand of the water-book is named and priced by the girl of seventeen herself: a penny a day for every day the water runs, sixteen weeks of seven days, a hundred and twelve pennies, nine shillings and fourpence, checked twice by her and once by a man who counts carts, and it is the first money anybody in this basin has ever paid anybody for looking at water, and about a fifteenth of the sluice-keeper's whole paid year.** The finding underneath it is a clerk's: the water-book has four hands in it and not one of them has ever stood at the frame, and on the third night of last week the mill hand and the Seat's hand disagree about that frame by about two hours, and both men were in the room and neither went up the hill. The order of the work goes on the paper in four lines, in the under-manager's mouth, and the timber is carried up the lane on the backs of about eleven people over two days and nobody writes it down except the man whose trade it is. Ends on a person doing their work: a barrow of stone up the lane, the long way round, on an evening when the wage was paid in full and on the day.

### Chapter 225 — A Man Who Lost A House Is Not A House
**Shelf day 95, the fifth day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 173. Day-count instance 11, at `225:59`.**
Nobody asks Coll Ferren anything for **eight days** after the counting — 173 − 165 = 8, and the chapter prints the subtraction — and the reason is that there is no form in this basin for standing in a doorway. The under-manager asks the wrong question in a lane, wanting a list of nineteen doors and numbers so that nobody can stand in front of the roofer and say he has done a roof he was not paid for, and gets four seconds of no. **If I am on that paper I am a thing on it, and a thing on a paper is a thing that gets looked at, and in four years there will be a man in this lane who says the number is wrong, and he will not be talking about the water.** He has been in that house since he was nine and it is gone, and a gone house is not a thing that is under anything. Then he says the sentence that changes the paper, **in eighteen words**, at the bottom of a lane: **a paper with a man's name on it is read out in a year when he is gone.** A man of thirty-one has put his own name at the foot of the draft in his own hand under three words, and says so out loud in a lane in about four minutes, and nobody asks him for a reason. **The houses come off the paper at the fifth hour and work and days go on: a roof is a thing you do to a house and a house is not a thing you do, and the day that lane has nineteen houses on a piece of paper is the day the twentieth house is a house that is not on a piece of paper, and there is a man in this valley who will be alive then and it will not be me.** **Fen Tregerran is asked to date the paper and refuses in nine words — his count is a count of dryings, the paper is about water, and a paper about water dated in a count of dryings is the two rows that do not meet — and puts his hand to it anyway, and says a hand and a date are two different acts.** The day on it is the water-book's, one hundred and seventy-three, written in a man's own hand. Ends on a person doing their work: a bed carried up out of a cart shed and put in a bottom room and not in a top room.

### Chapter 226 — What He Drafted
**Shelf day 96, the sixth day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 174. Block-quoted document 1, at `226:9`–`17`.**
**The draft, in the Seat's own hand, seven lines with the first struck through and left on the paper and three words under a name at the foot.** Five objections, in order, and every one made by a person the draft names or does not name, and not one by a man from four hundred miles off. **Wenna Skell, thirty-three, who copied it for nothing: you have struck it and left it on, and anybody who comes in here in a year will spend a month working out who took it back and why and will not get it right, because it was not a clerk who took it back.** **Ilma Treen, on the fourth line, in nine words: you have written *paid by the Anner and not by the Seat*, and the Seat did not fail to pay me, and nobody promised me the other four and six, and if you write *not by the Seat* then in a year somebody will ask the Seat why it stopped and the Seat will say it never started and both of them will be right, and I will be forty in that year and I will be the only person in it who knows which of the two is a lie.** **Garrow Lee, forty-one, on the third line: the frame does not want measuring again, it wants a gate, and if the paper says the frame is to be measured then the frame gets measured in the spring by a man with a rule and nothing happens and I will have measured it a third time in my life.** **Jory Vellan asks for the word *asked* and not *shall pay*, and wants his own hand on the line and says he would like it read out four times.** And a woman of about forty, on the seventh line: a copy kept in a lane by a person of the lane is kept by a man who cannot read it, and he is going to have it read to him every time it is read out, and every time it is read out it is going to be a different document, and you cannot put a clause in a paper about a thing that happens to a paper every time somebody reads it — and if you leave the line as it is she will not fight him about it, and if he puts her name to it she will fight him about it in this room and in the lane and in about four months. **Sera Quill, twenty-eight, refuses to put a hand to it at all, in nine words, and is right, and says her family's claim of six years is not filed and is not going to be filed in a valley, in about eleven words, and he may not speak for it and did not.** The strike is mentioned four times and the name at the foot is mentioned not at all. Ends with two documents on one wall that disagree with each other and neither of which is wrong.

### Chapter 227 — Six Lines, And Eleven Hands
**Shelf day 97, the seventh day of the fifty-third week. Basin day 175. The batch's System panel, at `227:53`–`54`. THE BATCH'S MIDPOINT.**
The paper takes the length of a working day and **the day was not in a room**: eleven people asked for a sentence, one at a time, in eleven places, and the four who could be found together did not sign in front of each other. The sheet on the wall is in eleven hands; the copy that goes down the hill is in one hand, the clerk's, because a copy has to be in one hand. Seven drafted lines become six, and the struck line stays struck with **three hands on it that do not agree** — his strike and his reason, a woman of about thirty-one with two children's argument that a house not on a piece of paper is not outside a piece of paper, and the clerk's sentence saying that two people in this lane do not agree. **And his name comes out, at the second refusal of a woman of about forty, in nine words: a paper with your name at the foot of it is the reason nobody came, in a year, when a woman at the eleventh house says a number went out of that lane and the roofs are not on nineteen houses, because a number can be asked for again and a name cannot.** He says *take it out* before she has finished, and then she refuses to let it be easy, and he says the reason, which is that he wanted a name there so that something would come back to, and he asks for it to be written down that a man of thirty-one said it in a lane in front of eleven people and was not asked for a reason. **Nobody asked him for a reason. Not one of the nine, and about thirty people alive in this valley have watched a man explain a thing he found once before into a room that had no use for it.** The space at the foot is not filled and a clerk of forty-four refuses to put a dash there, because a dash is a thing people put where a name used to be so that a later person thinks nothing was ever there. **The panel**, two plain lines, subject the finding: the six lines name six things and the eleven hands are on them, and the part of the sheet nobody will agree on is the part that says which houses are under the line; WHAT IS NOT DECIDED is whether a house put up after a line is drawn is inside the line or in front of it, and whether anyone in this basin will ever be the one to say. **And the count, said out loud unasked by a clerk of forty-four, who had watched six people go quiet: there are eleven hands on that sheet, and it is not the eleven houses and it is not the eleven marks and it is not the eleven feet and it is not the eleven seats in this room and it is not the eleven men at the pit, and if it were the same eleven it would mean something, and it does not mean the same eleven, and in nine years he has never once been able to say that about anything.** Ends with the copy going down the hill in a girl's hands to be read out in a lane.

### Chapter 228 — The Sheet In The Lane
**Shelf day 98, the first day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 176. Block-quoted document 2, at `228:13`–`20`.**
About forty people in the lane at the closing of the water because it has been said in three mouths in three rooms that there is a paper to be read out, and nobody in Hollow Sallow has ever had a paper read out in the lane. **The fourth line of the order on the wall has said since the hundred and fifty-fifth day that a copy is kept in the lane by a person of the lane, and nobody had ever asked what happens to a copy kept by a man who cannot read it, and the answer had been standing in a lane for a month.** The sheet, six lines, one hand, read aloud by the man it is about, who cannot read it. **Nobody stops him, and that is the finding, and it took forty people standing in a road to establish it and it could not be got any other way.** He changes two words: he puts in **and every week** after nine shillings a week, and says why, and says he was not in the room when a woman of thirty-eight said it and heard about it from a man who counts carts. And then he adds a line that is not on the paper at all: **and somebody to come and look at a wall before winter**, with no figure on it and not going to get one, because one of the nineteen asked whether the house was going to stand and has not been asked since. A woman of about forty says out loud that the sheet in Sallowby does not have it and the sheet in the lane has it and the two are the same piece of paper with one line on it that exists in one road, and she does not know what to do about it. **And she is also the woman who said the rest of it at `228:9`, in a room two days before, which is that a copy kept in a lane by a man who has it read to him is a different paper every time it is read; the first writing gave that paragraph to the clerk of forty-four and then called its owner *she*, and the review repair of 26 September 2026 gave it back to her.** **A clerk of forty-four, who came down because a copy is his job, says afterwards that he has stood in about forty roads in nine years making sure that what is written down is what was said, and watched a document acquire a line in about four seconds and not been able to do one single thing about it, and that the reason is that the man who acquired it is a person of the lane and the lane has a copy and the Seat has an original, and nobody has ever asked him which of those two is the document.** **The finding that closes it: two words and one sentence were added to a document in front of forty people and the document cost the same afterwards, and the two words cost nothing, and the sentence has no figure and will not get one.** Ends with a bed in a bottom room and a gate opened four miles off, and neither of the two people knows about the paper and both of them are in it.

### Chapter 229 — What The First Year Costs
**Shelf day 99, the second day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 177.**
The first roof comes off the second house from the bottom, the one with the door on its hinge, in about four days, four days longer than a roof on dry ground, and the man of fifty-six does not price that and is not asked to. The timber goes up on the backs of about eleven people over two days. The first wall is looked at on the second of that week, the chapter's own day: **two houses in the bottom half of the lane are not going to stand through a winter and one is going to have to come down and be put up again, and nobody in Hollow Sallow knew that and about six people have been saying since the spring of last year that they thought as much.** A man of about forty looks at it for nine minutes, says his hour is a shilling, and will not be paid by the village; the Anner offers and is refused and does not press it, **and about nine people noticed that he had offered and had been refused and that he was not offended, and that this was the first time in three weeks that anybody had seen anybody refuse the Anner and the Anner let it stand.** Then the sum, in full, on a bank, with the working. **£178 13s 4d a year, plus £16 14s once, is £195 7s 4d for the first year with everything owed in it, and the flood of nineteen roofs was £171, and the difference is £24 7s 4d — so the settlement of this valley costs more than the flood did.** And **a hair under one part in eight of the whole thing is not roofs**: a gate, three years of arrears to a woman of thirty-eight, and a hundred and twelve pennies to a girl of seventeen. And the other way of saying it: **three years and about six weeks more than the only wage anybody in that village has ever been paid.** And then the one thing that did not happen: **Hollis Nance puts it on the table in about eleven words and nobody argues with him. The bench is seized of the matter and will not hear anything else about this basin this year, and a paper taken nine days up a road costs five pounds and six and comes back as two paragraphs, and if it does not go, the paper is a paper of this valley and it stands or falls on the people in it, and nobody in Orison will be able to say in a year that a bench said so, and nobody in this valley will be able to say in a year that anybody anywhere said anything.** The under-manager supplies the first good reason anybody in that room has had in a month, and a clerk says he has been waiting nine days for one and had not told anybody because it looked like cowardice. Ends with a girl of seventeen paid seven pennies in a jar at the closing of the water, in front of about nine people, and saying the second hand of the water-book is now a job and not a favour.

### Chapter 230 — What The Sheet Does Not Say
**Shelf day 100, the third day of the fifty-fourth week. Basin day 178. Day-count instance 12, at `230:33`. The batch's close.**
The oak comes up on a cart and about nine people carry it the rest, and a joiner of forty-one who measured that frame in the fourth year after the marks were cut watches a thing he has charged for three times go past him, and hands the lath with five pounds eighteen on it in chalk to a girl of seventeen, who copies the figure onto the back of her own hand and throws it away in front of him. **The gate is hung in one day by two men, one of whom is a pitman of about thirty-five on ten shillings a week who was there on his own time, told nobody, and was not thanked for it. About thirty people came down a lane to watch a gate open, which is not a thing anybody has ever done in this basin, and about nine of the thirty were children and four of the nine had been under two feet of the Sallow in the week before last.** And the whole of what the six lines name is a roof, a gate, a wage, a penny, a payer and a reading, and the seventh line has no figure, and the struck line has three hands on it — **and not one of them names the height.** He had a pencil out and about four inches of space under the struck line and he did not write anything in it and put the pencil in his coat, **and he did not put it in because a recordwright said nine words and was right, and because he is not a party, and because there is no form in this basin for a man with nothing in his hands to have a paper in front of him, and because a man who has learned a thing once in a room in another county is not entitled to say it out loud a second time in a lane in a different county to a woman of thirty-four who lost a house.** He wrote it in his own book in four words and told nobody. **Nothing came up, and about eleven days ago he had begun, without noticing he was doing it, to expect it to say something, and on the third of that week it became clear that he had stopped expecting it, and he did not tell anybody that he had stopped expecting it, and there is no instrument in this basin for anybody to notice it in him.** The Shelf half of the book was not opened this week; the carrying is off nothing; the second notice is unpaid; the claim of forty-five pounds two shillings and eightpence is not paid and the carter of fifty-one is right; the clerk of thirty-four's letter is not opened; the entry is due in about nine months; and about four hundred and eighty-five pounds a year falls due at the close of a grain year in a county four hundred miles off and was not mentioned once in a valley that has just spent a hundred and ninety-five pounds and seven shillings and fourpence on nineteen houses. **The sheet is on the wall beside the four pages, which are still correct on their face and did this, and the two documents disagree with each other and neither of them is wrong, and the mine is a mine and the road is the road and the height is not on the paper.** Ends on a person doing their work: a gate opened at the closing of the water, a chair put back at a table, and a lath gone in a cart shed.
