## VOLUME 05 BATCH 0002 — Chapters 211–220, *The Four Pages, And The Water*. **The live block. Everything below is archive and is not edited.** Chapters 1–210 are canon; Volume 04 is closed, audited and repaired; `outline/volume-05.md` is the volume outline and `outline/series.md` outranks it.

### 211 — The Slow Is Down
**Shelf day 81, the fifth day of the fifty-first week. Basin day 159.** The causeway at Hollow Sallow is a hundred and forty years old and stood dry for the first time since the second shaking, and a carter of about forty is standing on it with a crowbar because the Anner shut it under an order that named a dam and a height and did not mention him: five days each way is ten days out of a hundred and forty, nine carters, the Anner paying all of it and rather not (**211:5**, **211:9**). **The slow had been down six days and there were about two feet of it standing in the lane.** The copy of the four pages has been on the doorpost of the third house from the top for three days, and **THE FINDING IS IN A GIRL OF SEVENTEEN'S MOUTH, IN A LANE, AND NOT IN HIS: it says how high the water is and it does not say high as from where (211:29).** She has been in that lane since she was born. The woman of about forty who washes the pen brings the finding up to the Seat's room and Hollis Nance has the chamber's abstract of three rulings out on the table and asks for both documents to be read aloud. **The order names a sill for the dam and not for the houses, and the chamber of plenty, in its third turn and nine years back, said that no order may name a height without naming the sill it is taken from (211:45, 211:49).** A voice from the door says *then it is void* and **Jory Vellan says it is not void and he is right, because the ruling is about a mark on a doorpost and not about a height named in an order (211:55).** **The finding of the whole day is that there is no form for asking a chamber whether its own order breaks its own ruling, and all three rulings are about this basin and none has been in that room except since the second of the week (211:61).** A second matter goes to Orison: **£5 6s, two of them £10 12s, nine days, and the clerk of the Seat pays his own five pounds and six out of a column that does not exist and says so first (211:69, 211:73).** The bag is dated on the outside with a day out of the water-book because a grain year does not exist in this basin. **Day-count instance 6 at `211:89`, day 159, and it is the first time in about a year that he has said the number out loud to anybody.** A girl of seventeen has read the four pages at all. Nine carts stand in the wet on the high road at the closing of the water and the clay goes on in the same order it has gone on in for eleven years.

### 212 — The Standing Order Nobody Has Read
**Shelf day 82, the sixth day of the fifty-first week. Basin day 160.** The frame at Hollow Sallow is oak and about twice the height of a man and has been in the same place since before the first shaking, the gate in it is four years old, and behind the gate is a second frame that came at the same time and does nothing, and the chalk on the lath in it says **four pounds ten for the frame and one pound eight for the oak, which is five pounds eighteen, and nobody will buy it (212:9)**. Ewan Troke goes down to Sallowby and comes back with **one page in the flat of his hand — block-quoted document one, the standing order of the sluice, four lines, at `212:21`–`24` — and it is the only order in this basin anybody has ever had to keep to and it has been kept to every year without anybody knowing it existed.** **THE FINDING: the order does not name a day, it names a weather — the day the pans are turned at Coldbeck — and a salting is a drying, seven weeks in a dry year and eleven in a wet one, and the only man in the basin who could say in advance which year it is has never been asked (212:34).** It is the eleventh salting of the forty-ninth year and the bond is the eleventh salting of the fortieth, and that is the same salting of a year nine along, and nobody has ever done that sum (**212:28**). The money comes out because it is the only thing about a sluice anybody can say: **nine shillings a week for sixteen weeks is £7 4s, the Seat owes four and six of it and three years of it is £10 16, and she is paid for a hundred and twelve days of the hundred and forty she works, and the twenty-eight is four weeks, and four weeks at four and six is eighteen shillings exactly (212:46, 212:48)**. The four hundred and eleven pounds a year is a kitchen figure and two people asked for it give two different numbers and one says she does not know it. **THE TURN, and it is in a book and not in a mouth: on the ninth the sluice was shut and the water was in the hollow and nobody came — in the mill hand, three weeks and a day old, written by the woman who has been the gate for eleven years, on the Seat's own book, in forty leaves of it, and nobody in nine years has ever asked her what is on them (212:64, 212:68, 212:70).** She says out loud that she has known for eleven years that the day the pans are turned is a different day every year. The gate is opened at the closing of the water in the ordinary way (**212:86**), and the lath with the five pounds eighteen on it goes back in the frame (**212:88**), and the four pages and the bond both say nothing whatever about a gate or a frame or an oak and both are correct.

### 213 — The Last Day Of The Fifty-First Week
**Shelf day 83, the seventh and last day of the fifty-first week. Basin day 161.** The water is against the ninth doorpost at the second light and about nine people are on the bank, which is four more than had ever been there at once. **A man of seventy-four comes up the lane with a bucket of tar and a ball of string. He was born in the second house up that lane, and everybody there knows it and nobody had said so to him.** He had been given the whole of it in the Seat's room on the first of the week and had not said a word during any part of it. **THE FINDING: he puts the water against the ninth doorpost and cuts a tar line at it, walks up to the fifth and does the same, and the two new lines are level with each other because water is level (213:13, 213:25). The water is a foot above the old mark on the ninth and a foot below the old mark on the fifth, which makes the two old marks two feet apart — and Garrow Lee, forty-one, who has had his own shoulder against both of them since he was twenty-six, says they are a foot apart, and neither man is lying, and one of them is wrong by a foot, and nobody can say which, because neither man has had water on both marks in the same hour (213:25, 213:31).** He asks whether the chamber's second ruling of nine years back was about this, and is told it was, **and he says they are nine years late and they are right, and that he is not going to start on the last day of a week by saying whether he cut the eleven (213:45).** A woman of thirty-three who copies deeds over a chandler's shop reads the third line out on the bank and puts her hand on the doorpost and asks the first question anybody in that village has ever asked about a document — **high as from where** — and gets an answer in the wrong shape from the only person on the bank who has ever put anything on a doorpost (**213:49, 213:53, 213:57**). **Day-count instance 7 at `213:69`, day 161, said out loud on a bank because a number said out loud in front of five people costs nothing and is worth something, and Garrow Lee writes it on the lath under the marks and puts a barrow against it.** The man of seventy-four puts the tar on the stone by the ninth doorpost, picks the empty bucket up and goes up the lane, and the water goes on doing what it is doing and a woman of thirty-eight opens a gate of oak in the ordinary way.

### 214 — Asking Eleven People
**Shelf day 84, the first day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 162.** The Seat's one room has **a table with nine things on it and no form in this basin for any of them** — a sheet, a second sheet, a stub of lead, twine, a pot of tar with a brush, a rule, the water-book, a sheet with the chamber's second ruling on it in Ewan Troke's flat hand, and a lamp, which nobody had lit and which is not on the list. Hollis Nance says in his first words that he is not a Bench clerk, not a recordwright and not an advocate, and that there is no instrument in that room that makes eleven seats decide anything. **Nobody in the party can compel a person, and there is no form at the Seat for asking a person of Hollow Sallow a question that matters, because a thing that is kept in this basin is a thing somebody can take away eleven years later, and the woman who keeps the sluice has not been in that room in eleven years for exactly that reason (214:19).** **THE FINDING, and it is the batch's: asking eleven people costs three days, and three days is not a figure, and a figure is a thing you can put in a minute and take out of it again (214:21, 214:23).** The Anner will not answer for the village; the village would not answer for the Anner and nobody asked; the Seat has eleven seats and eight of them have never had anybody in them. He spends the three days anyway, because the only two things anybody in this valley has ever been made are a mark on a doorpost and a page on a wall, and both were made without asking anybody — and his book says only this: **three days, day one spent, the water is two feet and rising, I have asked nobody anything and I am going to ask eleven people tomorrow, which is the same as saying I am not going to, because tomorrow I will be at a dam (214:43).** **Nobody in this basin has asked him a single question in thirteen days and he has got used to it, and he writes that down, and that it is not a relief, because a man nobody is waiting on is a man who cannot be held to the thing he came for (214:49).** The lane gets the order read to it at the closing of the water **by a clerk of a Seat who has no authority to read it in a lane and does it anyway, on eleven chairs carried down a hill, and nobody signs anything (214:55, 214:59)**, and it is the third thing he has done in eleven days that he has no authority to do and it is the worse of the three. A paper comes off the wall in Sallowby and goes back up on it, crooked, and the woman of about forty looks at it for as long as it takes to grind ink and then washes the pen.

### 215 — Eleven Feet, Held Exactly
**Shelf day 85, the second day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 163.** Four men and a barrow on the Anner dam. **THE HEIGHT IS HELD EXACTLY AND ON PURPOSE: eleven feet and an inch at the low end and ten feet and eleven inches at the high end, and it took a man with a barrow and a string and most of a morning, because the paper says eleven feet and does not say where along the dam (215:11).** The order's money in a mouth on a bank: **forty loads of clay at 9d and a hundred and forty of rubble at 3d is £3 5s a year out of the Anner's own book and has never once been in a bill to the Seat, and four men for a week on the Anner wage is forty shillings, which is £2, so the whole week's labour of the four men holding the height costs about twice what a year of material costs, and neither figure is in a document (215:15).** In the office with ochre worked into the boards: **a thing that is void and unread is not a protection, it is an absence — and the forty pounds in the box says that if the Anner holds eleven feet then Hollow Sallow will not be flooded, and the Anner has held eleven feet every day for eleven years, and every load and every week has come out of a pit that sells its ochre seven pounds a ton dearer in Sallowby than at its own mouth (215:27).** He is asked what the height is for and **answers that the height is for the road, which is the sentence he gave unasked on the sixth day of the fiftieth week and which is in a chain-book a week later because a man of thirty-one could not hold four figures and a hand at once (215:41).** **THE FINDING, NINE WORDS, IN HIS OWN MOUTH, IN OCHRE DUST: I HAVE BEEN GIVEN A NUMBER AND NEVER A REASON (215:43).** He is right. **A dam is not held by a decision, it is held by a number that everybody can repeat, and a thing held exactly is a thing held to a figure, and a figure is not a decision, and correctly is the whole of the danger (215:49, 215:51).** **The Anner is the only body in this basin with men enough to hold a dam, and a man with men enough to hold a dam is not looking at eleven houses, and that is not a fault, that is the arithmetic (215:55).** The bag is still in the gap in the wall, the man with the bag is not due for six weeks, the second matter went in on the fifth day of last week and the answer is about nine days off, **and the water does not wait nine days and has never in the history of this basin waited nine days for anything (215:59).**

### 216 — The Night
**Shelf day 86, the third day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 164. THE MIDPOINT, PART ONE.** Four men and a barrow and a string on the dam at the second light, and there have been four men on that dam in the working years of every year since the bond was lodged, and the Anner is about four hundred strong in the working years and about sixty in the off ones, **and the four were the four the pit could spare, and the pit had decided that at the second light and nobody asked it how (216:3).** The night dressing is put on in a man's own mouth at ten in the morning: **twenty loads of clay at 9d is 180d, thirty loads of rubble at 3d is 90d, and the two together are 270d, which is one pound two and six, out of the Anner's book for one night, against a year of three pounds five, and he has put a third of a year on a dam in a night and would like somebody to write that down and nobody ever writes anything down (216:9).** **THE REVERSAL: the height is held exactly, as instructed, lawfully, by the only body with enough men, and the four of them from the valley are on the dam and none of them was asked to do anything, because there is nothing to be asked to do (216:7).** At about the middle of the afternoon a carter comes down off the ridge and says that the Sallow is **coming up backwards**, because a river that rises has somewhere to go and a river that comes up backwards has had its somewhere taken off it, and what was taken off it was the causeway, and the causeway was taken off it by four lines on a wall in a market town (216:17).** Nine carters stand on a bank at the fourth light with nothing to do and the order does not say a word about them. The woman who keeps the sluice comes out of the third house from the top and opens the gate in the ordinary way at the closing of the water. **THE GATE DID ITS JOB, AND IT IS NOT A FIGURE OF SPEECH AND NOT A DEFENCE: it took the water off the Hollow and put it down the frame, and the frame took it, and the job ended at the frame (216:27). The water is going over the top of it (216:31).** **THE ARITHMETIC, PRINTED WHERE A READER CAN DO IT IN THEIR HEAD: the Anner's sill is the dam's own sill and it is the high one, the frame at Hollow Sallow is nine feet below it, eleven feet above the Anner's sill is therefore two feet above the frame's sill, and two feet above the frame's sill is about the height of the floors of the houses on the upper half of that lane (216:43, 216:45). And the finding in nine words: the eleven feet is the dam's number and not the lane's (216:49).** He goes down the bank to look at the frame and **his leg is what his leg has been since a morning four hundred miles and some weeks behind him, and he has not told one person in this valley what any of that is, and there is nobody here he is going to tell (216:51)**. **NOBODY DROWNED, and that is not a mitigation and is not going to be written as one: nineteen houses had water in them by the time the light went and about a hundred and forty people were in them, on a slow night in a wet year in a village of about four hundred and ten, and the girl of seventeen read the third line out loud to about twenty people standing in two feet of the Sallow, and the third line says that no person of Hollow Sallow is to be asked to leave any house, and nobody was, and it is the only one of the four lines anybody in that lane could have used and it is the reason they were standing in it (216:55, 216:57).** The nineteen that are under water are the nineteen that are under water for the next four months and the other three hundred and seventy went to bed. **Block-quoted document two, a page of the water-book, three lines, at `216:63`–`65`: the Seat's own hand on the sluice standing open, the mill hand on the side being up to the sill of the fourth house and the ninth house under to the lamp, and no hour against either line and no column in that book for an hour.** Ewan Troke reads it out on the bank twice and the two readings differ in nothing. **Day-count instance 8 at `216:73`, day 164, written in the dark with a stub of lead and his thumb for a rest, because there was no lamp oil left in the lane by the middle of the afternoon.** **AND THE CHAPTER DOES NOT END ON A COMPLETED BEAT. It ends with a woman of thirty-eight putting a barrow down in the road and not lighting the one lamp in that village and standing in the dark with her hands on the handles — the same gesture as at the end of Chapter 210 and not the same evening, and nobody in that lane is going to be told the difference (216:77).**

### 217 — Nineteen Houses
**Shelf day 87, the fourth day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 165. THE MIDPOINT, PART TWO.** They count it at the first light and the people who count it are the people who live in it, on foot, because there is nowhere in Hollow Sallow a cart can go that the Anner's carts could not have gone on the causeway nine days ago. **Eleven is what the order said and what the marks said and the eleven were right about the eleven. Nineteen is what is under. The eight are houses that came up after the marks were cut, one of them a barn that had a door and a hearth and a family in it by the year the third house from the top was rebuilt, and the man who turned the barn into a house cut no mark because nobody alive in the lane at the time had been told to, and he is forty-four and did not know for four days that his house was in anything (217:5, 217:9, 217:11).** **AND THE CHAPTER SAYS PLAINLY THAT NOBODY IN THIS VALLEY IS A VILLAIN, and sets out the three sentences of the bond: hold the dam to eleven feet above its own sill, Hollow Sallow not to be flooded by the Anner, the Anner not answerable for any flooding not held by that height. The first two are the promise and the promise was kept exactly by the party it names (217:13). The village the mine had promised to protect is flooded by the fulfilment of the mine's promise, and that is not a sentence anybody in this basin is going to be able to improve on this year.** About a hundred and forty people out of about four hundred and ten are in the nineteen; the rest had the water out by the noon light. **Nobody drowned. Nobody is ruined. Both of those are true at the same time in the same lane on the same morning and there is no word in this basin that holds both of them (217:21).** **A man of fifty-six who does roofs comes over the bank with a ladder, looks at nineteen roofs, and says about nine pounds and will not split it: a roof wet through, taken off and put back and the timber under it, and he has never given anybody a price in parts in his life and is not starting this year (217:23, 217:29).** **THE BATCH'S ONE SYSTEM PANEL, two plain bold lines at `217:35`–`36`, introduced by a narrative line saying the thing came up in the interface's own two plain lines: the four lines name a dam, a height, a day and a party to pay, and they name nobody else, and the part of the document that was never drawn is the water; and the second line is a WHAT IS NOT DECIDED line about whether a thing that was not named may be carried by a party that was.** It takes nothing out of him, it answers nothing, and nobody in that lane saw anything. **THE FINDING, IN HER OWN MOUTH, AND SHE IS NOT A LAWYER AND IS NOT A LAWYER BECAUSE THERE IS NO LAWYER IN THIS BASIN: it named a dam, it named a height, it named a day, it never named the water (217:48).** A man of thirty-three with a book in his coat does not write it down for about four minutes and then does, on the basin side of a page that has a day at the top of it. **THE MONEY, ONCE, IN THE MOUTH OF A MAN WHO COUNTS CARTS ON ROADS AND NOT ARGUED: nineteen houses at about nine pounds a roof is £171 — £9 is 2,160d, ×19 is 41,040d, and that is £171 with nothing over (217:60) — and £171 is 41,040d and a sluice-keeper's whole year is 1,728d, so £171 is 23.75 years of it, which is about twenty-four (217:66), and she is standing about ten feet away in the road and has been in the middle of that figure for eleven years and is in it again this morning with two feet of the Sallow in her own house.** The chapter closes on a door that is still on its hinge, because the hinge is above the line the water got to, and on **a woman of about forty carrying the Seat's hundred-year-old water-book down four miles in her own two hands because she was not going to wait, who does not open it in the lane and does not open it in the house and puts it on the sill of a house with two feet of the Sallow in it and turns round and goes back up the hill, where a clerk of the Seat is standing in the road with a lamp, doing his work.**

### 218 — The Person The Order Did Not Name
**Shelf day 88, the fifth day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 166. THE MIDPOINT, PART THREE.** The Sallow turned in the night and is falling about a foot a day, and there are nine people in the Seat's one room, four of them there on the day the four pages went on the wall, plus a joiner who came on his own and a girl of seventeen who came because she could not get a thing out of her head. **He gets to the thing nobody has said out loud in four minutes and it is not the thing anybody expected: they should come off the wall — and he says he is not going to take them down and that he has no authority and is not a party and there is no form in this basin for a man with nothing in his hands to have a wall in front of him (218:7).** **THEY STAY, and the reason is the clerk's: they are the only document this basin has produced in about a year, and the press is the only thing in that room that has ever been asked to remember anything, and the keys to it are in the inside pocket of his coat where they live, and a valley with nothing at all is a valley where the next person who comes up a road with a piece of paper is the first person anybody here has ever seen (218:17).** The second matter has not come back and the first has not come back and cannot come back before nine days, and nine days off that is this morning. **And there are about thirty clerks in a building with a yard in that city and every one of them is somebody's clerk and did a job properly and not one of them is going to do a ninth day's work for a basin that has not sent anybody to ask, and a distance is harder to be angry at than a man and it is exactly as expensive (218:21).** **HE NAMES THE FOURTH COLUMN OF HIS OWN INDEX OUT LOUD AND SAYS HE IS NOT GOING TO ASK ABOUT IT, that he has kept that book up to date for nine years and has never once asked what is in a column of his own index, and that he wants it on the record that he named it first and did not ask — and nobody says anything about that either (218:25).** The under-manager says the height is right, the dam is right, the party is right, the day is early and he would have done it eleven days early without the paper, and **there is not a single thing wrong with any of that (218:33).** **THEN THE CATEGORY, IN HIS OWN MOUTH, AND IT IS NOT THE SENTENCE HE SAID ONCE: there is a sentence I said once, in a room, in another county, about a category rather than about a place, and I am not going to say it again and I am not going to explain it and there is nobody in here who is going to ask me to. Here is the part of it that is about this wall — A RULE THAT NAMES NO BYSTANDER IS CARRIED BY THE NEAREST BODY WITH HANDS (218:39).** He does not quote the four words and he does not explain them and he does not relieve himself of the first time. **NOBODY ASKS HIM TO EXPLAIN IT, and the chapter says so and says why: there are about thirty people alive who have watched a man explain a thing he found once before into a room that had no use for it, and not one of them has forgotten it (218:43).** They argue for two hours and the argument is not about whether the four lines are right. **THE WOMAN OF ABOUT FORTY WHO WASHES THE PEN: if it comes off that wall, then in three months' time there is a woman in this lane saying a number went out of here and nobody in Sallowby has ever heard of it, and she will be right, and there will be nothing on any wall in this basin to say she is wrong, and somebody will come in six weeks and ask what the four pages were for, and the wall is the only place she can put her hand on anything (218:51).** Nobody takes the four pages off the wall, and there is no minute of it, because the Seat keeps no minutes. **HIS NAME IS NOT ON THE FOUR PAGES AND NEVER WAS, and not on the bond, the standing order, the marl-strip deed, the chain-book or the hand-book, and there is no line in this valley carrying his name on anything at all, and it is the one fact in this volume that has not gone wrong, and about six of the nine people in the room knew it, and not one of them said a word, because saying it would have been a kindness, and this basin has never in nine years done anybody a kindness in a room (218:63).** The chapter closes with the Sallow falling at the Anner and the four men on the dam, and four miles off **a man of sixty-one coming off the far side of the eleventh pan with a board, the sixth salting out and the pans in and the year turned over, a hundred and sixty-five notches in the upper edge of a board cut one notch a day for thirty years, and he does not cut one, because the day is not over — and nobody on the north side of the flats that evening knew that anybody in the lane at Hollow Sallow had spent the whole day in a room arguing about a word on a wall (218:71).**

### 219 — What Is Under, In Money
**Shelf day 89, the sixth day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 167.** There is no word in this basin for what a man does when his house is under water and no book that could be opened and no office nine days off that does this. **THE SHEET IS THE BACK OF A LEAF of the hundred-year-old water-book, and the front of the leaf has the sluice on it in the mill hand, and a hundred years of a river has been kept on one side of it and somebody is about to put a village on the other (219:5).** The money is done three times and gets three answers, all of them honest. **The Anner: about eleven hundred tons a year at £4 a ton at the pit's mouth and £11 at Sallowby, the difference of £7 a ton is £7,700 a year, and forty-five times £171 is £7,695, so nineteen roofs are a forty-fifth of the difference between what a ton costs at the mouth and what it costs in the market, and five pounds short of even that — and the £7,700 is not a profit, it is the road, and there is no figure for the Anner's road in any book in this valley, and the man who would have it is asleep in a shed four miles up the river because he was on a dam until the middle of the night (219:13).** The chamber does not do this. **And the Seat: it is said to have four hundred and eleven pounds a year, that is in a kitchen, about four hundred and ten people have heard it, not one can say where it came from, and of the three people asked to say the whole of it out loud two gave different numbers and one said she did not know it — and a hundred and seventy-one is NOT a quarter of it, it is a quarter of it and sixty-eight pounds and five shillings more, because a quarter of four hundred and eleven is a hundred and two pounds and fifteen shillings, and the more is a figure from a man of fifty-six with a ladder on his shoulder, and there is no more than that in this valley (219:25).** **THE TURN: the woman of about forty puts the sheet down on the wall and asks the wrong question on purpose — not what it costs, but what you need — and says she will write down exactly what is said, will not read it back, and that her sheet has no heading because there is no form in this basin for this, and that if it is a bad document it is a bad document and it is the first one in this valley that is about us and not about land (219:37). Nobody signed it either. She put a mark under every answer, not a tally of anything, and she did not add the marks up and nobody else did (219:39).** **THE NINETEEN ANSWERS, in the order she walked, written as they were said and not tidied, in running prose and not block-quoted because the batch has two block-quoted documents and not three (219:45).** They are about a dry floor, a bed out of the bottom room, a wall looked at before winter, salt out of plaster, a dead woman's chair, whether a house is going to stand, a roof before the frost, seed in a cellar, **to be told it was nobody's doing**, boards, a child's cot, which of two doors to shut at night, water in the well, a door still on its hinge, somebody to write down that it was nothing, nineteen years of ledgers, a cart to get ochre off a floor, **to be asked before the water and not after it**, and somebody to hold the other end of the sheet. **NOT ONE OF THEM IS MONEY, and that is the finding: two of the nineteen are about somebody being asked at the right time and one is about the other end of a piece of paper (219:47).** **He did not ask the nineteen anything, and the chapter says so, and the woman of about forty tells him why: you are not a party to this, and if you turn up at that cart shed and put your name at the bottom of that sheet then it is not a list of what nineteen people need, it is a list of what a man from four hundred miles off found out, and the four hundred miles is in it, and the leg is in it, and I have not asked about the leg and I am not going to (219:61) — and nobody in that road had said a word to him about the leg (219:63).** The list goes up the hill, is read by nobody, is not in the press and not in the chain-book and is not sewn to anything and has no other half nine miles away under a floor, and goes into a cart shed under a board with a stone on it, and **it is the first document anybody in this basin has ever written about themselves, and a man of thirty-one has not read it and is not going to read it, and it is the only page in this volume that is not a record of land (219:67).** A woman of thirty-eight comes up out of the Sallow and turns up the lane instead of going straight on, the whole three hundred yards of it, because the short way was still under, which is what she does every evening and which she did with two feet of water in her own house on the third night of that week.

### 220 — A Person Doing Their Work
**Shelf day 90, the seventh and last day of the fifty-second week. Basin day 168.** **The water is down and the mud is not, and the chapter is careful about the difference: the water goes down a bed that has a shape in it, the mud does not, and there is a crust on the top of it and mud underneath the crust and three inches of it in the fourth house and it is not going anywhere (220:3).** Eight of the nineteen are still under a foot and a half; the eleven on the upper half are out and full of mud; the third house from the top is the driest and has been since the second hour of the fourth night. **Nobody in the Red Basin is redeemed. The order is on the wall in the Seat's room and on a doorpost and it is correct on its face and there is no remedy on it and there is not going to be one this week and there is no line in it about a roof or a floor or a bed or a door, and the mine is a mine (220:9).** **The letter came up the Shelf road with a man who was going to Coldbeck for a horse and was in the room for about an hour before anybody opened it, and the clerk opened it in front of six people and said the thing first, for the third time in eleven days, and that nothing in this valley has changed to make the sentence shorter (220:13). IT IS TWO PARAGRAPHS AND IT IS SIGNED BY A CLERK OF THE CHAMBER AND HE DID HIS JOB PROPERLY: the Bench is seized of the matter and will consider it in its own time and no time is given, and the second paragraph quotes back the first of the three rulings word for word — that is nine years old — and the two matters together cost ten pounds and twelve, five of which was Ilyan's and seven of which was the clerk's out of a column that does not exist, and neither of them is going to be paid for or thanked for (220:21, 220:23, 220:27).** Nobody thanked anybody. **Day-count instance 9 at `220:33`, day 168, and it is the ninth time in nineteen days, and 168 − 149 = 19, the first instance being `201:78` on the day they arrived, and nine of the nine are out of the same book and the same count. THE CHAPTER SAID *SEVENTEEN DAYS* AND `220:61` SAID *SEVENTEEN DAYS*; both were corrected on the Batch 0002 review and the working is here.** **He then reads the Shelf side of his own book out loud to about nine people on a bank, which he has not done in another county and had not planned to do here: the notice of four sheets at five shillings and fourpence, never paid and not going to be forgiven; the claim of a carter of fifty-one with a boy, eleven miles off, forty-five pounds two shillings and eightpence, not producible, no form for asking, and he is right; a dead man in the fourth line of a list of two hundred and forty whose wife is on the fourth line and knows she is on the fourth line; the minute of the first of the forty-eighth week, one sheet, the only copy, in a drawer four miles off with nobody's name on it; the box of about nine hundred and forty forms, six miles off, not found, and not going to be asked for this month; and Nesh Arrad, thirty-nine, and the clock on her side of this is running, and he is not printing the figure because the figure is a figure of the other side of the book (220:37).** He stops there, a man of about forty says *there is one more*, and **he says there is one more and he is not going to say it (220:39) — and that is the new question, and it is not asked and not answered and not compressed into one word, and nobody in the Red Basin asks him which year it was, and he is not relieved of the not being asked (220:41).** **The other side's year turns in about forty weeks and he is not printing the figure, and when it turns then four hundred and eighty-five pounds falls due on an account of nine thousand seven hundred and the district of Ryefold is at nothing and it does not stop and it is not a Red Basin figure and there is no column in this basin for it and there never will be and he has stopped hoping for one (220:45).** The last two hours are four ordinary things and none of them is a decision: the four men and the barrow on the dam for the ninth day, the Sallow falling and the wet workings dry; a joiner who does not measure the frame again until there is a fund and leaves the lath with five pounds eighteen on it in the frame; a woman of thirty-eight who comes up out of the Sallow, puts the barrow down first, and opens the gate; and a clerk who washes the pen, turns the board over because it is the end of a week, puts a chair back at the table and squares four pages that are crooked and does not take them down. **The System puts nothing up and says nothing whatever about any of it (220:61).** And the batch ends on a person doing their work: a gate at the closing of the water and a chair put back at a table, a hundred and sixty-eight days of river in a book in a cart shed, about a hundred and seventy-one pounds of flood under the lane, the order on the wall, and the mud not down (**220:63**).

## VOLUME 05 BATCH 0001 — Chapters 201–210, *The Red Basin*. **The live block. Everything below is archive and is not edited.** Chapters 1–200 are canon; Volume 04 is closed, audited and repaired; `outline/volume-05.md` is the volume outline and `outline/series.md` outranks it.

### 201 — The Road That Is Not Where It Began
**Shelf day 71, the second day of the fiftieth week. Basin day 149 since the second shaking.** Three people come to the end of a nine-day road and the basin is red and low and has a floor. **Tarin Keel measures the road twice, throws the first set away, and refuses to say which of three explanations it is (201:13).** Ewan Troke, a chainman of twenty-nine, has come up the Shelf road with a case of papers because he heard about them at a market; nobody sent him (201:21). The road crosses the **marl ridge**, the only ground in the basin a house will stand on above the flood line, and about four hundred and ten people and eleven houses are in the story before anybody sits down. **THE FINDING: one word, *common*, defined in the margin of each of two deeds and not in the body of either, eighty-two years apart in one margin and nine turns in the other, and the two definitions are incompatible and both men were telling the truth (201:39, 201:46, 201:50).** The four pages are planned on the road in three mouths, in nine words each, and nobody improves on it. Ilyan says what he is and does not say the other half of it, which is that he could not have drafted the four pages. **He writes the day at the top of a page and it is a day out of a water-book and not a day of the Shelf (201:78), and tells nobody what the number is.** **The last line is Ewan Troke's and it is the volume's problem in a form nobody can act on: there is nothing wrong with your four pages, and there is nobody in this basin who can be in the room when they are read, and he has been trying for eleven years to get one and has not got one (201:98, 201:102).**

### 202 — Fifty Saltings, And A Count Nobody Keeps
**Shelf day 72. Basin day 150.** The salt-pans above Coldbeck at the second light, and a man of sixty-one drawing a board through the fourth pan, and he talks because they came up a bank for water and he had a kettle. **A board with a hundred and forty-nine notches, one a day, and two heaps of stones, eleven a day, and the large one at a thousand six hundred and thirty-nine (202:11).** **THE FINDING, said once, in his own mouth, by a man scraping salt, without knowing he has said anything: the pan-book year, the turn-count and the day-count do not convert, and there is no arithmetic to do it with, because a salting has no length and no first drying and the pans' year does not begin on the same drying twice (202:45).** The first eight turns were numbered on a door frame by a man four short of the true one who corrected it himself in the front of his own book, in a better hand, because he was frightened of it, and **about nine people in this basin know that and about four hundred do not care (202:31).** Wenna Skell asks the first question anybody has asked him in eleven years, in nine words. **The finding is credible because the pans are the only count in this basin that is not about land.** A hundredweight of salt is a pound and fourpence, which is twenty-four shillings, and fifty-two of them down the bank on a barrow is sixty-two pounds and eight of salt a year, and the man who does the barrow gets five pounds and four of it and is seventy-one and is on no document anywhere (202:81). **Day-count instance 2 at 202:83.**

### 203 — Two Halves Of One Deed
**Shelf day 73. Basin day 151.** Sallowby, a room over a chandler's shop, Wenna Skell, thirty-three, who has copied about six hundred and forty deeds in eleven years and about ninety for the Anner, at a penny a page and threepence a sealed copy, and who **says the price before the fact because the price before the fact is the only price there is (203:11).** **THE FINDING, said while copying, in her own mouth, and she does not know she has said it: a deed in this basin is not a paper, it is an agreement between two papers, because the strip is longer than a skin and each man drew the half he could see from where he was standing, and a person who loses one of them has not lost a thing — they have become one of two people each holding half, and neither half is a lie (203:29, 203:31, 203:70).** Nobody in this basin has ever lost a deed. **What they do is stop bringing the halves to each other.** The second half is nine miles away under a floor at Coldbeck and a woman of seventy there says her grandfather asked the same question in the first year and let it go and that she is not going to be the one to start it (203:50). Jory Vellan, fifty-two, comes to the door and does not come in, and the second half carries his wife's name, Ruth, dead four years, drawn a year after, in a hand that is not his and not the scrivener's, **and there is a word at the foot of it under her name and he has read the piece nine times in three years and has never once asked anybody to read it out (203:88).** **SERA QUILL REFUSES HIM ONCE, IN NINE WORDS, AND SHE IS RIGHT, and the reason is a recordwright's reason and it is about four hundred and ten people (203:94).** She is owed eleven pence by a woman two streets down who has said every market day for two years that she will pay it, and she has never written the eleven pence down (203:104).

### 204 — The Sluice, And The Half Wage
**Shelf day 74. Basin day 152.** Hollow Sallow, nine feet from the sill of the sluice to the bed. **Ilma Treen, thirty-eight, eleven years in the job, says the whole of her wage before she is asked anything: nine shillings a week for the sixteen weeks the Sallow runs and nothing the rest of the year, which is £7 4s, of which the Anner gives four and six and the Seat owes four and six and has owed it for three years, which is £10 16 (204:21).** She has never been in the Seat's room and there are two women in this village who have. The water-book comes to the bank in the flat of a chainman's hand and it is read out, and the last entry in it is in her own hand, because she has a mill on the Anner water and writes on the Seat's book since the Seat cannot make her buy one. **THE FINDING: she has been opening the sluice eleven days early in every one of eleven years to keep nine carts a day off a causeway that the water goes over, and she lost that causeway nine years back with a cart and a mule on it and nobody in either, and the Anner shut the road for nine days and said so in four rooms and the Seat said the sluice was open and nothing else (204:73).** She has held the water in that Hollow for a hundred and forty days a year and been paid for a hundred and twelve of them, which is four weeks of water she holds and is not paid for, and Ilyan does the sum out loud in front of her: twenty-eight days is four weeks, and four weeks at four and six the week is eighteen shillings exactly and there is nothing over (204:77, `204:91`, `204:97`). **THE QUESTION NOBODY HAD ASKED HER WAS ASKED BY TARIN KEEL, IN NINE WORDS — how many days a year are you paid for, and how many days a year do you work (204:81).** He does the arithmetic out loud twice because she tells him to say it again and not to say it to a page: **a hundred and forty days and a hundred and twelve paid is twenty-eight days, and twenty-eight days is four weeks; a wage is a week's wage; four weeks at four and six is eighteen shillings exactly and there is nothing over (204:97).** **This line said *twenty-five days is three weeks and four days, and thirteen shillings and six*, out of a chapter that has been corrected, and every part of it was wrong: ninety paid and a hundred and forty worked leave fifty days and not twenty-five, and fifty days is seven weeks and a day and not three weeks and four days. She is owed more than this line said and the money is exact.** **Day-count instance 3 at 204:93.** He tells nobody what the number is and there was no reason on earth why he was going to start in a village four miles from a chandler's shop (204:95).

### 205 — A Bond Keeps A Thing True By Costing Somebody Money
**Shelf day 75. Basin day 153.** The water-seat's one room, eleven seats, eight of them never used. **Hollis Nance, forty-four, says in his first nine words that he is not a Bench clerk, not a recordwright and not an advocate, and that the price of taking a paper to Orison and bringing it back is five pounds and six (205:7).** The bond is forty pounds, on two skins, lodged in the third salting after the first shaking, binding the Anner to hold the dam to eleven feet above its own sill, **and it is void on the death of the person who lodged it, which is written in at the back in a different hand and has been read once (205:17, 205:20).** The forty pounds has sat under a floor since the first winter after the first shaking. **The ink has run across the words about not being answerable and the fourth line is clean (205:40).** **THE FINDING: a bond keeps a thing true by costing somebody money, and the money stopped in the fourth year and the thing did not stop, and nobody noticed for three years, because a thing that keeps being true does not announce itself. The dam has been held for eleven years by four men and a barrow for three pounds and five of clay and rubble a year out of the Anner's own book (205:32).** Jory Vellan says the volume's scale figure out loud for the first time in nineteen years and it is the whole of what is being argued about and neither party has ever said it: **eleven hundred tons a year at four pounds a ton at the mouth and eleven at Sallowby, and the difference of seven pounds a ton is seven thousand seven hundred pounds a year (205:76, 205:84).** Nobody writes it down; a chainman does, a week later, in a book of his own, because a man of thirty-one said he could not hold four figures and a hand at once (205:86).

### 206 — The Eleven Houses
**Shelf day 76, the seventh and last day of the fiftieth week. Basin day 154.** Eleven roofs on a lane four hundred yards below the sluice, a mark cut on each doorpost about the height of a man's shoulder, cut in one day in a year when the Sallow came up nine feet in a night by a man with a stick and a string and a bucket of tar, **and nine at one height and two at another and nobody has ever asked him why (206:33).** **Garrow Lee, forty-one, a joiner, has measured the same frame for a second time: the frame is four pounds ten, the oak is one pound eight, and the five pounds eighteen is his and there is not a part of it that is anybody else's, and nobody will buy it (206:15).** **THE FINDING, in his mouth, with a rule in his hand: a height is a height above something, and there are three sills inside four miles, and eleven feet is eleven feet, and the mark is not a level, and if you write eleven feet on anything then whoever reads it in nine years will take it for a level and it will be the only level anybody in this basin has ever had.** **THE SECOND FINDING, also his: the eleven houses are not a category, and the reason nobody has asked them is that asking eleven people costs three days, and three days is not a figure, and a figure you can put in a minute and take out of a minute and argue with (206:57).** A day is a day and a penny is a penny. The sluice-keeper lives in one of the eleven and is owed ten pounds sixteen and nobody has told her, because there is no list. **The week turns over at the closing of the water and about nine people in this basin notice it and every one of the nine is at the pans and about four hundred and six do not (206:89).** The frame is measured and not built.

### 207 — The Four Pages
**Shelf day 77, the first day of the fifty-first week. Basin day 155.** Nine people in the Seat's one room, four more than have ever been in it, none sent for, and one of them walked up with a barrow and left it in the lane. **Hollis Nance says the order is his hand and not a clerk's before anybody has said anything (207:11).** Three hours of ordinary wanting: the Anner's four pages are about the road, the village's are about eleven houses and cannot be written, the Seat's are about a date. **THE QUICK RULING IS FOUR LINES AND ALL FOUR ARE FINISHED (207:37), naming the Anner as the party bearing it, the high road at the Anner's cost, eleven feet, and the eleven houses below it, and nobody to be asked to leave a house, and the copy in the lane kept by a person of the lane (207:39).** **THE TURN, and he says it out loud before anybody else has worked it out: there is no hole in it, and the hole is the most useful thing in a document, and this is the other thing, and it is going to hold because it is complete (207:45). Nobody notices (207:57).** The Anner's copy is taken by Jory Vellan, who says the two words that will do and leaves before anybody can ask him anything, **and he knows what it is going to cost and has never once said it out loud in a room that was writing it down (207:61).** **THE ONE SYSTEM PANEL OF THE BATCH, two plain bold lines, the second a WHAT IS NOT DECIDED line (207:67–68), and it says the height is a height above a sill and no sill is named in it, and it does not say one word about the nine people in the room.** The leg has done nothing whatever in seven days and it is going to go on doing nothing for as long as he is carrying the thing he is carrying, and he tells nobody that (207:72). **He says that it is the fourth time in about a year that somebody has tried to put a person in the middle of a sentence to protect somebody else, and that the first three cost the person in the middle of it something, and that this one will cost him the most, and that he does not know that yet (207:80).** **Day-count instance 4 at 207:76.**

### 208 — Three Rulings And A Column Head
**Shelf day 78. Basin day 156.** A rider's bag addressed to the Bench of Orison **at** the water-seat of Sallowby, in that order, which is not an address, and it came on the morning of the first of the fifty-first week, the same morning the four pages went on the wall, and it was on the shelf from about the second light, and nobody opened it because it says Bench on it. **This line said *nine days*, and the chapter said nine days three times over, and none of the three could be true: the four pages went up on the first of the week and Chapter 208 is the second of it. The bag is one day old and the review repair made it so.** **Hollis Nance says he has no authority to open it and opens it anyway in front of five people (208:7).** Inside: a printed abstract of three rulings of the chamber of plenty, four sheets, threepence the sheet, sixty-six sheets a time for nine years, two bundles opened and neither read. **The first says the Seat is competent and needs no seal and the nine days are not to be spent on a matter the Seat can hear. The second, entered in the third turn, nine years back, says a height marked on a doorpost is not a measurement and that no order may name a height without naming the sill it is taken from. The third, entered in the ninth turn, says the first half of a deed, sewn to its second, is the deed, and the Seat must require both halves before it enters any matter of ground. And the referral upon all three is of one name, P. Holloway of Orison, who has not been in the basin since the first shaking and is not a party to any of them (208:17–21).** **THE FINDING: the Bench has been consistent and the basin has been consistent and the two consistent things do not meet, and a record can be perfectly kept and still be wrong about a place, and the reason is that the only channel between them has been a man who was not of the basin and was right every time and nobody ever checked that he was the only channel (208:49).** **The second ruling is nine years old and the four pages on the wall breach it, and nobody in that room knew it existed (208:45, 208:47).** Folded into the fourth sheet, unopened, is a letter of about nine lines in a clerk's hand, and nobody in the room asks for it to be read, and the clerk does not read it, and then he says who wrote it — a clerk of thirty-four who wrote to ask about a fourth hand — and gives the room a form for somebody else's letter and not for his own (208:63 and about). **The index on the same shelf has a fourth column with a heading that means not sent, and it has no entries under it and the other three have four hundred and sixty, and Ilyan sees it at the fourth light and asks nothing (208:85).**

### 209 — A Trench Taken Out In A Straight Line
**Shelf day 79. Basin day 157.** Anner Pit, the under-manager's office, the chain-book about nine hundred pages in a hand nobody in the valley can read, and a man of twenty-six who has been in the oldest workings since she was seventeen and who was not asked to be anywhere and came because four people went down the ramp past her. The oldest trench on the lowest level is eleven chains and sixteen links and it is **straight**, and there is nothing in nine hundred pages about a straight line taken out of red stone by hand before there was a bench in Sallowby. **THE FINDING, in her mouth, and nobody had ever asked: six cuts in the floor off the side of it, in a line, there since before she came, a chain goes in about four inches and comes out on a shoulder, like a joint, and she has never seen a man make one (209:23).** Page eleven of the chain-book (209:33–35): the take-out is along one straight line and **there is no column in that book for anywhere**; the six marks are cut in a hand not the page's, on the sixth salting of the eleventh pan-book year, **which is a date the book has no means of entering**; the low end of the pit is four hundred and six feet below the sill stone, and under it there is a void of depth not yet found, **and the figure of four hundred and six is the figure of the pit and not of the void.** The Seat's list of drains has forty-one lines and its ninth is the Anner overflow, dated the ninth turn, with a note saying the turn was taken from the Anner's own book. **THE POSITION IS IDENTIFIED BY TWO ORDINARY RECORDS THAT DO NOT MEET: a drain was aimed along a line older than anything in this basin can date, and the interval between the two is a span this basin has no instrument for naming and the chapter does not name it, **which was printed here as *a hundred and ten years older than it* and was out of a corrected line: a hundred and ten is less than the hundred and thirty the chain-book's binding is old, and `209:53` says out loud that there is no way whatever on earth to say how much later**, and nobody in the basin has ever noticed that it was aimed, and the answer is nine degrees and a quarter off the Anner's own heading at more than four hundred and six feet (209:63).** **NOBODY GOES DOWN. He says he is not going down four hundred feet and that the reason is not the water and is not the steps, and he tells nobody what the reason is, and the reason is a leg that has not been his own since a morning four hundred miles and some weeks behind him (209:75, 209:79).** **The System puts nothing up and says nothing whatever about it (209:83).** At the second light Jory Vellan rules a line at the foot of page eleven and writes the position on it, in his own hand, in a book belonging to the Anner, and puts it on the board and not in the book, because the book goes to Orison on a schedule and the board does not (209:85).

### 210 — A Person Doing Their Work
**Shelf day 80, the fourth day of the fifty-first week. Basin day 158.** Four days after the four pages went on the wall: the causeway shut, nine carts a day on the high road, the dam dressed with forty loads of clay and a hundred and forty of rubble in about four days by four men and a barrow, three pounds and five out of the Anner's own book, **and the wet workings of the Anner are dry for the first time since the second shaking.** Nobody is ruined, no house is wet, and the eleven did not know there were four pages until the second of the week, when a woman put the lane's copy on the doorpost of the third house from the top, which is hers. **A man of thirty-one buys a penny exercise book and divides the first page down the middle with a straightedge he made out of a lath, and writes two heads, and under the second of them he puts the day, and the number that goes on the page is one hundred and fifty-eight, and it is the fifth time in ten days a number out of that water-book has been at the top of a page in this valley, and he has not told anybody in this basin what any of the five is — which is the batch's fifth day-count instance and it is the first one written in a book bought in the valley (210:19).** The reason for the division is in the first line: there are two numbers in this basin and they are not the same number and nothing on earth converts one into the other (210:15). The Shelf half carries the whole inherited list in his own hand — the second notice of five shillings and fourpence, the claim of forty-five pounds two shillings and eightpence and the carter of fifty-one who is right, the dead man in the fourth line and his wife, the minute in a drawer, the blank in the third line, the fourth hand, the box of about nine hundred and forty forms, Nesh Arrad's name with **no day figure printed for her and the reason given in his own hand**, and four hundred and eighty-five pounds a year that does not stop (`210:27`–`210:35`). **AND THEN THE NEW QUESTION, ONCE, WITH A PLACE AND A FORM OF WORDS, AND HE DOES NOT ASK, and the reason he gives is that the last lane he stood in had nine people in it and not one of them ever said a word about what they had watched happen to a man in it, and that is how the thing in that book got there (210:39, 210:41). The sentence breaks off in the middle and it is the only broken sentence in two hundred and eleven days of that kind of book (210:43).** Nobody in the valley knows what is in that book and nobody is going to. **A woman who maps a country without asking anybody is named once, in a mouth, by a man who has not met her, and one person in the room repeats the name as Vaynn, and nobody in that room has heard of her (210:55, 210:59).** **The batch's refrain, once, in a new basin and in a book bought for a penny: It is mine to write down and it is not mine to decide (210:73). The hundred and fifty-seven at `210:69` is a notch count on Fen Tregerran's board and runs one behind the day on this volume's own convention, which is why day-count instance 5 is at `210:19` and not there.** The chapter ends on a person doing their work: four men down to the dam, clay in the same order it has gone on in for eleven years, a woman up out of the Sallow, and a lamp not lit until the barrow is down.

## Chapter 0151 — Three Days East

He leaves the Saltglass coast on the second day of the fortieth week with four shillings and a bag. **Fenn Ordram, fifty-four, thirty-one years on the water, asks him nothing for three days and then says four sentences about the second mouth: it is the cheapest grain in the county, in about six weeks it will be the only grain anybody has, there is a district called Ryefold six miles down the towpath with about six hundred in it holding a granary on a lease, and the lease is up in a fortnight.** He asks why the man is telling a stranger that, and is told that he is going to look like a man going somewhere to be useful. He lands, works out that four shillings is five weeks and that he is not going to be on a river for five weeks, and is told by a man in a coat with a stamp on a chain the one thing about a man with no paper: **nobody can prove anything about him, it cuts both ways and it cuts them the same distance, and about ninety people in that building like it and about nine do not.** The rendering comes up on a towpath and does not move. He walks six miles, the leg goes alone on a bank, and he gets into **Ryefold**: eleven hundred yards of quay, a beam nine feet over a door, sixty carts, eleven hundred yards of stone. He sits down twice and a man notices. **Sena Ollet, thirty-one, a slate on a three-legged frame, tells him the granary is shut, the weighbridge shuts at the fourth, and that she goes up the towpath once a month, six miles each way, paid three shillings a week in the cut and nothing the rest of the year, and that she carries numbers and does not read them and there is nobody in the district who does.** She tells him there is a basket and it is there if he wants it, and she is not asking, she is telling him, because in about four days the lease is up and about nine people in the district cannot read what is going to be put in front of them. He sleeps in a cart shed for a penny, and the sixth of the six torn-out pages says what the man in the coat said, and the page after it is blank and stays blank. He works out the only door available to him: **a wage, in chalk, by name, at the moment of the work**, which is the ninth bridge's tenth term, and being paid is the only thing that will make him a person in a record instead of a thing in one, and it will put his name in a fifth book in a district he has never been in, and he decides that on purpose. **The chapter's honest sentence is written on the page: he chose this place because a stranger told him where the hunger was, and he told nobody, and nobody asked, and the not-telling was in his coat and would come out about four months later in a shed, in a different argument entirely.**

## Chapter 0152 — The Fourth Term

**Sera Quill releases the ninth-bridge matter on the public record** at the second bell on the sixth day of the fortieth week, in a room of the chamber of Plenty above one that smells of wet wool, with Ilyan standing in the doorway, having walked four hundred miles in under four weeks. Her reason is that **it is finished — not that it went well** — and she names the history of her own fourth term: drafted by Sel Harrow on the court's motion at her own asking, used against her four times, twice by benches, once by a clerk and once by Harrow himself, and all four entered in her own book with the fact that he drafted it. The cost of the release is named: **she may in about four months file a claim of six years for a page that may not exist, and that is hers.** Then she refuses him the claim, in about six minutes, with four reasons and none of them a kindness: it is hers, it is unfiled, it is not in any bridge or city case, and when it is filed she will be a person in a matter. **And the fourth reason is the volume's method in one sentence: *I know exactly what you do with a person in a record. You do not put them in it by asking. You arrange it.*** She has read the three sheets from the coast and there is not one word of them he arranged. **He says he is not going to ask her about the claim, because she has not offered it, and because if she has not offered it the answer is no and he would be asking her to say so twice.** Then she asks for her own sheet back — the one with two questions on it in a hand he asked her not to write in, one of them about consent — and he gives it to her, **and does not say *you can leave it*, and that is the whole of the first relationship beat in a hundred and sixty chapters.** She then says the thing that governs the next four hundred miles: **she is not going to ask him about the shed, and he is not to tell her, and in about four years she is going to ask him again and he will have to do it properly, and she is warning him now so he cannot say later that he was not warned.** She writes in a public book, as a recordwright, that **the bench of Ryefold** is four out of four occupied by persons who cannot read a form, and *and none of the four has said so*, and says the last clause is the most useful sentence anybody has written about that district in nine years and none of the four will ever know. At the end she gives him a Bench abstract of a forbearance and tells him one thing in it — **it has an end on it, and every one of them has an end on it, and that is what the word means and the word is not on it** — and asks him a question she does not answer: **when a thing a district was given for a year ends, and nobody in the district is told, and the only people who know are a person in a city and a man in a record he cannot read, and a basket-runner being paid ninepence a day to carry a number up a towpath, then who has the duty to tell them, what is it called, and does anybody in this world have a name for the person who does it?** He walks the four miles back, the leg goes on a bridge, and the seventh page of the exercise book carries his first finding about Ryefold and the first finding of his life about paper with a word at the top of it.

## Chapter 0153 — A Building With No Name On The Door

**The counter is the whole of the chapter, and it has been open for four years and nobody has ever walked into it.** Dessin Nahl tells him where it is and warns him that the man in it sweeps and is not waiting for anybody. **She works out that he cannot read**, in about four seconds, in a counter — which makes seven people in the world who know it, four of them on a coast four hundred miles away who worked it out and have never said a word — and says one sentence: eleven years of reading that paragraph four times a day to men who cannot get a word of it on the first pass, and I slowed down the second time because I thought you had a cold. And then: *you are the wrong man for this and I am not going to say so in here*, and the one courtesy anybody in that room has ever shown him. **He is the third person in the world to know.** In the building: a passage that smells of cold stone and lamp oil, a man on his knees with a broom, and **Corrin Vask, forty-one, nine years, ninepence a day, right hand six years gone at the wrist.** He tells Ilyan the third shelf is not the old one and the old one went in a cart and nobody wrote down where, and then says: *I can tell you a thing was printed in a year I have not been in. If you want to know what it says you want a person who reads, and there are about nine of them in this city and none of them is in this street.* The cold room: nineteen shelves, a plate and a year on each, a series of everything the county has printed in four years, and **a standing instruction that any person may read any of it at fourpence a sheet.** The price of a volume out of the case is a shilling, in no minute, on nobody's order, entered in the day book in the column with the sweeping of the floors, and a man who holds it open for you is not sweeping, and there is one man for the floors and he is the man with the lamp. He reads for three hours by a lamp he cannot read, guessing, and gets about one word in four, **and then at the sixth bell a man of thirty-four comes in off the street with a slip and says *I want to read a form* and *I don't know, that's the thing* and *I paid two shillings and eightpence for this. I want to know what it says.*** Corrin Vask names it — a prize, two sheets at a shilling and fourpence, the price the same in every county and the price of the sheets, and he is not the office that entered it and cannot say who was — and then does the most careful thing Ilyan Vester has seen anybody do in a year: **he does not pick the slip up.** He tells the man the register is shut, apologises for it in a way he has been apologising for four years, and then points out that whatever the paper does was printed under a plate in that building, on a shelf with the man's year on it, and may be read tonight for fourpence and taken away, and nobody will stop him and nobody will know. **The man is Iven Brack and Ilyan recognises him and says nothing, and the chapter says the reason plainly: it is the only time a person is made safer by anything Ilyan Vester did, and he did it by not being useful.** On the street he works out that a thing on a road is a person and a person is produced by whatever is nearest, **that he has been produced five times and said four of them out loud before anybody else did, that this is the first that cost nobody anything, and that it was still the same.**

## Chapter 0154 — The Bench of Four

The bench sits in two rooms above a chandler's shop. **All four seats are filled and all four are named: Perrin Gant, sixty-one, nineteen years in the bench's own book; Osa Trin, thirty-nine, the second, who does the notices; Nevin Hake, forty-six, the third, a carter before he was a bench; Wil Tamworth, thirty-three, the fourth.** It is four miles from the court, eleven from the ninth bridge, seven from Nethergill and six from a low street of counting-houses, **and it is not on the way to anything, and that is the whole of its geography and the reason nothing has ever happened to it.** Gant says *useful* when he means *right*, and notices himself doing it, and says the bench's own book is the only book in the room nobody can read. **He makes the offer once, in the plainest words he has: whatever happens about the lease, the bench will have to swear something in this room, in public, on a day the bench appoints, on its own page, and the only reason he is offering it to a stranger is that a man who is a person of no district is a man no district can answer for, and the only two people in the county talking about that had both noticed him.** Ilyan says yes and says the price, and **says out loud, before anything is agreed, that his name is in four hundred and sixty-three forms eleven miles off a bridge and a sledge has been used on it once, and that he has been produced five times by whatever was nearest him, and that none of the five cost a stranger nothing except two, and that he came here because a man on a boat told him where the hunger was and he did not ask and nobody asked and that is the worst thing about it.** Gant writes both facts down and says he has not written a stranger into that book since the year before last and did not enjoy it either. Then the chapter's turn: **the man of thirty-one cannot read, and the only person in the room who can read it is thirty-nine and has spent her life reading things out loud for nothing, and three of the four admit it.** Nevin Hake says it first, and says he is not going to be the second person in that room who is cheaper than the stranger, **and the truth of that sentence is that he has been in that bench eleven years and has never once said he could not read, and he says it because a man has been honest in the room and the price is that he will never sit in it and not know it, and he decided in about four seconds that knowing was cheaper than not knowing.** Ilyan names the hammer on the coast and the woman of twenty-four and the man of sixty-one, and says both of those are true at the same time. He carries the basket on two days and **Marda Fen, fifty-four, twenty-two years a granary reeve, pays him ninepence in chalk on a board with his name on it, having read the board before she wrote on it**, and refuses to write that he carried it six miles each way, because a wage line is not a place for a man to be generous about his own distances. **Then she tells him the whole of it: the year was worth four hundred and sixty-two pounds and the carts cost four hundred and sixty and the carts were not theirs, and the hiring went on the account, and the year is over, and she found out a fortnight ago because a man off a boat asked her for a basket, and she is going to keep it from the bench for about a week and then has to say it, and if he repeats it to any of those four she will stop his wage in chalk where they can read it.** The leg goes on the quay at the fourth bell in front of about forty people and is his own again three hours later on a towpath, and he tells nobody.

## Chapter 0155 — The End On It

**The towpath, six miles each way, about two hours of light in the middle of it, a basket about forty pounds full.** He carries it and **the leg is his own for about four hours of the six, unremarked, and he thinks about it for a mile: the leg goes when he is carrying a thing somebody else will have to read, and this time there is no woman in it at all, only a basket of numbers nobody at either end of the towpath can read, and it does not resolve into anything.** The abstract is four sheets and he cannot read it and has got one word in four, and the word is *year*, three times out of four, and the fourth time he got it wrong and spent twenty minutes wishing he had not looked. **He works out for himself why he does not simply put it on the table: because the only person in that room who can read it is a woman of thirty-nine who has read things out loud for nothing nine hundred times and has never once been asked, and the room decided ten minutes earlier that this was a thing that had been done to her too often.** Osa Trin refuses to read it out — **not because of the truth of it, because the difference between reading it out and not reading it out is about four hours of her life** — and agrees to take it away for a night; Perrin Gant backs that from the chair and says he will take whatever she has to say however bad it is and will not ask her to be careful, and says the reason he asked for the night is *because it will not be careful about it.* At the fourth bell next morning, before he has sent for anybody: **the year ended fourteen days ago.** The block-quoted fourth sheet is on the page, and he has had it in his coat for two days. **The account is four hundred and eighty-five pounds a year and has been since the carts went on it, and it was four hundred and sixty-two before that, and nobody ever told her either figure, and she has signed a paper in Orison that says the account and read every line of it, and she knew what the hire cost and nobody told her what the year cost.** The rate is not on the abstract: it is in another book in the counting-house street, and she has known for eleven years and has never been, because it is an hour and fourpence and two miles in a cut month and a reeve's wage of two pounds ten. **Then the chapter's hard problem: one copy or two. A copy is four sheets and sixteen pence, and the district has about nine pounds. Two copies means asking a man with a bad hand to carry four sheets out and then four more, and he will remember her, and she does not want to be remembered by anybody in that street until she knows what she is doing.** So it is one copy, and she is going to take it up the lane herself, and she is going to tell those four that it has ended and that she has known for eleven days and did not tell them, and that the reason is that she could not work out what to tell them. The eighth page of the exercise book is the longest he has written and says three things: the mechanism he has still not got a name for, **that a thing which can only be carried by a person is a thing the district cannot be without, and this district cannot be without Osa Trin, and therefore this district cannot be without her** — and, in advance and on purpose, that he is not going to have the fourth sheet read to him, and that the next four days will prove that to be both the correct thing to do and the thing that costs the most.

## Chapter 0156 — A Decision Is A Thing A Person Makes

**The lease notice arrives on a boy's back and goes on a nail and three of the four people in that room cannot read it and nobody had asked for it.** Gant says it has been coming since the middle of the cut before last and that his father told him the same thing. **Osa Trin reads it off the nail with her thumb under the line, and the finding is four things: it is up; the renewal is at the discretion of the account; the price is a fortieth of everything in the granary, payable in grain and not in money, before the cut; and there is a line saying a district may not sell the lease and no line anywhere saying what a district may do instead.** Nevin Hake says four weeks, and then three and a bit, and says he has been doing that sum every day for a year. **Nobody thanked Osa Trin and nobody asked her to take it off the nail.** Then the errand: six miles down and six miles up and three hours at a counter, and the only question he has, which is whether a forbearance that has run out can be had again. **Roald Tern, twenty-six, two years at the chamber of Plenty's counter, has read the same eleven hundred forms twice as many times.** The answer: **once a year, at the fourth sitting, on notice to every party, the application made by a person of the district, the district represented at the sitting, notice eleven days out at a shilling and fourpence a sheet, and four sheets for a district of six hundred people is five shillings and fourpence to say that it is still poor.** And the category: **a party that does not appear is carried as uncooperative, and that is the word on the wall, and it means the party did not come and not that it was angry or wrong, and a court that goes and finds out why has stopped being a court and started being a man with a cart.** Tern also tells him the one form in that building where a man of no district can stand without being an inconvenience to anybody — a sheet and a shilling and fourpence, naming him as a person and not as somebody's hands — and says, honestly, that he has found Ilyan interesting and that he would rather what he enters today say a true thing than a kind one. **Then the plant.** Ilyan finds the flaw in the category out loud in about a minute and is right, and then says the sentence that the whole of Batch 0002 is built out of: **a district that sends nobody has decided it has nothing to say, and a decision is a thing a person makes, and I will not stand in a room and call that anything else.** Tern enters it in a clerk's hand on purpose and says it saved him four minutes. The chapter then sets out **the order of the three things he did** — the question, the flaw, the comfort — and names it as the whole of what he is, since a city four hundred miles behind him with a bad coffee machine in it, and as the reason a woman of twenty-four refused him and a man of sixty-one told him he kept being careful in the wrong direction, **and says it is going to be read back to him in a room in about three weeks out of a deposition in his own words by a person he has not met, about six hundred people who cannot read anything that has happened to them.** He wrote none of that down. The ninth page is about a basket and about a man of twenty-six and about a sentence he cannot account for.

## Chapter 0157 — The Difference Between Those Two Things
