At the turn he holds the paper up so the people near the stone can see there is a thing in it, and asks: **is there anything in that paper that is wrong about the water.** She looks at him for about two seconds, says *that is a question about the water*, and tells him that he gets one and has got one and nobody may ask a second and she is not going to make him walk back down nine hundred yards of wet shingle with nothing because he asked it in the wrong words. **And then she answers it, out loud, in front of about seventy people, and it takes about a minute and a half: there is nothing in that paper that is wrong about the water. The water at the north end on a good day goes out to about four inches at the lowest of the ebb and about six on the bar, and the bar is a bar and not the channel, and the channel on a good day lies across that shallow and not along it; on the fourth, the sixth and the seventh the sea stands over the crown of that bar and there is no lowest at the north end at all, and the crossing four hundred yards south of him is the road on those three days and this flat is not.** And then the one thing she will not do, said plainly and not unkindly: **she will not stand on a stone and say whether the table on a wall a mile up the hill is right about that morning or whether the paper is, because she has never had those two things in front of her at once, and if she tried it she would be guessing about the water, and she does not guess about the water.** Somebody at the back says the word *four* and somebody else says the word *feet*, and about nine people on that shingle have a number in their heads that has just been contradicted out loud by the only person on this coast who is allowed to say a number about the water, and about sixty understood the shape of it and not the size. **Nobody asks her a second question. Nobody refused anybody. The paper was right about the water, and that was the whole of what was wrong with his week.** Then, in the ordinary way and not unkindly: **you did not spend it on the water… that has cost you the only thing you have ever had on this coast and it has bought you a thing you could have got by standing on your own flat with your own eyes on it for a day… that is the whole of what this stone is. It is for the water. There is no second door. There is one stone and two days a week and me on it, and you had it.** He goes down to the chain with the slate in his hand for the rest of the day and says nothing to anybody, and about nine people on that flat would have given a great deal to have heard it. The boy of eleven goes over for the ninth time at a penny; Corrie Tallow is at the far stones with her slate for the ninth crossing, unpaid and always there on the ninth; the post and the board are there and the nails hold and nobody puts a hand on it. **Seth Garrick comes out of the oil shed when the ninth crossing is done, looks at the flat, says one word out loud to nobody in particular — "Well." — and shuts the door, and that is all he ever says about it to anybody for the rest of his life.** Ilyan heard all of it, and could have said that this stone is not the way to put two records side by side and never was going to be, **and did not, because he has no standing on this coast and the only two things he can give a person here are an argument and a piece of paper, and the argument was refused in a yard in the fifth of a tide and the piece of paper was in the man on the chain's breast pocket and had cost a carter a day. He does not put it down anywhere; there is no place on this coast for a fifth page, and he has known that since about the third of a tide and has not found one.** At the ninth bell the water goes off the flat, the chain goes into its sockets, and **the man on the chain took the slate out and put a stroke in it for the last of the nine and went home. He kept the paper and never took it out again.**

## Chapter 0134 — The Two Days a Week

**The seventh of the seventh tide, a bar day, and the day there is no appeal at all, and the chapter is the day: water, weather, the ordinary work of a seventh.** The strait is shut, the water has been on the crown of the bar since before the light and is not coming off it, and every cart that has to come round this coast is on nine hundred yards of shingle. **Gell Roke, seventy-one, is on the staff at the harbour mouth with a pot of paint and his hammer in a bag and a boy of about ten holding the pot for him**, because the turn on a seventh is the only moment in the week a man can put a mark on the bar staff at two feet under; he has a second coat on the mark from about four years ago and it has gone thin at the two-foot line. *Hold it up. Not down. There is no arm in a man that holds a pot down.* **The mark under the water is the same width as the mark above it and has been for nineteen years and it is a long way from where the thing it marks now is, and about two hundred people on this coast have worked that out and not one of them ever said it, and this morning nobody said it either because it is a bar day and there were seventy people on the flat and every one of them had a load.** The chain goes up and comes down nine times and rests an hour between the fifth and the seventh, and the seventh is the day it rests and the eighth is the day the man with the bar has to hurry, and that is how a seventh is made. Corrie Tallow counts forty-one crossings, about half of them people on foot; Nim Hask, eleven, goes over for the ninth time at a penny with a hand-lead in his fist and nobody thinks anything about it, including him. **The tally post is there with its chain and its board with two numbers and a difference and a line under them, and it is inspected at about the turn on a seventh once a year by a man with a hammer, and it had been inspected in the turn of the year and will not be inspected again until the turn of the year after, and nobody had any business at that post on a seventh morning and nobody had.** **Danno Ray, forty-five, with a load of lime and two men on, crosses on the seventh and stands at the chain: there is a stone you can ask one question on, and a song at the stone this afternoon, and a number cut on a post that a man counts with a hammer once a year, and there is a board on the front of it. And I have worked out that a rule that cannot be changed for a year is not a rule, it is a season. Nobody answered him** — the boy with the board, two carters, a man in his fourth crossing — **because about nine people heard the same sentence from the same man standing in the same place in the fifth of a tide and nothing has happened on this coast since. It is not the rule I am complaining about. You have had that crossing a hundred years. I am complaining about the season.** He goes to the hard. **At about the turn Seth Garrick sang at the stone — four lines, a tariff, sung every seventh at the turn by one man, not written down, not on any board, four or five people in on the chorus, which they do. The stone was bare behind him. Nobody stood on it that day and nobody could have, and there is nobody on this coast who has ever explained that to the guild or to anybody else, and the guild has never asked.** The person it lands on is **the man on the chain**, who spent his question on the sixth, got a true answer out loud in the open in front of seventy people, and **had known for six days that it would be about the water and spent it anyway** — and what he has instead is the fact of it, that a man who has held a chain for nineteen years without once not knowing where the going was has been told by the only person on four hundred miles allowed to say it that he was right about the water, **which is not nothing, and which he thinks about about twice a day for the rest of that year and never says out loud, and about four people work out that he spent the stone's question and never said so.** Then, to a carter who asks when the next one is, in the ordinary way: **the first of the eighth, and the third, and the fifth, and the seventh, and then the first of the ninth, and it goes like that and there is no more to it. The sixth is there and the fourth is there and the first, the second, the third and the fifth are not. There are two days a week when the stone is there and a woman on it, and about four hundred thousand days a week when it is not, and I have never once heard anybody on this coast work that out in a sentence until just now.** Nobody is going to be able to use that. *It has got a stone in it and no more.* Ilyan's finding, on a head of flat in the dark: **the whole working life of every person within four hundred miles of that shingle is arranged around two days a week and a question about the water, and not one of them has ever been asked for a single thing in return for it, and that is the only arrangement on this coast with no form in it and no counterparty and nobody to complain to and nobody who can be got at.** Gell Roke comes past with the hammer in the bag and the boy with the empty pot and neither of them says a word, and neither of them ever did.

## Chapter 0135 — Two Hundred and Sixty Yards of Stone

**The first of the eighth tide, a good day, the flat takes six, and the defence the guild built is on the page, and the guild is right about it.** At the north end, four hundred yards up the lane from the crossing, the ebb out of that deep runs long and soft and two hundred yards of gravel stands out of it in the low like a floor. **Halse Tarrant, fifty-eight, has been on that wall for thirty-one years and was one of the hands that laid the first of it.** The wall: two hundred and sixty yards, laid in courses, nine courses at the inner end falling to about two at the outer, and the outer end standing out into the deep on purpose. **What it is for is one thing and it has been one thing since the year it went down: the deep is nine feet on a good day and it is a hole the ebb has cut in a gravel bar, the wall stands along the seaward side of that hole, and where the ebb and the outside are close the water makes a hole in the gravel. In the year before they laid it, it had gone back eleven yards in two winters and taken a hut and a boat slip with it, and the slip had belonged to a man called Teel and there is nobody on this coast who was ever taught by him.** Eight men, one season, about seven weeks, **the last course nineteen years and eight months ago, in the same year the guild had a thing fired in a shed at Thornglass for the room upstairs of the office at the Reach — two things paid for out of the same season, about two miles apart, and there is not one person on this coast who has ever put them in the same sentence.** **Four things he says, in the open, on a good day.** First: **the guild was right.** He has watched that ebb every day since he was twenty-seven; take the wall out and there is no north end inside three winters; nobody was wrong and it has not been looked at since. Second, the thing he has not got: **a wall of stone does not stop water, it stops gravel; the wall is worth exactly what is behind it, and what is behind it is about two feet of gravel, and those two feet are the whole of that point, and if they go the wall is a wall standing in the sea about eleven yards from where anything is. And the toe of the seaward face is the part that goes, and he has not been at it since about the fourth year — on a good day it is under nine feet of green water, and on a fourth and a sixth and a seventh the ebb brings the sand out of the channel and packs the middle of the bar flat and the deep fills and a flat boat can be stood over the top of it, and on those three days the sea outside is standing on the crown and the wind is on the quarter and a man out there has about an hour and a quarter and then is sitting in nine feet on the flat, because it holds about eleven times in twenty and the nine is somebody's cart in nine feet of water and it would be his fault for being there.** **He has the four things short of one: a lead line, a boat, a man who can sound, and a day.** The lead line is the guild's, in a box in a shed since the wall was laid; the boat is his own and has not been out in about a year; he can sound to a foot inside of forty yards. **He has wanted the day since about the sixth year and has not asked anybody, because a wall does not ask for a boat.** Third, the thing nobody is going to like: **the water has moved.** Not a fright, not a discovery, not anybody's fault. The line where the ebb works along the outside of that wall is outboard of the outer end now, and it has been going outboard for a good many years, and he can see where it is working and has no number for where it worked then — the number anybody has is on a wall a mile up the hill, a morning about three months old, a photograph of a morning taken by a man standing beside a fire, the only instrument anybody will act on, and it does not come out of that building; the other one is on a wall two miles along this coast and is three years old and is a different morning, and the man who made it cannot get at the first one and cannot get the first one to him and has not been sure his own is right since he made it. Fourth: **he has been in charge of it since the fourth year and nobody has ever asked him whether he would like to be, and he is not complaining, and he would not have said yes the first twenty times, and he has not thought about it in six years, which is the same as not caring except that the wall and the man are two different things and he has only ever been sure about one of them.** And then, to a stranger who asks *who do you ask when you want a day*: **nobody… the last man who asked me for something was a man in a good coat who asked for a year, and the answer to that was a woman's back for eleven months, and he did not ask her, and he was right not to… a person who wants a thing off a person who has not got it to spare does not ask the person. The person finds out afterwards or does not, and either way the person is standing there with it and nobody has said yes to anything. And I have watched that happen four or five times on this coast since you came and I have not liked any of it and I have not been able to do one single thing about any of it, and I am fifty-eight and I am the man who keeps two hundred and sixty yards of stone and there is not one part of that I am allowed to spend on anybody.** The ordinary business goes on round it the whole time — six crossings on the flat, a boat standing along beyond the point, a man not sorting his bait, a carpenter planing a hull on his ways — **and nothing on this coast is alarmed and nothing is threatened and the ebb goes out long and soft and does exactly what it has done every good day for thirty-one years.** Ilyan is forty-four days on the coast, puts the lead down about four seconds after picking it up, hears the whole of it, and says one stupid thing and is told, at length and in the trade's mouth, why nobody on this coast asks anybody for anything. He has the four things in his head already — a glassmaker named them at a bench ten days ago and would not buy them with a woman's back — **and there is no way on four hundred miles of this coast to make a man hold them, and he has known that for forty-four days.**

## Chapter 0136 — The Third Column and the Eighth

**The second of the eighth tide, a good day, and the two columns that are places and not depths are read aloud in a shed.** The second fire is let in at the second bell and Sabra Trew stands at it because it cannot be left once it is let in; the arch is cold behind two feet of brick; **the guild's order is on the bench under the batch book with a date against it and no figure against it, and it was under the batch book since a cart came up the coast road with a load of oil and it is going to be under the batch book at the turn.** **Hollis Thrale, sixty-one, forty-one years at the fire, deaf in the right ear as his father was and his father's father was**, has his own pane on the wall of that shed, three years old, eleven places for every tide. **The two columns are the third and the eighth, the two that record a place and not a depth. Sabra Trew is the only other person who can read them and she reads them out.** Third: the outer end of the north wall, a place and not a figure — **two hundred and sixty-one yards from the post at the inner end, along the line of the wall**, and then the height at the top of the inner end, which is the ninth course, which is the six-foot one. Eighth: the toe of the seaward face — **the gravel stands against the seaward face to the second course for the whole length of the wall, and at the inner end it stands to the fifth.** The exception is at the inner end and not the outer, because the wall is nine courses there and about two at the outer, and it is at the inner end in the prose because a repair pass had put it at the outer end, where nothing can stand to a fifth course on a two-course wall. **Nine of the eleven are depths, taken from a boat at the lowest of the ebb with a line, and they are for a morning; the two that are not depths are the two that are about a wall, and a wall is not a depth, and whoever made these two columns knew it.** Hollis has the guild's two figures **in his head in a clerk's hand and has had them for two years**, and says how he got them: **the harbourmaster read him two columns off her own wall in a yard on the fourth of a tide and would do nothing else, and she was within her rights, and she was right to refuse him the other nine, and he did not go back.** The guild's third says two hundred and sixty-four. **The guild's eighth says the toe stands to the fourth course for the whole length and does not give the inner end at all.** So: **the third column is three yards in nineteen years and eight months on a wall laid in seven weeks by eight men, and that is not three yards of nothing — that is the water moving along that wall, and the outer end is three yards further in than it was on the guild's morning, so something has taken the gravel off the outer end of it, and he cannot say how much or when, because a number about a wall is not a number about water and you have to be in a boat to get one of those.** And the eighth is the whole of the trouble: **mine says two courses for the whole of it, theirs says four; a course is about the thickness of a hand, so four is two feet eight and two is a foot and four; if theirs is right the wall has had two feet eight of gravel standing against its face for nineteen years and is doing its job; if mine is right the toe has come down by a foot and four along two hundred and sixty yards and there is no bottom under that bottom course in places and the ebb is working round the foot of a wall instead of past the end of it. And he cannot tell you which is true, and the only way there has ever been to try is to put the two panes on one bench, and the only instrument anybody will act on is theirs, and it is on a wall a mile up the hill in a frame and does not come out of that building and the next one is a year off and there is no money in the arch.** Then **a third pane**, and Sabra Trew puts the bar down in the middle of the fire, which she has done once in three years, and refuses him again: **a third one is a third morning. It settles nothing. It is harder to argue with and no more true, and the water will have moved three times instead of twice, and a year of somebody's back is the price of it, and the price is me, and the price was me the first two times as well, and one of those two is on a wall a mile up that hill and one of them is on this one and they do not agree in the eighth column, and there are two photographs on this coast and no room to put them side by side in.** She refuses to say it a second time in this chapter. And she gives him the other half, in her own hand's knowledge: **the eighth column is worth everything and worth nothing at the same time, because it is a record of a morning… and the only thing on this coast that will tell you how much gravel is standing against that wall this morning is a man in a boat with a line on the day the sea is doing whatever it is going to do** — and then the thing nobody has said out loud: **he has said that to me and to a man off a road who came up this road twice in three days and stood at that bench, and he has never once said it to the man who keeps the wall, because he is two miles along this coast and has never been there, and neither has the man been here, and the two of them have been four feet from the same argument for two years and neither of them knew it.** Ilyan has the true answer and does not say it, because he has been wrong about the same shape of thing three times on this coast and every one of the three times he put it in a building. He says the stupid thing instead — that there is a man up the coast with a lead line in a box and a boat and the ability to sound who needs a day — and is told that Hollis Thrale has known that since about the fifth of a tide, and did not believe a word of it and then did, and has not been up there and has not sent anybody and is not going to: **because the last time anybody on this coast got a person to stand on a thing for a year they did it without asking her, and I am not going to be the man who starts a second one in a season where the passage money is short; and because he will not say yes.** She goes back to the fire. **The order stays under the batch book with a date and no figure. The arch stays cold. And nobody on this coast is going to be asked which of the two columns is right.**

## Chapter 0137 — Would You Like to Be the One Standing There

**The third of the eighth tide, a good day, the flat takes six, and the volume's relationship milestone is delivered: the question Chapter 130 set up for the man at the fire is asked of the woman who stands on the stone, and she says no, and the truth is not the answer he wanted, and he is wrong out loud and she is right out loud and the coast does not treat it as an event.** **The stone is bare, because the stone is bare five days in seven and this was one of the five** — and he asks her anyway, in daylight, with people about, because doing it in an office would be a conversation and doing it on a bare-stone day would be a complaint, and there was one in a week of them when she came down a hill in daylight past about forty people. **Bettany Rook comes down at about the fourth bell with a board under her arm and a hood up to see the near end of a flat that takes six, and she knows what he is before he says it, and says *no* before he says it, and then lets him ask it properly, because he has told her twice in a month she is not going to invent a reason for him.** He asks: **would you like to be the one standing on it.** And she says **no**, and answers it in the open at four in the afternoon, in three parts. **The first half is the one he expected and it does not decide anything:** a stone is worth what the person on it is worth, take her off it and it is four feet of flat stone and about a hundred years of people respecting a habit, the guild has never interfered with it in a hundred years and never will, and that is the whole of what it is worth — and *you are a man who has spent a month on this coast learning that the shape of a thing is not the thing, and you have learned it four times and got it wrong three.* **The second half is the one he did not expect: she would not give it up, and that is not a smallness.** In nineteen years in that office nobody in that building has asked her for one thing; she is the harbourmaster and she has never once been asked by anybody to stand in a particular place; **the stone is the only thing on this coast that has ever happened to me, and what happened was that nobody made me do it… the whole of what that gives you is that nobody can ever say you agreed to it.** And if she stands down, in about a month a man on a bar road four miles along this coast finds out what happens to a road with nobody on it, and he will find it out the way a carter finds it out, and it will be a person and not a rule, and she is not going to be the reason. **The third part is the one she wants in his own words: I do not want to be a person doing it. I want it to keep being the coast.** As long as it is the coast it is a hundred years of everybody respecting a habit and nobody has to be brave and nobody has to be asked and no day comes when a woman of fifty-one with one eye has to say to a room that she is going to stop. **The day somebody asks is the day it stops being the coast and starts being a woman on a stone. And then it is one woman. And one woman goes blind in the eye she has got and then she is tired, and then she is a person in a chair in a building a mile and a flight of stairs above a flat, and the stone is bare for about a year while somebody works out what to do, and in that year a man on a bar road finds out. I would rather be a coast than a woman. That is not a noble thing to say. It is the true thing.** And the last thing: **do not write it that I stood on that stone for six years out of duty. Standing in somebody's habit is not duty. Duty is a thing you agree to. I never agreed to it, and if I had agreed to it I would have had to be asked, and nobody asked me.** And then **he is wrong out loud, in front of nine people who can hear it, which is the fourth time in a fortnight he has been wrong in front of strangers and the first time he has said so before he was shown:** he had wanted her to say yes because he had it that the hundred years of habit was the fragile part, **and the hundred years of habit is the strong part; it has outlasted every record anybody on this coast has ever made, including three glass ones, and it went on while a man of sixty-one sat on a bench two miles along this coast being right about photographs, and it is the only durable thing out here and it has never once been in a room.** And he is wrong about the other half too: **you are not standing in a habit. A habit is what people do without anybody asking. You are the person in it, and the habit is the hundred years of everybody else, and I have had those the wrong way round in my mouth since the sixth of a tide, and that is the difference between a woman doing a job and a coast doing a thing with a woman standing in it.** She answers: **that is the first thing anybody has said to me about it… you may have noticed that we have not agreed about a single thing in the last six minutes and we are still both going to be here tomorrow.** *Yes. I did notice.* **They walk round the far stones and say nothing else about it. The tide office gets its woman back at the sixth bell and she does four hours' work and gets it out inside an hour and nobody in that room asks her one question. There are two panes on the north wall of that room in oak frames and they have not been out of that building in nineteen years and were not out of it that afternoon, and nobody asked her to bring one down and he did not ask her to bring one down, because he has been wrong about that three times and was not going to try it a fourth time with a woman who had just told him the truth about herself in the open at the near end of a flat.** He is **forty-six days** on the coast, and the leg had been his own for about four hours once, on the fourth of the third tide, at a fire two miles along this coast, and had not been his own since.

## Chapter 0138 — The Driven Mark

**The fourth of the eighth tide, a bar day, mostly water and weather, and the record that is in the world and is useless.** **This chapter's opening and its whole wheel sequence were lifted from Chapter 124 in the first draft — the boat and the ebb and a hand flat on the boards under him, the sound of the wheel going, the man out of the shed, the one word, the instruction to the driver, and the line at four places — and the first repair pass claimed to have rewritten them and did not. All of it is rewritten in the third pass and what is left is three short echoes, all marked in Brann's own mouth. Read `state/batch-summary.md` under *Third pass* before quoting any of it.** The ebb out of that deep is about an hour and a quarter and hard and it is coming out carrying sand and putting the sand into the hole, and for the length of it the hole is not a hole. **Sorrel Gannock, thirty-six, the only one of the three brothers who will take a boat over that shallow on a bar day, eleven years in her father's place and for nothing, takes the flat boat off the hard at the fourth bell with the towrope in the bow and nothing else in her at all, and a man with a bad leg goes in it because there was nowhere else to be**, and the leg goes — from the hip down, all of it, in about four seconds — **and nobody in the boat says anything about it then or afterwards, and she does not look round, and she had not looked round the last two times either.** They cross, and then they go round the point, because that is the way the boat lies when the ebb is still running, and neither of them says that was the plan. **It held: about the eleventh time in twenty that the deep packed and stayed packed for the length of a crossing.** The training wall is on the seaward side of that deep — two hundred and sixty yards, nineteen years and eight months old, nine courses falling to two at the outer end — and it stands up out of that deep on a fourth, and a flat boat can be stood over the top of the whole of it and the courses walked and the seaward face looked at from the ninth course down to a foot and a half of brown water and sand. **Halse Tarrant is on the inner end with a bar, doing the only thing there is to do to a wall that is out of the water, and there is an iron stake in the seaward face about the thickness of a wrist, with a plate on it, gone the colour of a coin.** Ilyan does not lean over it: **say the number out loud. You can see it. I cannot, and I would rather you said it than that I looked at it and guessed.** **Hundred and thirty-nine.** And then the whole of what a driven mark is, in the trade's mouth, in about four minutes: **a chainage — a hundred and thirty-nine yards along something from something, a place and not a depth, and there is no depth anywhere on it. The guild drove those along the whole wall on the last two days of the job, one every five yards, off a chain, with a boy and a book, and the book went up the coast road and the book is in that building a mile up the hill with a lock on it and he has never seen it and was not in the gang that did it because he was on the inner courses putting the big stone in. So I can tell you what kind of number that is and I cannot tell you what it is a number of.** And: **it is a man saying the water was working here this morning and I have put iron in the ground so that the next man knows where here was. And that is worth having, and it is worth having for about three years, because the next man does come and look… and after that it is a piece of iron with a number on it. The water does not come back to the same place because a man was in a boat and put iron in the ground, and if it did then none of us would have to sound anything.** And the whole of it, on the ground: **it is a place and not a depth, and nineteen years old, and about two feet under the ninth course where it stands out of the water on a fourth and a sixth and a seventh, and nine foot under on a good day, and there is not one boat on this coast that will come out here on a good day and there is not one cart in the world that can reach the foot of that face on a bad one. So it cannot be produced — at the moment anybody needs it, which is every single time anybody needs it. And there is a second thing worse than that: a thing that is written down can be produced; a thing cut on a post can be counted, and it took a man of seventy-one two hours and eleven minutes the last time anybody did it; a thing fired in a fire can be brought out of a building in an oak frame if anybody in that building ever says yes, and nobody ever says yes. This is the only kind of record on this coast that cannot be produced at all, because it is not in a room and it is not on a bench and it is not in a cart. It is in the wall.** **Nobody put the two together**, and the reason is the plainest thing on the coast: a thing in a wall cannot be put side by side with a thing in a room, the man in the boat did not know a third of what was in that shed, the man in the shed had not been told there was a man in a boat, **and the number was not even a number that matched one — a hundred and thirty-nine of something is not the same kind of thing as a column on a pane, and there was nobody on the flat to say it ought to be, and a man who cannot say that ought to be cannot go and ask. It settled nothing, it was not evidence of anything, it was not a discovery.** Then **a cart's wheel comes off on the shingle above the flat and seventy people do not look up.** Ostre Brann, fifty-eight, is up the road with iron and has stopped to get a collar cut; he says *sprung* once, and gives the driver the instruction short — *up the hard, and take the disc off, and get that iron off the shingle, and I am not going to say the rest of it, because I said the rest of it on this flat a fortnight ago to a man who is not standing here* — and does the line at four places and puts his thumb in the gap and leaves it there until the carter has put his own thumb in it, **because you cannot argue with a thumb**, and finds the crush in a pair of felloe ends with shingle in it. And he calls the instruction back at the end of it — *twice now, in about a fortnight, both the same way, on that flat, in the worst of the week* — and says the three he always says in the same words, with *I said that to the last man who came in here* in front of them, and then the thing that is his and is **new**: **you can get a number off a wheel. Nobody has ever told anybody that and it is not any use to anybody. Everything in that nave above the axle line took the load and everything below it did not, so the wood above the axle line is a record of how deep the going was and the wood below it is a record of how deep it was not, and if you take a wheel to pieces and put a rule on it you can tell me within about four inches what the going was like on the last crossing, and I have done it, and I have never once told anybody, because it is a fact about the last crossing and about nothing else in the world.** And the rest of his trade's speech: a repair is not a date, a punch is Ness Tarn's and Ness has been dead nine years, a mark says who bought the iron and the iron does not know anything about water — **but the number I can give you is four inches, and it is about the ground, and it is about one crossing, and it is about the axle height of one cart. It is not about the water. Your water is a different thing entirely and it does not touch a wheel.** A woman of thirty-six stands at the mouth of the yard with the towrope on her shoulder the whole time and says nothing about the wall or the mark or the number, and **is not asked to solve anything and does not solve anything.** The water comes back into the deep at the ninth bell, and by the next morning there will be about nine feet of green water over a hundred and thirty-nine of something, in a wall, in the dark, for another six days.

## Chapter 0139 — A Day Given Away

**The fifth of the eighth tide, a good day, the flat takes six, and the batch's cost is priced and paid for by somebody who is not thanked.** **A lead line, a boat, a man who can sound, and a day.** Slee has three of them: the guild's own line in a box in a shed since the wall went down, a boat of his own that has not been out in about a year, and thirty-one years of sounding that bar to a foot inside of forty yards. He does not launch until the sixth bell because a boat in the water for two hours is a boat doing nothing. **Nobody has the money for it and the only thing missing is the day.** And the day is given away in about nine words in a lane four hundred yards from the crossing: **Cleve Gannock, thirty-one, who does not go on the water and deals in what the flat boat brings in, comes down with a pair of beasts yoked and a cart behind them on his way to a landing, and says he has got two hours before the turn, the beasts and the cart are by the day, he has paid for both whatever happens to him, the only thing his day buys is him standing at a landing being useful to a man at the Quay, and the man does not need him until about the ninth bell. And: you are not going to ask me. Right. Then I will tell you what I have got… take the day. And you are not to say anything about it, and if anybody in this yard starts on about it I will tell them it was the beasts that were late.** **Halse Tarrant did not ask him for it, and that is the whole of what happened and it is worth being exact about, because it is the shape of every single thing on this coast: the man who had the day and the man who needed the day were standing in a lane and neither of them asked the other for anything.** Cleve takes the cart to the landing and is two hours late and tells the man at the Quay it was the beasts, **and nobody said thank you — not the man with the bad leg, not the man in the boat, not the three people at the yard — and nobody thanks him then or afterwards.** And **Ilyan's part is what he cannot do:** he cannot refuse it, because he has no standing on this coast and a man who is not from this coast does not get to decide what a Gannock's day is worth to a Gannock, and a thing he is not owed is not a thing he is entitled to hand out; he cannot say the man in the boat should not spend a day somebody else lost on a question nobody asked him about; he cannot say the answer will be a number and that a number is the right instrument. He says none of it, and **being the person standing nearest is not a qualification and has never been a qualification and cost a woman of eighty-one nothing and a clerk of twenty-two nothing and a man of thirty-one the best part of a day four times.** What he does is take out the penny exercise book and write four lines: the date, that Cleve Gannock gave a day to Halse Tarrant, that it was his cart, his pair of beasts and his own day and he was two hours late at a landing because of it and told the man there it was the beasts, and **nobody asked him for it and nobody thanked him for it — it is mine to write down and it is not mine to decide.** The date on it, and that it was his, and no reason on the page, for the fifth page running, and he noticed himself not putting one and did not stop. The sounding goes over the seaward face from the inner end, every nine feet, for an hour and a half, and the result is: **the toe of the seaward face is gone along about eleven yards of it, in the middle, not at the ends, and gone to about two feet of depth. There is no bottom holding gravel under the bottom course of that wall for eleven yards. There is stone in courses and then there is the sea.** And then, in the trade's mouth, and it is worth more than a stake with a number on it and worth nothing at all tonight: **I have got that in a book in a shed with the date on it and the number in it, and I will swear to that book in a room in front of anybody who wants me to, for as long as I am alive, and that is the whole of what it is worth… and nobody on this coast will do anything about a number in a book. There is a table on a wall a mile up that hill that is the only instrument anybody will act on and it does not come out of that building, and there is a pane on a wall in a shed two miles along this coast that is about the same wall and is three years old and disagrees with the first one in two columns out of eleven, and the two columns are the ones that would settle this, and the man who made the second one cannot get at the first one and the first one does not come out of its room. So I have got a number and there are two photographs that do not agree, and one of them is nineteen years and eight months old and the other is three years old, and my number is from today, and today is the best day anybody has had on that wall in about fifteen years, and none of the three of them is going to travel to meet either of the others.** The post comes up the coast road in the afternoon and **Seth Garrick reads it out twice in the lane.** The guild's own four lines are correct and are a refusal: **that a record of a moving thing is a working instrument; that instruments do not travel, and a man who has one is the only man who can use it, and a body two hundred miles from a wall cannot act on a number taken from a boat; that the guild will sound that wall at its own cost and in its own season, and the season's money is not in the arch, and it will not be this season, and the guild does not send a copy of a working instrument to a person who has one; and that the guild is not in dispute that the wall is nineteen years and eight months old and that it is to be walked.** And Slee: **that is four sentences of the truest thing anybody has said to me in a year, and it is a refusal, and every part of it is right, and I want it written down that I have not got one single thing to say against any part of that, and I am not going to argue with a guild about the one thing they know best.** And: **the fourth line — they want to be walked. That is the first sentence anybody in that building has written to this coast in about two years that was not about a sum.** The second letter is short, sealed, from a city four hundred miles behind this one, from **a woman who is a magistrate and who was out-voted in a room and has not been out-voted since and is not going to be.** It asks two questions — what body stood behind the crossing at Wether Cross, and what instrument governed the counting of it — **notes that both have been answered in the return for the last quarter and that both answers are the same answer, and that the same answer has been given for eight years** — and it asks for one thing: that a person ought to be able to be told no by the harbourmaster's office in a place where the refusal is written down and can be shown to somebody else, **and that she does not care in the least what the answer was and only wanted it to be somewhere.** Corrie Tallow reads it once and gives it back: **we have not got that and we are not going to have it… she has asked for it in the only way anybody ever asks for anything that is not money, and she is right, and a body two hundred miles off asking this coast to have a box for refusals in is a body that has not noticed what this coast does with a person who says no to a question she was never asked. It has got a stone. Four feet of it, a hundred years old, and she answers about the water, and nobody may ask a second, and that is the only door anybody on this coast has ever had and it is not a door anybody can write a refusal on. And we are not building one, and I would say so to her office as well as to her and I would not put a name at the end of it.** And the letter goes back up the road and **nobody on this coast was any nicer or kinder about a magistrate than she had been about them, and nothing about it softened.** Then, in the same post, **the guild's quarter, and the line in it for a person to be paid two pounds a year out of what the crossing takes, to count the crossings in persons and not carts, has had no name on it since the fourth of the fourth tide, and the office read it and chose the one of its two options that writes nothing.** And then the finding, in four hundred words and no speech: **the vote of a council of nine sits in a book two hundred miles up this coast for a year and does nothing at all. It will not be reopened. Nobody in that building has asked the office here to fill it in and nobody here has written and asked. In about a month the next quarter will go up in a cart on the coast road and a clerk will read a line with a wage on it and no person on it, and he will leave it, and the next one after that he will leave it too, and by the turn of the year the paper with the vote in it will be in a drawer with last year's… and a man of thirty, who is the only person on this coast that line is for, has a lamp-oil shed at the head of the lane and counted that post in his head for four years and got it wrong by about nine hundred and said so out loud in front of thirty people, and he has not asked for it, and nobody is going to ask him, and nobody in that building two hundred miles off is ever going to know that there was a man on this coast the wage was voted for, because the line is blank and the quarter does not say.** And the last sentence of the chapter: **That is what a blank does. It does not stop a thing and it does not refuse one… and in about a year somebody in that office will go looking for the minute that voted it, and will find that the minute says a person is to be paid, and will not be able to find the person, and will put the minute back. Seth Garrick shut the door of the oil shed behind him and did not say anything, and nobody asked him, and nobody is going to.**

## Chapter 0140 — The Sixth

**The sixth of the eighth tide, a bar day, the flat takes nine, and the tidal breach opens in the last third of the chapter and the batch closes on a decision.** The westerly has been getting up two days; by the first bell the sea is over the crown of the bar at the north end and the whole two hundred yards of gravel is gone under, **and there is nobody on this coast who is surprised by that and nobody who is frightened of it.** Then the volume's spine, untouched: **Alma Gannock, eighty-one, four miles above the north end, on the stool with her back to the water and the chain round her knees, the boy of eight on a board with a slate and a stick of chalk putting something on it and getting it wrong, and she is not correcting him, and the one thing he had put in front of her in six weeks she had said no to in about four minutes and had not asked him for a reason, and she did not know what was under any of it, and nobody on that road was going to tell her — and he had been up the lane before the light and had not gone into the hut, and he was not going to do it on a sixth, and nobody on this coast is owed a page by him for that and nobody has asked for one.** Nine crossings; the chain rests an hour between the fifth and the seventh; about seventy people; a good sixth said twice. **The training wall, and the guild is right about it, said out loud by the man who keeps it.** At the fifth bell Slee walks the wall, and about a hundred and forty yards of it has four or five people on it. At the sixth bell he is about nine yards along it from the inner end, at a driven mark about two foot under the top of the ninth course, with his hand on it, **looking at the water in the deep, which is going down** — the ordinary end of the bar day: the ebb has done its hour and a quarter, the sand has packed, the bar has been a road, and the flood has come back in behind it and the sand is going out of the deep again. **Pell Cawley sees it first** — the boat's carpenter of fifty-two (corrected at the volume close; this line said fifty), thirty-one years at that hard, with a slip of his own a long way inside the gravel and a plane in his hand, standing on a hull — and says *Slee, come here and look at that*, and puts the plane down. **He is named, because he is somebody the reader has met and a person who does work in a chapter may not arrive from nowhere. The first draft gave him a lost slip in a year when a hole went the other way; the slip was Teel's, and Teel is dead, and that is gone.** **Nobody was in it. That is the first thing about it and it is the whole of why it was possible for six people to stand on a wall and look at it.** In the middle of the seaward face, for about eleven yards, the water was not going down the face; it was going out through it, and the surface of the deep was doing what water does when it is pulled through a hole about the size of a doorway, **and a man who works the water says what it means in the trade's mouth: that is the water going out through the middle of it.** And Slee: **it is not the wall failing. Do not anybody say that. The wall is doing what it was built to do and it has been doing it for nineteen years. That is the bed going out from under the bottom course in the middle of eleven yards of it, and I found that yesterday with a lead line in a boat, and I have got it in a book in a shed with the date on it, and there are three people on this coast who knew I went out yesterday and not one of them knew what I went out for.** **Those three are not the three who could act, and this line was rewritten by the first repair pass into four people who had all been told by him, which was a story-level change made as a wording fix, contradicted the batch record, and named four people no chapter identifies. It is reverted, and `state/batch-summary.md` under *Third pass* has the account.** And then the two things he wants said, in the open: **the harm is not the hole. The harm is the gravel. That wall is worth the two feet of gravel behind it and the two feet is the whole of that point, and the wall is not holding the gravel up, it is holding it sideways against the ebb, and where the bed has gone out the ebb comes through the wall now instead of past it, and the first thing it does on the far side is take gravel, and the second is go round the end, and the third is have a wider hole to work on next time, and none of that is a disaster. That is a shore going. It took two winters the last time and it will take less than that this time, because this time the guild is putting stone in a hole instead of taking a wall out, and there is a difference and it is the only good thing anybody can say about it. And the guild was right. I want that said too, and by me, and in the open, and not once in the next year by anybody else.** Then, at about the eighth bell, about four people come off the wall and across the flat, and **by the time they are on the shingle the story has four versions in it and none of them is about the gravel and all four of them are about the hole.** Jory Vance, twenty-two, four years on the counter, writes down what happened while it is happening, and makes the entry standing up at the chain:

> THE SEA STOOD UP OVER THE BAR AT THE NORTH END ON THE SIXTH DAY OF THE EIGHTH TIDE. AT ABOUT THE SEVENTH BELL THE WATER WENT OUT THROUGH THE SEAWARD FACE OF THE NORTH WALL FOR ABOUT ELEVEN YARDS. A MAN OF FIFTY-EIGHT WHO KEEPS THE WALL SAW IT FROM THE HARD. NO BOAT WENT OUT. NOTHING WAS DONE.

**And the batch's one System panel, the sixth thing on this coast that was a record of a thing somebody had entered nowhere in particular, reaching him on the wet shingle at about the ninth bell, rendering the entry and nothing else** — no mechanism, no join, no cause, and it ends on the two things nobody has decided. Then **the forward pull, and it is a link and not a monster. There are three people on this coast who could do something about the eleven yards of it and not one of them can see the other two, and nobody has asked any of them for anything.** Sorrel Gannock at the north end with her boat, who had been in that deep twice that day in a flat-bottomed boat with a man in it and had stood on that wall at the fifth bell and had not been there at the seventh, and who is **not asked and is not going to be told anything about the ninth bell because nobody in that yard is going to think of it.** Bettany Rook a mile and a flight of stairs up the hill, told in about a minute and a half, and asking the only question: *how many feet* — and being told that nobody had measured it in front of anybody — and then: **that is a number somebody is going to want, and there is not one instrument on this coast that will give it to him except a man in a boat… I have wanted to see that number for about a week and I am not going to send a boy up that lane for it, because that is what this coast does to people, and in about a week it would come back to him from a room and it would be the worst thing that has ever happened to him.** And Hollis Thrale two miles along the coast, at a bench, with an order under a batch book with a date and no figure, a pane three years old on his own wall, **and the eighth column of it saying that the gravel stood against the seaward face to the second course, which at that moment was the only figure anybody on this coast had in their head about that wall** — three years old against nineteen years and eight months, and the two of them cannot be put in one room, and the arch behind two feet of brick is cold. Then **the rendering, on nine hundred yards of wet shingle at the ninth bell, at the height and the distance it has been at since the third of the second month in a city four hundred miles behind him** — the boards, the table, the lamp with the wick down, the window with the wrong weather, four people at the table, one of them about forty-four with her back to him — **and the leg goes at the same moment, from the hip down, all of it, and does not come back inside two hundred yards and comes back the rest of the way worse, and he tells nobody then or afterwards, and about nine people on this coast have now seen something happen to him on a shingle or in a boat and not one of them has said a word.** And the decision, in the dark at the near end, four minutes of it, and it is the ending: **he is going to go and ask three people things. Not to tell them. Not to fetch them, and not to carry a sheet to any of them, and not to write one. He has no standing on this coast and has never had one and there is no way on four hundred miles of it to get one, and he has been produced four times on this coast, every one of them by a thing that was simply nearest to him, and he is not going to be produced a fifth.** The three are **a woman of thirty-six in a yard with a boat and a towrope and eleven years of a thing nobody has ever asked her the name of; a man of sixty-one who has been at a fire for forty-one years and has never once been asked; and a woman of fifty-one who said on a shingle four days ago that she would rather be a coast than a woman**, and he does not know what any of them will say, and **his one guess is that at least one of them will say no, and that the no will be right, and that it will be right in the way a thing is right when it is about the person saying it and not about the wall.** And he has no page for it and is not going to write one, because a page with a date on it and that it is his is a thing he has done five times in forty-nine days and every one of the five was a thing he wrote instead of going and standing in a yard. And **there is a fourth road he is not going to go up at all — four miles above the north end, a hut, a woman of eighty-one knitting, a boy of eight with a slate — and he is not going to knock, and that is because of the second of the seventh tide and a page in his coat, and it is the hardest thing in that paragraph and it is not one of the three, and nobody on this coast knows that he worked out where he was going and left that road off.** Close: the ninth crossing goes over, the boy of eleven goes over for the ninth time at a penny, about four people are carrying a story about a boil in a wall and about nine are carrying the same story without the boil in it, Corrie Tallow writes the ninth down and nothing else, and **a man of thirty-one stood at the near end in the dark with his weight on his good side and had not asked anybody for one thing in forty-nine days and was going to ask three of them.**

**THIRD PASS ON BOTH 164 AND 165, and the one that mattered.** Chapter 164's last three sentences told the reader, in a narrator's voice and in the first half of the batch, that eight days later he sat in a room and read out a sentence and that it was his own hand and the room did with it what rooms do, and then said *he did not know that yet*. **That is the batch's own placement rule broken on the page, and two earlier passes certified it clean because their scan looked for five vocabulary words and this sentence contains none of them. All three sentences are cut and 164 now ends on the thank you.** The sentence was also wrong: the deposition is in Kellock's hand, the whole of it, which is what the prompt requires, and 165's testimony about *the last three lines of the third box* and *the last two lines of the fourth box* contradicted the form's own printed boxes. **165:71 is rewritten: the whole sentence is in his hand and not the deponent's, and he wrote down *decided* because *decided* is the word on the memorandum in front of him, and he did not choose between *decided* and *refused* — there was one.** And 165:127's *four words are missing* is now **twenty-one words and one substitution**, checked in a script.
